title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: tight end Dalton Kincaid
summary: Back in the early aughts, when the Buffalo Bills were firmly mired in the midst of a long, miserable playoff drought that was still going to be worse before it was better, I used to read a lot of Bill Simmons’ work. Admitting that now feels far less cool then it was at that point—or […]
full_text: ROCHESTER, NEW YORK - JULY 29: Dalton Kincaid #86 of the Buffalo Bills makes a catch during training camp at St. John Fisher University on July 29, 2026 in Rochester, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images Back in the early aughts, when the Buffalo Bills were firmly mired in the midst of a long, miserable playoff drought that was still going to be worse before it was better, I used to read a lot of Bill Simmons’ work. Admitting that now feels far less cool then it was at that point—or at least as it seemed, anyway—but Simmons had a unique way of blending humor, pop culture, and sports together to create entertaining bits of writing. One of his bits that has always stuck with me centered on the “if Player X can stay healthy” trope that often surrounds the discussion of athletes. He began talking about injuries that way in earnest with a young Detroit Lions quarterback named Matthew Stafford, a player who hadn’t reached his potential due to a slew of early-career injuries. But the player it always stuck out most with to me was former Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Josh Freeman. Simmons used to call him “Josh Freeman If He Can Stay Healthy” as if it were his actual name. The joke, of course, wasn’t really at the expense of the player, but instead at the expense of fans, pundits, fantasy football players, and others with a rooting interest in the player performing to a level he had yet to unlock. Much of that discourse amounted to something like, “If Freeman can stay healthy, he can be a top producer in the league.” In today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days,” we discuss a tight end who can be a top producer in the NFL…if he can just stay healthy. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Dalton Kincaid Number: 86 Position: TE Height/Weight: 6’3” 246 lbs. Age: 26 (27 on 10/18/2026) Experience/Draft: 4; selected by Buffalo in the first round (No. 25 overall) of the 2023 NFL Draft College: Utah Acquired: First-round draft choice Financial situation (per Spotrac): Kincaid enters the fourth year of his rookie contract, and he carries a cap hit of $4,272,234 for the season. The Bills have already picked up the fifth-year option on his deal, so he’s under contract for 2027 with a cap hit of $8.162 million, as well. 2025 Recap: After missing time in 2024 thanks to a PCL tear, Kincaid started the 2025 season on a great pace. In Buffalo’s first five games, he totaled 20 catches for 287 yards and three touchdowns. Extrapolating that out to 17 games, it would have put him on pace for a 68/976/10 for the season. However, Kincaid missed Buffalo’s Week Six loss at the Atlanta Falcons due to an oblique strain, and he wasn’t the same upon his return. Kincaid had one big game—Buffalo’s 28-21 win over the Kansas City Chiefs in Week Nine where he caught six passes for 101 yards and a score—but that single contest made up nearly all of his remaining regular season production. A hamstring strain caused him to miss three games in November, as well. In Kincaid’s final seven games, he caught 19 passes for 284 yards and two scores. That comes out to a 46/690/5 pace over 17 games, which is remarkably close to what his regular-season numbers ended up being. In 12 games, Kincaid totaled 39 catches for 571 yards and 5 touchdowns on 49 targets. In the playoffs, he was exceptional, totaling nine catches for 11 yards and two scores on 11 targets. For his efforts, he was named to the Pro Bowl Games, replacing Chiefs’ tight end Travis Kelce when he dropped out. After the season, it was confirmed that Kincaid never had surgery to repair his PCL after the 2024 injury, instead dealing with the tear and rehabbing the injury through joint-strengthening physical therapy options. Positional outlook: Kincaid is one of five tight ends on Buffalo’s current roster. Shane Zylstra, Keleki Latu, Jackson Hawes, and Dawson Knox are the others. 2026 Offseason: Kincaid played in Buffalo’s preseason opener, but he was not targeted in the 29-14 victory. He held up well as an in-line blocker on at least one long play, as he took on outside linebacker Trevis Gipson and gave Josh Allen time to hit Khalil Shakir downfield on a second-quarter touchdown drive. He also was instrumental blocking downfield on a long gain for James Cook on a toss on that same drive. 2026 Season outlook: Kincaid definitely bulked up this offseason, as I admittedly had a hard time figuring out whether it was him or Dawson Knox on the field during Buffalo’s preseason opener. It used to be a little easier—just look for the bulkier fella and it was Knox—but with some added muscle, Kincaid looks much stronger entering his fourth season. He’s going to need that strength to translate to durability if he’s going to reach his full potential. When Kincaid is on the field, Buffalo’s offense is extremely hard to stop. He was the single best tight end target in the game last season in terms of quarterback rating, as Bills quarterbacks had a 149.2 rating when targeting Kincaid in the passing game. He also led all tight ends in yards per catch, notching 14.6 yards per reception. The issue for Kincaid has never been his ability; it has always been his availability. With San Francisco 49ers wideout Ricky Pearsall undergoing PCL surgery this offseason, a procedure that is likely to sideline him for 9-12 months, we see why Kincaid chose a more conservative treatment plan to mitigate his injury. Granted, we don’t know if the two issues are exactly the same, but they do impact the same ligament. Kincaid understandably wanted to play last season, and while he was certainly limited by his knee injury and the other muscle issues he encountered over the course of the season, he still showed himself to be an elite receiver when he was on the field. If he can become a better blocker—and early returns are certainly encouraging—then he can take the next step towards becoming the player Buffalo thought he would be when the chose him No. 25 overall in 2023. All of it starts with one thing, though, and it’s the Bill Simmons corrolary to Kincaid’s actual surname. With any luck, “Dalton Kincaid If He Can Stay Healthy” can become a thing of the past just like it did with Matthew Stafford. Less pain for Dalton Kincaid plus an alpha wideout in DJ Moore equals more pain for opposing defenses. That’s the kind of math equation I can get behind heading into the 2026 NFL season.
author: Sean Murphy

title: NFL free-agent wide receivers Buffalo Bills could sign before Week 1
summary: Ahead of the Buffalo Bills’ joint practice against the Cleveland Browns on August 20, injury reports and questionable statuses clouded the team’s wide receiver situation. Sal Capaccio of WGR550 shared a list of “(w)ide receivers I either don’t see at all or are here but NOT practicing: Khalil Shakir, Keon Coleman, Skyler Bell, Dante Pettis” […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - JANUARY 17: Ja'Quan McMillian #29 of the Denver Broncos fights for the ball with Brandin Cooks #18 of the Buffalo Bills during overtime of an AFC Divisional Playoff game at Empower Field At Mile High on January 17, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Ahead of the Buffalo Bills’ joint practice against the Cleveland Browns on August 20, injury reports and questionable statuses clouded the team’s wide receiver situation. Sal Capaccio of WGR550 shared a list of “ (w)ide receivers I either don’t see at all or are here but NOT practicing : Khalil Shakir, Keon Coleman, Skyler Bell, Dante Pettis” — a large chunk of the wide receivers room. Brady has indicated a lack of long-term concern for Coleman’s availability even though he’s dealing with a sprained toe/foot, (per ESPN ’s Cameron Wolfe) . We don’t yet know what’s bothering Shakir, and Bell was seen doing sideline work with a team trainer on Thursday in Cleveland. But if you stop and do some math, the injured list renders roughly 30% of the Bills’ 13-man receivers group unavailable for the joint session, and their status for Saturday’s Week 2 preseason game against the Cleveland Browns in question. NFL teams don’t have to disclose injuries at this stage of the proceedings, but during head coach Joe Brady’s press conference Tuesday afternoon we learned that Shakir was injured ahead of the joint practice in Cleveland. Capaccio then shared a look at wide receivers participating for Buffalo, which encouragingly included DJ Moore Joshua Palmer, and a handful of other mostly expected depth options. Once the joint practice began, the bulk of news and video highlights shared were plays to the Bills’ group of tight ends. A look at the Bills wideouts who are practicing, including DJ Moore. But we will see how much he does during offensive team work. pic.twitter.com/9VajXOBwHh — Sal Capaccio 🏈 (@SalSports) August 20, 2026 President of football operations/general manager Brandon Beane can’t sit idle hoping the injury bug exits stage left soon. He made a concerted effort to bring Moore in via trade, which so far has the looks of a potentially great move. However, Moore’s effectiveness will be limited if the surrounding starting cast around him is unavailable. Is it time for Beane to go back to the free-agent pool, or better to roll with the options in-house and available? That depends on the team’s confidence in those who are injured returning in time to be ready for Week 1, and the pool of rostered receivers. Apart from Moore and those currently injured, it’s a group that consists of Mac Dalena, Stephen Gosnell, Mecole Hardman Jr., Ja’Mori Maclin, Joshua Palmer, Trent Sherfield, Quentin Skinner, and Max Tomczak. Like any fan base, Bills Mafia can equally be talked into the idea of rolling with that roster set, and with signing someone in free agency. Perhaps Palmer takes on a featured role in tandem with Moore, and maybe Hardman helps fill in admirably as Shakir’s understudy. That said, Beane is probably making calls. There’s no way he wants to risk fielding a compromised group of wide receivers again. Right? With that in mind, let’s take a quick glance at the available free-agent wide receivers. We’ll dive in from least likely to the one(s) who make the most sense. As of publishing this article, Spotrac lists 17 free-agent wide receivers . It’s an interesting list, to say the least. Without looking, many may guess it’s a trip far down the NFL’s depth chart. That assumption may best be viewed as incorrect. Sure there are a fair number of players who might struggle to crack any team’s 53-man roster, but there are plenty of intriguing names. Let’s dig in and round up the most notable options. It’s a group that includes 11 players who are 30 years or older. Tyreek Hill We could simply point out his public image and the police reports as proof enough that Hill would be an awful signing by One Bills Drive. That said, his game is nearly incomparable and he brings speed that only cornerback Maxwell Hairston can match. The other big problem, however, is the injury that Hill sustained during a Week 4 game last season — which included significant knee dislocation and multiple ligament tears to his left knee that included a torn ACL. Even if Hill is fully recovered, it’s worth wondering how his prior explosion and speed will be impacted in what would be his age-32 10th NFL season. Oh, by the way, Spotrac lists his current market value at more than $15 million. No thanks. Zay Jones Zay Jones has dealt with some very real personal troubles off the field , and that’s reason enough to guess that Beane would keep his distance in any reunion with the former second round pick of the Bills’ 2017 draft class. It’s true that Beane didn’t draft Jones, but the point remains. What is true is that Beane did orchestrate the trade to send Jones to the then-Oakland Raiders in 2019. The bigger current issue is that Jones suffered an Achilles tear last November while playing for the Arizona Cardinals. Spotrac lists Jones’ market value at $1.3 million. Curtis Samuel (Insert Michael Scott screaming GIF.) It’s tough making a case for Curtis Samuel’s return to Buffalo. He was a priority free-agent signing by Beane, and an expensive one at that. Looking back, the details of the contract weren’t even the biggest concern with Samuel’s tenure. Instead, it was how often he showed up on the injury report, or unavailable as a healthy scratch or otherwise. By all accounts, Samuel was the consummate teammate, and he does have a rapport with quarterback Josh Allen. Samuel’s best contributions came during more than of the team’s playoff runs. None of that can be discounted. The Bills cannot afford, however, to sign a player with a known and recent injury history. Samuel’s current market value with Spotrac is around $1.8 million. DeAndre Hopkins Will he or won’t he. That’s what all of Bills Mafia wanted to know when rumors first swirled around DeAndre Hopkins being made available by the Arizona Cardinals ahead of the 2023 NFL season. During that year’s annual NFL owners meeting, Beane exacerbated the drama when responding that he’s always going to check in on every good player when asked about Hopkins. Later on, and as only he can do, Von Miller fueled speculation about Hopkins signing in an appearance with Kay Adams in April 2023. Then a few week after that nugget, DeAndre Hopkins was reportedly in the vicinity of Toronto, Ontario, CA, which only added fuel the signing fire while he was looking for a new team following his release from Arizona . As we now know, Hopkins never signed with Buffalo because they simply didn’t have the salary cap space to make something stick . Beane was, as it should be noted, very interested in adding Hopkins . Hopkins played with the heartstrings of the fan base, intentional or not. The latter isn’t reason enough to avoid signing Hopkins. He’s now 34 years old and has taken up coaching at the college level for Georgia Tech. One has to wonder what Hopkins would have to give if he was interested in playing this season, while also considering whether or not he could turn away from his new responsibilities as a coach. As a means of housekeeping here, Hopkins’ current market value per Spotrac is listed at just under $1.5 million this season. While the former three-time NFL First-Team All-Pro and two-time NFL Second-Team All-Pro would no doubt bring a massive level of excitement to Bills Mafia, his best seasons are in the rearview mirror. Gabe Davis It’s no secret that Gabe Davis’ best NFL seasons came while he was a member of the Bills. The man eventually known as “Big Game Gabe” was a fascinating WR2 to Stefon Diggs’ WR1 role. He was also exceedingly hot or frighteningly cold as a starting receiver catching passes from Josh Allen. When Buffalo had a litany of injuries to contend with during the 2025 season, they brought back Davis following his release from the Jacksonville…

title: Buffalo Bills fans grade signing of DL Greg Gaines
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bills fans and fans across the country. There’s been no shortage of discussion about the Buffalo Bills’ plans along the defensive line. After a nearly 10-year run in former head coach Sean McDermott’s […]
full_text: Aug 23, 2025; Tampa, Florida, USA; Tampa Bay Buccaneers defensive tackle Greg Gaines (96) tackles Buffalo Bills running back Frank Gore Jr. (20) during the first quarter at Raymond James Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Kim Klement Neitzel-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bills fans and fans across the country. There’s been no shortage of discussion about the Buffalo Bills’ plans along the defensive line. After a nearly 10-year run in former head coach Sean McDermott’s 4-3 base, nickel-heavy scheme, the Bills are changing things up beginning with the 2026 NFL season — which includes along the defensive line. There are a lot of familiar names set to reprise roles in Buffalo’s defensive trenches, but there’s plenty of new opportunity and some new blood to the room. However, after finding out the team will be without defensive tackle Phidarian Mathis thanks to a suspension for the first three games of the upcoming season, there was new urgency to add talent to the room. Since early in the offseason, when president of football operations/general manager Brandon Beane added defensive tackle Zane Durant in the 2026 NFL Draft, many have wondered what the plan was to stop the run. Durant profiles more akin to Ed Oliver, and the big man set to stuff the middle of the trenches as the team’s starter is Deone Walker. He’s shown a ton of talent, but he’s more in the mold of a freakish disruptor than someone who should be asked to clog rushing lanes. There had been enough buzz around Tommy Akingbesote to guess he had a path to the active roster as a depth player who profiled as a space-eating one-tech defensive tackle. But two things appeared evident: The Bills may not prioritize space eaters, and they also needed to further address the defensive tackle position. Recently, we heard rumblings of Buffalo’s front office reaching out to check on Tampa Bay Buccaneers defensive tackle Vita Vea . The now-former disgruntled DT was the talk of NFL circles after expressing discontent over his current contract. Vea’s staying in Tampa Bay, having agreed to a one-year, $30 million deal. It all seemed a bit rich for the Bills to meaningfully approach a trade, but Beane will always check on talented players. It would seem, however, that their chats with the Bucs’ front office proved fruitful enough for roster needs. Earlier this week, Buffalo signed free-agent defensive lineman Greg Gaines to a one-year contract . Gaines fits the mold of a traditional space eater at nose tackle. He’s played eight seasons in the NFL since being selected by the Los Angeles Rams during Round 4 of the 2019 NFL Draft. The Buccaneers connection here comes via Gaines’ three-year tenure with Tampa Bay, where he started nine of 49 games played from 2023 through 2025. The 6’1”, 312-pound Gaines isn’t pegged to be a starter with the Bills, instead taking on a reserve role. His game provides a much-needed specialized skill set as someone who will likely see action in obvious run situations. The addition of Gaines saw Buffalo release Akingbesote, but it remains to be seen how his presence affects the depth chart elsewhere. Now including Gaines, the Bills currently roster 10 defensive linemen/tackles in DeWayne Carter, Travis Clayton, Zane Durant, Landon Jackson, Zion Logue, Phidarian Mathis, Ed Oliver, T.J. Sanders, and Deone Walker. That list includes seven players selected by Beane and company in recent drafts (Carter, Clayton, Durant, Jackson, Oliver, Sanders, Walker). It would appear that despite their efforts, the Bills still felt a need to add talent from the outside . How do you rate the signing of Greg Gaines? title: T.J. Sanders is the ultimate X-factor on new Buffalo Bills defense
summary: The biggest X-factor on the Bills 2026 defense is hardly discussed by fans or media despite the fact he was an early-round pick a year ago. It’s T.J. Sanders, and I’m writing this piece to raise awareness of his importance to and potential within Buffalo’s defense under Jim Leonhard. Think about it — in back-to-back […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 20: T.J. Sanders #98 of the Buffalo Bills looks on prior to an NFL football game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on November 20, 2025 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The biggest X-factor on the Bills 2026 defense is hardly discussed by fans or media despite the fact he was an early-round pick a year ago. It’s T.J. Sanders, and I’m writing this piece to raise awareness of his importance to and potential within Buffalo’s defense under Jim Leonhard. Think about it — in back-to-back years the Bills made early second-round picks in the NFL Draft. People can’t help themselves with Keon Coleman. He’s the most hot-button topic on this Bills team. Entering his second season, I wouldn’t blame you if you forgot Sanders was on the roster. Of course, receivers will naturally garner more attention than defensive tackles, yet given Buffalo’s defensive struggles in the playoffs and Buffalo’s new defensive coordinator fresh on everyone’s mind, you’d think the former No. 41 overall selection would be generating some semblance of buzz before Week 1. And his quiet rookie season — that did feature a reasonably serious injury — may be the main cause of the general apathy regarding Sanders right now. He missed five games with a knee injury and appeared on just 30.2% of the Bills defensive snaps. And, yes, there were some ugly reps once he returned from said injury, particularly when anchoring against double teams against the run. But that’s not why the Bills drafted Sanders, to devour blockers and free up second-level teammates. Having thoroughly scouted him at South Carolina — and loving him as a prospect — I believe Brandon Beane traded up to snag Sanders at No. 41 to be the upfield penetrating understudy to Ed Oliver. Sure, there’ll be an uptick in read-then-react asks of trench players in Leonhard’s scheme. However, Oliver will still be the primary one-gap backfield disruptor. And he needs a rotational piece behind him. That’s where Sanders can be an asset on this new-look defense. Despite those ugly run-game reps, plays in which Sanders was easily displaced from the intended running lane, he did generate 13 pressures on 164 pass-rushing snaps in the regular season as a rookie, good for a respectable, bordering-on-encouraging 7.9% pressure rate. At defensive tackle in the NFL, once you’re pressure rate hits double digits, you’re a darn-good rusher. And the talent is undeniable with Sanders. Here’s a reminder of how athletic he tested before the 2025 draft: He’s an explosive dude at close to 300 pounds. In his final two seasons at South Carolina, Sanders tallied 16.5 tackles for loss and 8.5 sacks. The production was there in the SEC, no doubt. The general indifference surrounding him, I think, is due not just the lowlights but the long stretches of invisibility and reps with average-at-best effort during his debut NFL campaign. Now, of course, his knee injury must be considered on those fronts. But if a now fully healthy Sanders can play motivated and taps into all of his natural talent, he can become a seriously valuable member of Leonhard’s defensive front that features a plethora of new players. And the flashes were there against the Panthers in the preseason opener. At 3-technique, check the efficiency of Sanders’ counter move that resulted in a pressure of Kenny Pickett: pic.twitter.com/OTnxSfuboX — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) August 20, 2026 And even that wasn’t the quickest one-on-one win from Sanders in Buffalo’s exhibition opener. And, sure, he did miss a tackle in this game and didn’t record an official stat — yet these reps provided a glimpse of what he’s capable of in a pure pass-rushing role: pic.twitter.com/eIMaRWITwi — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) August 20, 2026 If, when Oliver needs a rest, Sanders can jump into that 3T spot and provide lightning-quick wins like those, it’ll be an enormous development for Leonhard’s defense. Defensive tackles with that first-step explosiveness and powerful hand work aren’t easy to come by in the NFL, and those attributes are exactly why he was a Top 50 selection a year ago. Here’s the abridged version of my pre-draft scouting report on Sanders: T.J. Sanders is a tall, athletic interior defensive lineman who excels with a mix of counter moves and relentless effort across all three downs. His rushes are often high, which limits his power, but he compensates with strong hand usage and savvy technique. He shows a good burst off the snap and demonstrates excellent hand placement, frequently utilizing the swipe and arm-over move. Despite his height and frame, Sanders possesses impressive lateral mobility and flexibility, allowing him to squeeze through gaps and perform well on stunts. His strength is a work in progress for NFL double-team situations. As a run defender, Sanders stands out for his relentless pursuit from the backside and reliable tackling. He was my No. 3 IDL with a late Round 2 – early Round 3 grade. Over the past close to a decade now, the Bills have done a masterful job developing raw-ish talents within their program. Josh Allen is, quite obviously, the shining example. Sanders is Buffalo’s latest project with immense upside. And if that upside is realized in Year 2, the Bills defensive front will be a lot better than everyone is expecting, which is why Sanders is the ultimate defensive X-factor on this team.

title: Buffalo Bills Superfans: Final paint, spaulders
summary: You got a tease of the paint on the armor before, and if you’re like I was, once you saw the first color coat go on, you were eager to see the final result. Anyway, I have the spaulders complete, including final paint. Right spaulder – Mafia means family Remember that each of the supplemental […]
full_text: You got a tease of the paint on the armor before, and if you’re like I was, once you saw the first color coat go on, you were eager to see the final result. Anyway, I have the spaulders complete, including final paint. Right spaulder – Mafia means family Remember that each of the supplemental armor pieces was meant to tell a bit of a story. This one is a bit convoluted. Way back in college an episode of The Simpsons came out. One of their Halloween specials. In the intro Mr. Burns puts out “the” decoration. A little red bat named “Batsy.” After circumstances lead to the demise of the Simpson family, Mr. Burns attributes it to Batsy, though he seemingly didn’t do anything. Or did he? The sequence ends with the crappy looking, little, red bat coming to life and flying away. For one reason or another, I decided that was as close to a deity as I needed to see. There are more steps to the story, but eventually Batsy became not just a “god” but a football god. My sister, my friend, and I who have attended games together (I mainly mooch off of them) for forever have now taken to pleading with Batsy when the Bills need something big and/or praising Batsy when the something big happens. The right spaulder is my tribute to Batsy and my immediate football family. There was a reason I chose a red bat to practice things several chapters ago. One of the reasons I didn’t cheap out on my painter’s tape was because I knew I was going to be doing some hand stenciling. How did I get this little guy on the spaulder? Frog tape! The first picture is me marking off how much space I have to work with. The second is my free-hand drawing of Batsy, and the third is after I cut it out with a razor knife. Now, you do still need to worry about the paint already on the item you’re putting your stencil on, so before anything else, I made the tape less tacky by placing it on my couch a few times. Anyway, Batsy needed a face and some lines in his wings… Now you might say that this looks kinda crappy, and you’d be right. Batsy by default looks a bit crappy and I wanted that to come through. It’s part of the joke. He’s crooked you might say. Yes he is! He’s taking flight! He’s supposed to be crooked. There’s a thumb print where you must have gotten paint on your hand. Ah, crap. To be fair, my hands got a lot of paint on them. How in the world did THAT happen? It’s common to get a little paint on your fingertip with a spray can but this is ridiculous, right? I needed something more than Batsy on this so I took matters into my own hands. My fingertips really. That entire border is made of fingerprints. I figured lean into the Halloween vibe a bit and thought this would be cool. This is before I made it wearable, so there’s one more embellishment you’ll see in a few moments. But first… Left spaulder – Buffalo Polish My actual name isn’t a closely guarded secret and my last name is preeeeetty Polish. My dad grew up Buffalo Polish and I grew up with a Dom Polski club as a lingering part of that tradition. I won’t lay claim to being “very Polish” all things considered, but it’s a part of me and my story. I already showed you the left spaulder and it’s haute-piece. The intended design element for this one was to borrow from medieval armor, much like the Japanese-armor inspired tasset. You might remember I painted the base color red, a striking contrast from the base blue of nearly everything else. In fact, it’s the only item that will feature ZERO blue paint. If you’re also of Buffalo Polish heritage you likely know the Polish flag is red and white. It’s got a bird on it. What type of bird? A white-tailed eagle! Time to get to work. Okay, you’re hard at work Skare. On what? I’m introducing a new plastic type. Type 7. What’s type 7? It depends apparently. This is from a Frank’s Red Hot jug (notice the 1/2 marking). It’s flexible, multiple layers apparently, and way different to work with than polypropylene. That still doesn’t explain what I’m making though. That center line I’ve drawn on is the area I WON’T be scoring with my X-Acto chisel. Yeah, but that still isn’t telling us what you’re making Skare. Feathers! Tail feathers. They’re not yet white-tailed eagle feathers though. A can of spray paint can fix that though. Here they are! My white-tailed eagle feathers on the medieval-ish left spaulder. A quick detour. You might have started noticing mechanical attachments that aren’t your typical rivets. When I was trying to make the armor wearable, I had made small washers from the polypropylene to attach elastic straps and well, the rivets ripped through the washers. So I bought Chicago screws, aka “screw rivets.” They did the same job, allowed me to dial in the torque, and they look awesome. Back on track, I said I wanted Polish inspiration. Many regions of the world developed scale armor. Overlapping pieces of metal attached to something underneath it. Polish scale armor, called “karacena” is notable for using rivets rather than the more common wire or thread. Karacena was also less protective than plate armor available at the time and was often worn by nobility (since they’d hit the front lines less) or as ceremonial armor. Mine, lorewise mind you, is over beskar plate so being decorative is surely not an issue. Like I did with the tassets, I wanted to make sure the pair looked good together, so here’s a look at the side-by-side. Two final thoughts. Like the Zubaz print tasset, I wanted the Batsy piece not to look so flat, so I added a strip of extra “beskar” to look reinforced. Finally, I did a bunch of test runs on the feather design and was not happy with any of them. Even the final design. I was quite confident I had over-committed to the left spaulder design and was going to wind up with a piece of armor I hated. Then it hit me. A single feather might look unsatisfactory, but perhaps layered they’d start to look more like what I wanted. I think I proved myself wrong. I don’t hate that armor piece at all. In fact, I love how it came out. Praise Batsy!

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: cornerback Christian Benford
summary: The Buffalo Bills have some question marks in the defensive secondary. While they have plenty of talented players, there’s a fear that both of their likely top corners are somewhat prone to injury. Perhaps it’s unfair to designate a player who’s only been in the NFL for a season as injury prone, but for Buffalo’s […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 02: Christian Benford #47 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates after making a sack during the second quarter in the game against the Kansas City Chiefs at Highmark Stadium on November 02, 2025 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills have some question marks in the defensive secondary. While they have plenty of talented players, there’s a fear that both of their likely top corners are somewhat prone to injury. Perhaps it’s unfair to designate a player who’s only been in the NFL for a season as injury prone, but for Buffalo’s other top corner, he’s yet to play a full season in his four years in the league. That penchant for injury has led to some unfortunate substitutions at inopportune times over the years—hello, Dane Jackson—and was also a reason why general manager Brandon Beane added a high draft pick to Buffalo’s stable of cornerbacks in April. You can never have too many corners, and while the Bills have some good ones, their availability on Sundays is never guaranteed. In today’s installment of our “91 players in 91 days” series, we discuss Buffalo’s CB1, a player with immense talent who overcame a poor start last season to play lights-out football when it mattered most. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Christian Benford Number: 47 Position: CB Height/Weight: 6’1” 205 lbs. Age: 25 (26 on 9/21/2026) Experience/Draft: 5; selected by Buffalo in the sixth round (No. 185 overall) of the 2022 NFL Draft College: Villanova Acquired: Sixth-round draft choice Financial situation (per Spotrac): Benford signed a four-year, $69 million contract prior to the start of last season. Of that total, the deal includes $$37.636 million in guarantees. For the 2026 season, Benford carries a cap hit of $7.396 million if he’s on the 53-man roster. Buffalo would carry a dead cap charge of $35.036 million if they were to release him. 2025 Recap: Benford’s 2025 season did not start well, as he was routinely beaten in Buffalo’s season-opening victory over the Baltimore Ravens. Pro Football Reference had him allowing six completions and two touchdowns on eight passes where he was the closest defender in coverage. In fact, throughout the season’s first five games, Benford was not good. He allowed opposing quarterbacks to go 19-for-27 (70.4%) for 177 yards and four touchdowns; he had neither an interception nor a pass breakup in those first five games. After that stretch, though, he locked in and played the way we all know he’s capable. He did not allow another touchdown in the regular season, finally breaking in the Wild Card Round against the Jacksonville Jaguars. Including the postseason, Benford allowed opposing quarterbacks to complete just 16-of-36 passes (44.4%) for 207 yards with one touchdown. Benford had two interceptions and six pass breakups over those final 11 games that he played. One of those interceptions came against the Pittsburgh Steelers, and he also recovered a fumble and returned it for a touchdown on the first play of the second half of that contest, swinging the momentum in a game Buffalo ultimately won running away. The following week, he made Buffalo’s play of the year, making a leaping interception of Joe Burrow and returning it 63 yards for a touchdown against the Cincinnati Bengals. On the regular season, Benford played in 14 games, totaling 43 tackles, two interceptions, four pass breakups, two sacks, two fumble recoveries, and four tackles for loss. In the postseason, he totaled five tackles and two pass breaups in two games. He missed Buffalo’s November loss at the Miami Dolphins due to a groin injury, and he also missed the Bills’ December loss to the Philadelphia Eagles thanks to a toe injury. He sat the regular-season finale against the New York Jets, as well. Positional outlook: Benford is one of nine players listed at cornerback on the current roster. Dee Alford, Maxwell Hairston, Davison Igbinosun, Toriano Pride Jr., D.J. Miller, Anthony Kendall, Jordan Dunbar, and Kani Walker are the others. Te’Cory Couch is listed at defensive back, but he plays corner. Jordan Hancock is also listed at defensive back, but he is a safety/cornerback hybrid. 2026 Offseason: Benford is fully healthy and embracing a role as a vocal leader now that he is the veteran in the room. 2026 Season outlook: Benford’s talent is not a question, as he has proven himself to be among the league’s best corners when he’s playing at his highest level. The question is whether Benford can line up every single week, as he has yet to do that in his pro career. Buffalo’s cornerback depth has been tested this summer, as Maxwell Hairston has dealt with an injury that has caused him to miss plenty of practice time. Kani Walker, who has been a pleasant surprise this summer, is also hurt, so Buffalo has added some players to eat preseason snaps in order to preserve others. Benford has primarily played in a zone-heavy scheme throughout his career, as that’s what Buffalo ran under head coach Sean McDermott and it’s also what he did at Villanova. Coming out in the 2022 NFL Draft, Lance Zierlein wrote that Benford could play zone or man, but that he might need “scheme protection” in man coverage. With new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard looking to play more man and match coverage, can Benford continue to thrive? I think the answer is yes. Even though the McDermott scheme was known to be zone-heavy, there were signs over the last two seasons that more man coverage was coming. The Bills continued to load up on plus-athletes, and they did play a heavier percentage of man coverage over the last two seasons than they did early in McDermott’s tenure. Even though they still played zone 70% of the time, Buffalo was thirteenth in man coverage rate, running it nearly 24% of the time. That percentage is likely to increase this season. Benford has the ball skills and the physicality to match the league’s best wideouts regardless of scheme. Yes, he might need some help over the top against burners, but rare is the cornerback who doesn’t need that kind of assistance. As long as he can stay on the field, Benford is sure to help the new-look Bills defense charge into a new era this season.
author: Sean Murphy

title: Panthers vs Jaguars: Defensive Preview
summary: The Carolina Panthers will enter their 3rd preseason game this Friday, meeting the Jacksonville Jaguars in their stadium after a week of team practices to build up some tension. This might be the most we see of the Panthers starters on both sides of the football, and the Panthers defense is still working out some […]
full_text: CANTON, OHIO - AUGUST 06: Zakee Wheatley #38 of the Carolina Panthers looks on during the first quarter of the 2026 Pro Football Hall of Fame Game against the Arizona Cardinals at Tom Benson Hall Of Fame Stadium on August 06, 2026 in Canton, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images The Carolina Panthers will enter their 3rd preseason game this Friday, meeting the Jacksonville Jaguars in their stadium after a week of team practices to build up some tension. This might be the most we see of the Panthers starters on both sides of the football, and the Panthers defense is still working out some depth questions there. They should get a fair amount of the Jaguars first team offense, so this one should be a nice measuring stick for how this defense is going to look in the regular season. Let’s dive in. Pass rush continue to stand up Jaelan Phillips looked every bit as productive as you’d expect for the highest paid free agent signing on the market from the off-season, logging a sack on Josh Allen and generally being the disruptive force for the limited snaps he got. It was nice to see Phillips flash, and the real question is going to be depth at that position. Cam Gill, Trevis Gipson, and DT Aaron Hall accounted for 2 more sacks between them against the Bills, and I was particularly impressed with all 3 of them. Gill was a pass rush specialist with the Louisville Kings with 10 sacks and being named UFL Defensive Player of the Year earlier this season, so continuing that momentum could earn him a real shot at being part of the pass rush rotation for the Panthers in 2026, following a couple of stints with the Panthers since 2024. Jackson Kuwatch a name to observe for ILB competition? The Panthers are allowing Trevin Wallace and Claudin Cherelus to fight it out for the open inside linebacker position opposite Devin Lloyd during the preseason, and neither seems to have pulled a head of the other so far. Kuwatch, meanwhile, has been all over the field when given snaps, and while that is nice, he definitely needs some seasoning as far as functional strength and getting pushed around by opposing blockers. Still, the 2026 7th round pick is showing enough that he may very well make the roster at a position of relative weakness. Obviously, every rookie’s challenge is usually catching up to the speed of the NFL from college. His snaps may be ones to really monitor during this game. Lathan Ransom and Zakee Wheatley continue to impress at safety Tweets have been abound on social media about Ransom and Wheatley making plays throughout the off-season, and both could very much be vying for more first team snaps come the regular season. The Panthers have devoted mostly late round picks and UDFAs to the safety position behind Tre’Von Moehrig, and Nick Scott, while serving as the veteran presence, could see his snaps eaten into if these two continue on an upward trajectory. Watch the back end of the defense during this game, folks, it could be fun. What do you want to see from the Panthers defense on Friday?

We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - SEPTEMBER 20: Jon Beason #52 of the Carolina Panthers is introduced before a game against the New York Giants during play at Bank of America Stadium on September 20, 2012 in Charlotte, North Carolina. The Giants won 36-7. (Photo by Grant Halverson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #24. Jon Beason The Carolina Panthers have been spoiled with off-ball linebacker talent throughout their existence. Jon Beason is just one of the many dominant backers the team has had, and boy was he dominant at his peak. The Panthers selected Beason 25th overall in the 2007 NFL Draft out of the University of Miami. (Spoiler alert: he won’t be the only first round linebacker from the U on this list). Starting all 16 games his rookie year, Beason put the league on notice, using his athleticism and playmaking ability to rack up 140 tackles, eight passes defended, a pick, and a fumble recovered. That performance landed him second in the Defensive Rookie of the Year voting, losing out to fellow linebacker Patrick Willis. Beason’s first four seasons in the NFL were about as good as anyone could have hoped for: he started every game in that span, earned three Pro Bowl selections, and First Team All-Pro selection, and a Second Team All-Pro selection. He didn’t have less than 121 tackles in a single season in that span, and had over 100 SOLO tackles three of the four years. The Panthers rewarded his dominance with a five year, $50 million contract extension in 2011, making him the highest paid middle linebacker in NFL history at the time. Unfortunately, 2011 is also when the wheels started falling off physically. The previously Iron Man type of player tore his Achilles in Week 1 of the 2011 season, causing him to miss the rest of the year. Beason worked hard to return to the field in 2012, but a combination of cartilage damage in his knee and a torn labrum in his shoulder combined to limit him to just four games that year before landing on IR again. The timing on that second injury was not ideal for Beason as he was replaced in the middle by a Hall of Famer. Beason returned in 2013, but didn’t really fit with the defense anymore. After just three games, the Panthers traded Beason to the New York Giants for a conditional 7th round pick. Beason finished that year relatively healthy, but succumbed to multiple ailments that ended his 2014 and 2015 seasons (e.g. fractured foot, knee sprain, concussion, lingering ankle injuries). Beason ultimately retired following the 2015 season. Had catastrophic injuries (and competing with Luke Kuechly) not derailed Beason’s career, he was well on track to finish in the Top Ten on this list. As it stands, the highest of Beason’s highs were tough to beat. Those first four seasons had Panthers fans excited on a level not seen since Dan Morgan’s early dominance at the position. By all accounts Beason was great in the locker room and did not make any waves when moved outside, at least not until after he retired. Despite the ride coming to a sudden and disappointing end, Jon Beason’s on-field dominance when healthy earned him this spot in our countdown.

title: Left Tackle Struggles, Red Zone Success, and More at Bears-Bengals Joint Practice
summary: The Chicago Bears held their first joint practice of training camp with the Cincinnati Bengals earlier today, and there’s a lot to get to! Ben Johnson is a big fan of joint practices, and he outlined why with reporters before practice here. “They’re controlled reps here,” Johnson said via the team site. “It’s exciting because […]
full_text: Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson, left, and Cincinnati Bengals head coach Zac Taylor, right, share a conversation during a joint training camp at the Kettering Health Practice Fields, Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026, in downtown Cincinnati. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Chicago Bears held their first joint practice of training camp with the Cincinnati Bengals earlier today, and there’s a lot to get to! Ben Johnson is a big fan of joint practices, and he outlined why with reporters before practice here . “They’re controlled reps here,” Johnson said via the team site. “It’s exciting because we know there’s ground rules to stay away from the quarterback. We’re thudding up and things of that nature, and so we can just make sure it’s safe, it’s controlled, and yet the competition goes up, the intensity goes up.” After poor play in the first preseason game by Jedrick Wills Jr. and Kiran Amegadjie led Ben Johnson to shift both players over to right tackle, Theo Benedet was featured as competition for Braxton Jones at left tackle. Ben Johnson noted that Benedet is an asset in the run game but that he is “a little behind” in pass pro. That weakness was on display in practice today. It reportedly did not go well for Benedet in today’s live practice period, and Braxton is the frontrunner to win the LT1 job. Adam Jahns of CHGO observed that it was a “bad finish to practice” where “Caleb Williams was sacked twice by Myles Murphy. Second one for a safety.” Jahns noted that Murphy beat Theo Benedet on both sacks. Beat reporters took note of a poor ending to the practice for the Chicago Bears offense against the Bengals defense. Nicholas Moreano of REKAP reports that there were no passes completed by the Bears first-team offense in one of the 11-on-11 sessions. Patrick Finley of the Chicago Sun-Times noted that the Bears offense was dominated in the last drill of practice. The last play of the practice was a Caleb Williams interception by Jalen Davis over the middle. Adam Jahns reported that Dexter Lawrence was a “serious problem” for the Bears offense. Dan Hoard, the radio voice of the Cincinnati Bengals, observed that “Dexter Lawrence was a force, consistently collapsing the pocket and tipping a ball to himself for an INT.” Here is Hoard’s tweet with video of the interception: Five observations from today's joint practice with the Bears: 1. After only playing three snaps against the Lions, Dexter Lawrence was a force, consistently collapsing the pocket and tipping a ball to himself tor an INT. “Yeah, it felt good going against another team for more… pic.twitter.com/cUopCXbffG — Dan Hoard (@Dan_Hoard) August 20, 2026 Patrick Finley gave some attention to the battle between Jaylon Johnson and Ja’Marr Chase at practice today. Reportedly, Ja’Marr Chase was “fuming” over the lack of targets in practice due to Johnson’s blanket coverage. Finley reported that Chase complimented Johnson after practice. Chase remarked, “Real good corner. Pretty aggressive on a couple plays.” Dillon Thieneman had the play of the day for the defense when he picked off Joe Burrow, according to Adam Hoge. “Burrow forced it into tight coverage, and it went off Gesicki’s hands. Thieneman was right behind to snag the ball.” Hoard acknowledged that the Bears offense had success early in his observations of the practice. Adam Jahns said the Bears offense scored three touchdowns during the red zone drill. Larry Mayer called it the “highlight of the day,” noting that the first of those touchdowns came when tight end Colston Loveland high-pointed a ball with safety Jordan Battle “draped all over him.” Jahns believes that Kaden Davis is going to make the team. Mayer reports that Davis made a diving TD catch just inside the front right pylon of the end zone during the red zone drill. Rookie Zavion Thomas got in on the touchdown action, catching a pass in the right corner of the endzone from Case Keenum. Summing up the practice, Kelley Peter of blogintheback.com noted the best news that comes out of practice – despite an early scare when Kromah had to leave practice briefly – there were no serious injuries suffered during the practice by either team. A few other nuggets from the day. Bears head coach Ben Johnson chatted with Bengals head coach Zac Taylor before practice: The #Bengals and Bears are on the field and gearing up for today’s joint practice. Observations to come… #WhoDey pic.twitter.com/eDJ8FSDg83 — Dan Hoard (@Dan_Hoard) August 20, 2026 The Bears saw the return to practice of both Tyrique Stevenson and Terell Smith, according to Alyssa Barbieri of USA Today’s Bears Wire in her 9 takeaways from the joint practice: Geoff Hobson, the senior writer for Bengals.com, reports that Bengals linebacker Demetrius Knight Jr remembers the Bears’ last-minute comeback win this past November as a “dagger in the heart” in his quick hits . That’s how a game between two top offenses should be. Dexter Lawrence and the defense has had their fair share of wins. The Bears D has had wins too. But yes, two top offenses would’ve put up a lot of points. Tee Higgins has been the best player on offense for Cincy https://t.co/ghue7ifCjJ — James Rapien (@JamesRapien) August 20, 2026 Unbelievable play by Caleb Williams in redzone 11v11. Dexter Lawrence beat the double team. Had a hand in his face. Williams threw a laser that whizzed over Jordan Battle’s head to Colston Loveland in the endzone. An impossible completion and he made it. — Jeremy Rauch (@FOX19Jeremy) August 20, 2026 The #Bears defensive line put a lot of pressure on Burrow in 11 on 11. In a game might have been 2 or 3 sacks. #Bengals @FOX19 — Gabi Sorrentino (@GSorrentinoTV) August 20, 2026 Bears WR Ray-Ray McCloud throws a punch at a Bengals DB. McCloud was surrounded by Bengals DBs with no backup, he chose to take a swing anyway. Skirmish ensued. Bengals piled onto McCloud. It eventually calmed down. — Sean Hammond (@sean_hammond) August 20, 2026 And a few videos from the day. The definition of threading the needle 🪡 pic.twitter.com/9z2GHatSMj — Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) August 20, 2026 Bears receiver Kalif Raymond pic.twitter.com/TsKJaLPlwV — Larry Mayer (@LarryMayer) August 20, 2026 . @colstonlovelan1 is a problem 😮‍💨 pic.twitter.com/4mB9CCYVs0 — Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) August 20, 2026 Good day for the Johnsons 🤝 pic.twitter.com/hGa1EpBIIw — Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) August 20, 2026 Bengals-Bears joint practice recap: – Caleb Williams starts fast – Mixed bag from Bengals offense – Bengals defense closes strong – Joe Burrow applies Super Bowl pressure @WLWT | @char_cliff pic.twitter.com/kjnaLhUs9d — Jaron May (@jaron_may) August 20, 2026 Joe Burrow on #Bengals ’ Practice Scuffle with #Bears : “Sh*t happens.” Yes, Joe was involved. Here’s what happened: Joe Burrow got into it with a Bears defender after the defender didn’t let go of his jersey. Burrow pushed him. It led to a small scuffle that was quickly broken up.… pic.twitter.com/l1efxngcgU — James Rapien (@JamesRapien) August 20, 2026 Recapping Bears v Bengals joint practice with @JeffJoniak and Tom Thayer. full_text: Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams (18) throws a pass during a joint training camp at the Kettering Health Practice Fields, Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026, in downtown Cincinnati. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Chicago Bears and Cincinnati Bengals met up today for a joint practice at Kettering Health Practice Fields, and it sounded like each number-one offense had some explosive moments. We’ll have the practice recap later this afternoon, but in the meantime, feel free to discuss that and anything else in this Open Thread (Rated WCG-MA). Quarterback Caleb Williams met the media after practice, and he hit on a variety of topics, but he was asked how he would assess his individual performance. “I think I’ve done a good job taking the coaching, taking the hard coaching, good coaching, whatever the case may be. I think that’s how I’m judging it. Just being able to go out there and execute, and you know there’s going to be mistakes and things like that, but it’s being able to go back into the film room, learn from them, and then when it comes to game day, when it comes to all of that, we’re executing on a high clip.” Middle linebacker T.J. Edwards also met the media after practice, and one of the questions he was asked was to explain what Kyler Gordon means to the defense. “I think Kyler’s one of the best nickels in the game. I really do. I think when he’s on the field, he changes the game. His ability to blitz, his ability to stop the run, his ability to cover when needed, play the pass. He does it all, right? And I know he’s working his butt off, and I talk to him every single day, man. He’s just itching to get out there. So you know, we’ll be ready when he gets back, and we know who he is when he’s on the field.” Here’s the full Caleb Williams press conference. And here’s the full presser from T.J. Edwards.

title: Don’t expect to see any Bengals starters play again this preseason
summary: Cincinnati Bengals head coach Zac Taylor spoke with the media Thursday morning before the joint practice with the Chicago Bears. There, Taylor revealed the Bengals would not play any starters on Saturday, regardless of how they perform during the joint practice sessions. And because teams don’t typically play starters in the third preseason game, this […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - AUGUST 13: Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow (9) passes the ball during the game between the Detroit Lions and the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Cincinnati, OH. (Photo by Ian Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Cincinnati Bengals head coach Zac Taylor spoke with the media Thursday morning before the joint practice with the Chicago Bears. There, Taylor revealed the Bengals would not play any starters on Saturday, regardless of how they perform during the joint practice sessions. And because teams don’t typically play starters in the third preseason game, this all but assures we won’t see Joe Burrow and other starters play again until the September 13 regular-season opener vs. the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. When the Bengals scheduled joint practices, it seemed like sitting the starters would always be the way to go. I cannot disagree with the decision to play it safe, especially coming off of some spirited practice sessions right before. This should give plenty of opportunities to the guys behind the starters that are trying to carve out a spot in the rotation, along with a spot on the 53-man roster, or the practice squad on Saturday night. We should see plenty of action from the young rookies, including in that. Cashius Howell isn’t technically a starter, but is expected to be a key rotational player for the Bengals. Tacario Davis was held out for precautionary measures last week, but is expected to make his debut against the Bears on Saturday. Colbie Young could continue to push Andrei Iosivas for playing time; Landon Robinson and Jack Endries could solidify themselves on the 53-man roster. While there is plenty to still look forward to, this all but guarantees we won’t see the starters in preseason action for the rest of the way. The last preseason game has never been one that the starters play, and I can’t imagine that changing this year, even though there are only three preseason games now. The Bengals’ preseason finale is August 28 on the road vs. the Philadelphia Eagles. The next time we will see the Bengals starters will be against the Bucs on September 13, as they kick off the regular season at home. Do you agree with Taylor’s decision to keep the starters out of the next two preseason games? Sound off in the comments section!

title: Joe Burrow is done saying ‘Next Year’; Bengals QB is manifesting a Super Bowl this season
summary: Joe Burrow isn’t interested in talking about the Cincinnati Bengals’ Super Bowl window as something that might still be open down the road. He wants it to happen now. And he’s making sure everyone around the Bengals hears him say it. Following Cincinnati’s joint practice with the Chicago Bears on Thursday, Burrow spoke to reporters […]
full_text: Jan 15, 2023; Cincinnati, Ohio, USA; Cincinnati Bengals wide receiver Ja'Marr Chase (1) and quarterback Joe Burrow (9) warm up before an NFL wild-card playoff football game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Cincinnati Bengals during a wild card game at Paycor Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Kareem Elgazzar-USA TODAY Sports Joe Burrow isn’t interested in talking about the Cincinnati Bengals’ Super Bowl window as something that might still be open down the road. He wants it to happen now. And he’s making sure everyone around the Bengals hears him say it. Following Cincinnati’s joint practice with the Chicago Bears on Thursday, Burrow spoke to reporters about the team’s championship aspirations and made it clear that he isn’t shy about putting those expectations into the universe. “I’m trying to put it out into the world. I’m trying to manifest it,” Burrow said when asked about the Bengals’ pursuit of a Super Bowl. But the quote that followed may have been even more revealing. “I’m trying to show our guys the urgency that I have and that I want us to have as an organization, to go and make it happen.” That’s the mentality Burrow wants inside the Bengals’ locker room heading into 2026. Not someday. Not next year. Now. Joe Burrow speaks to the media. https://t.co/Rnv6ka1at8 — Cincinnati Bengals (@Bengals) August 20, 2026 Burrow is tired of pushing it down the road There’s a reason Burrow’s comments feel different from the standard preseason quarterback optimism. He’s not simply saying the Bengals have enough talent to compete. He’s talking about urgency. Cincinnati has been in the AFC Championship Game twice during Burrow’s career and reached Super Bowl LVI following the 2021 season. But the Bengals haven’t been able to get back to the Super Bowl since that breakthrough run. Burrow is clearly tired of talking about what Cincinnati could accomplish. “You can keep pushing it down the road, or you can talk about it now and say this is the year,” Burrow said. Then came perhaps the most striking part of his comments: “I’m tired of saying next year, next year, next year.” That statement says plenty about where Burrow’s head is entering his seventh NFL season. The Bengals have spent the offseason making significant additions to a roster that already possessed one of the league’s most talented offenses. The biggest splash came on the defensive side, where Cincinnati acquired superstar defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence and added veteran defensive tackle Jonathan Allen. Now Burrow wants the results to match the investment. ‘This is it’ Burrow’s next comment was even more direct. “This is it,” he said. “Your life is too short to keep pushing things down the road, and I’m trying to instill some urgency and some intensity in everybody to go and be great every day and try to go make it happen.” It’s a fascinating evolution for a quarterback who has never exactly been shy about his expectations. Burrow has consistently talked about winning championships since arriving in Cincinnati. But there’s a difference between believing you’re capable of winning a championship and openly telling the entire organization that this is the year to make it happen. Burrow appears to be trying to create that distinction. And he isn’t limiting the message to himself. Burrow wants the entire building to feel the urgency Burrow also acknowledged that the Bengals’ defense has taken a major step forward with the offseason additions. “We have to step up and make something happen this year,” Burrow said, specifically discussing the defense reaching a championship-level standard alongside the offense. But the quarterback also challenged his own side of the football. “We have to be more consistent on offense,” Burrow said. It would be easy for Burrow to point toward the additions on defense and say the Bengals have finally given the offense the help it needs. Instead, he’s putting pressure on everyone, including himself. The offense has an incredibly high standard, and Burrow acknowledged that the standard exists because of what the unit has already accomplished—and what it believes it is capable of doing. “Our standard is so high, but it’s so high because of what we’ve done and what we can do,” he said. That’s the message of this year’s Bengals team. The standard isn’t being lowered because of what happened last season—it’s being raised because of what Cincinnati believes this roster can become. The timing of Burrow’s message matters There is also something significant about when Burrow chose to make this declaration. The Bengals had just completed their first joint practice of the preseason against another NFL team—a Bears team that won the NFC North and nearly beat the Rams in the Divisional Round of the playoffs just last year. The intensity was noticeably higher than a normal training camp practice, and Cincinnati’s offense reportedly had a productive day against Chicago. Meanwhile, Dexter Lawrence came away with one of the biggest defensive plays, intercepting a tipped pass. Cashius Howell and Myles Murphy also generated would-be sacks. In other words, Burrow isn’t speaking about an imaginary roster. He’s seeing the pieces come together in front of him. The Bengals have a veteran quarterback who is healthy. They have Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins. They have one of the league’s most explosive offensive cores. They added Lawrence and Allen to a defense that desperately needed more star power. And now Burrow is seeing something he wants to turn into a championship. That’s why he’s talking about manifesting it. Manifestation only gets you so far Of course, nobody wins a Super Bowl because they talked about it enough. Burrow knows that better than anyone. The Bengals still have to stay healthy. They have to become more consistent offensively. The defense has to prove that its offseason transformation translates to Sundays. The offensive line has to hold up. Cincinnati has to navigate the AFC, which remains brutally competitive. And ultimately, all of the talk has to become football. But that’s precisely why Burrow’s comments are interesting. He’s not presenting manifestation as a substitute for work. He’s using it as a way to establish the mindset he wants from the organization. Talk about it. Believe it. Expect it. Then work like it. The Bengals’ franchise quarterback isn’t asking his teammates to wait for their opportunity. He’s telling them the opportunity is already here. And he’s tired of saying “next year.” For Joe Burrow, 2026 is the year.

title: Ja’Marr Chase reacts to Bengals’ scuffle with Bears over contact with Joe Burrow
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals had a joint practice with the Chicago Bears this afternoon, and almost everything went off without a hitch. Of course, a few scuffles popped up during these things, but one in particular involved Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow. Reporters on the scene said that Dayo Odeyingbo held onto Burrow’s jersey and refused to […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - DECEMBER 15: Joe Burrow #9 of the Cincinnati Bengals smiles with Ja'Marr Chase #1 prior to an NFL football game against the Tennessee Titans at Nissan Stadium on December 15, 2024 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals had a joint practice with the Chicago Bears this afternoon, and almost everything went off without a hitch. Of course, a few scuffles popped up during these things, but one in particular involved Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow. Reporters on the scene said that Dayo Odeyingbo held onto Burrow’s jersey and refused to let go, causing a brief scuffle that thankfully did not escalate further. Dayo Odeyingbo got hands on Joe Burrow and didn’t let go causing a minor ruckus around the Bengal quarterback. Burrow intercepted on the play on a pass intended for Mike Gesicki. Burrow with six completions on six targets for Tee Higgins, including a red zone touchdown, one… — Mike Petraglia (@Trags) August 20, 2026 You imagine there will be fights over contact. Especially the guys constantly colliding in the trenches, but for a defender to make contact with an opposing team’s quarterback in this situation is fairly uncalled for. I won’t go as far as to say it was dirty as much as it is just a dumb thing to do. It is not surprising to hear this led to a fight. When recounting what happened, Burrow and his top wide receiver Ja’Marr Chase had two very different reactions. “We better f***ing protect Joe,” Chase said of the incident. Joe Burrow said “sh*t happens,” when asked about the contact and dust up during today’s joint practice with the Bears. Ja’Marr Chase on the other hand? Not a fan of QB1 being the target of late contact: “We better f***ing protect Joe.” pic.twitter.com/1974KWm9LU — Chatterbox Sports (@CBoxSports) August 20, 2026 It is safe to say we are all Chase in this instance. At best, he was trying to simulate blocking on an interception despite the very obvious rule of not touching the quarterback. At worst, he was trying to look like a tough guy, which is somehow even dumber than the first thing. No team that has a quarterback of Burrow’s caliber wants any defender doing something dumb like this in a joint practice. Nothing good comes from it, but thankfully, nothing bad came from this incident.

title: 7 Bengals players who could be surprise cuts
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals have a problem NFL teams generally like: They have too many players who look like they belong. That was evident in the Bengals’ 16-14 preseason victory over the Detroit Lions, when several players fighting for roster spots made legitimate cases to stick around. Dohnte Meyers, Colbie Young, Jack Endries and others helped […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals running back Tahj Brooks (25) celebrates the Bengals win over the Jacksonville Jaguars at Paycor Stadium on Sunday, September 14, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Cincinnati Bengals have a problem NFL teams generally like: They have too many players who look like they belong. That was evident in the Bengals’ 16-14 preseason victory over the Detroit Lions, when several players fighting for roster spots made legitimate cases to stick around. Dohnte Meyers, Colbie Young, Jack Endries and others helped make the roster decisions more difficult, while the revamped defensive line showed just how much the talent level has improved across the board. That also means some players who looked relatively safe earlier in the offseason may not be as secure as they once appeared. Cincinnati still has two preseason games remaining before the Aug. 30 roster deadline, so plenty can change. But based on the current depth chart, offseason additions, and what we saw against Detroit, here are seven players who could become surprise cuts. Tahj Brooks Brooks might be the most obvious name on this list, but cutting him would still qualify as a surprise given the investment Cincinnati has made in him, and the lack of clarity behind the top two backs on the roster. The Bengals selected Brooks in the 2025 NFL Draft, and he entered the summer with a legitimate opportunity to establish himself as Chase Brown’s primary backup. Instead, his development has been fairly quiet. Cincinnati’s official roster outlook entering training camp had Brooks as one of five returning running backs, with undrafted rookies Kentrel Bullock and Jamal Haynes joining the room. The Bengals also identified Brooks as someone who could contribute as a punt protector. But after the first preseason game, it’s still difficult to point to much that Brooks has done to separate himself. That’s particularly concerning because the Bengals have several other backs competing for relatively few spots. Samaje Perine is a safe and still-productive veteran presence behind Brown, but the remaining jobs could come down to special teams, versatility, and who simply makes more plays over the final two preseason games. Brooks doesn’t necessarily need to have a bad preseason to lose this battle. He just needs someone else to make the Bengals believe they can get similar production elsewhere. T.J. Slaton Jr. This one would be considerably more surprising. Slaton started all 17 games for Cincinnati in 2025 and produced career highs of three sacks and 52 tackles. Entering this offseason, he looked like an important part of the Bengals’ defensive line. Then Cincinnati went out and dramatically upgraded the position. Jonathan Allen and Dexter Lawrence now headline the interior, while B.J. Hill (freshly returned from the PUP List), Kris Jenkins Jr. and rookie Landon Robinson have all given the Bengals legitimate options. McKinnley Jackson, Jordan Jefferson and Howard Cross III are also competing for snaps. And yet, here’s the strange part: Slaton actually had a good preseason opener. According to Bengals.com, Slaton was the team’s highest-graded defender against Detroit, despite playing only six snaps, including a tipped pass. So why include him? Because roster decisions aren’t made in a vacuum. Slaton’s performance probably makes him safer than he was entering the preseason, but the Bengals could ultimately decide that they don’t need six or seven defensive tackles on the initial 53-man roster. It’s not only a numbers game in terms of position, but salary cap implications as well, after the team made such heavy investments. It would be a genuine shock if Slaton were released after what he showed last season and against Detroit. Many (including this writer) would be against it, as depth up front is crucial in the NFL—and, particularly in the AFC North. But that’s exactly what makes him a surprise-cut candidate. Mitchell Tinsley What a difference six months make. Tinsley was already a player worth watching before the preseason opener. Now, things have gotten considerably more interesting. The Bengals gave Tinsley a one-year extension through the 2026 season after he spent the previous two seasons on Cincinnati’s roster, and he entered camp competing for a larger role behind Ja’Marr Chase, Tee Higgins and Andrei Iosivas. The problem is that Dohnte Meyers has arrived. The former CFL standout was one of the biggest stories of Cincinnati’s preseason opener, producing four touches for 42 yards and adding an 11-yard punt return. Bengals.com noted that Meyers appears to be leading the competition toward the back of the receiver room. That creates a fascinating numbers game. If Chase, Higgins, Iosivas and Charlie Jones are considered safe, there may only be two remaining spots. Tinsley is competing with Meyers and Colbie Young for those jobs. Young had two catches for 28 yards against Detroit and continues to show the type of size and physicality that could make him difficult to leave off the roster. And because he was a fourth-round draft pick this year, he’s already likely to make the 53-man roster, leaving just one spot between Tinsley and Meyers to earn. Suddenly, Tinsley’s previous experience and 2025 regular season highlight-reel catches may not be enough. He could absolutely make the roster. But if Meyers continues to produce and Young keeps flashing, Tinsley could become the odd man out. Charlie Jones This might be the most controversial name on the list. Jones has already established himself as one of the Bengals’ most valuable special-teams players, and his three career return touchdowns aren’t insignificant. Bengals.com specifically noted that those touchdowns continue to loom large in the roster equation. But Jones didn’t exactly help his case as a receiver against Detroit. He finished the game without a catch (was close to making a long one from Joe Flacco) and had one fair catch. Meanwhile, Meyers made plays on offense. Ke’Shawn Williams had a 48-yard kickoff return, a seven-yard punt return, and an eight-yard end-around. Colbie Young continued to make plays downfield. And that’s before considering Tinsley and the other receivers competing for limited spots. This is why Jones is an interesting potential surprise cut rather than an obvious bubble player. Jones’ special-teams value could ultimately save him. But if the Bengals decide they can replace his return duties while gaining more offensive versatility from another receiver, Jones could suddenly become vulnerable. He has earned his place in the final roster conversation. That doesn’t necessarily mean he’s guaranteed a place on the 53-man roster. Tanner Hudson Hudson might be the quietest surprise cut candidate of the bunch. He’s been around. He’s been productive. And he’s earned the trust of the coaching staff. But Cincinnati’s tight end room has changed. Mike Gesicki and Drew Sample offer established veteran roles. Erick All Jr. is finally returning to the field after his ACL injury, and the Bengals like his potential. Rookie Jack Endries just had three catches and a touchdown against Detroit and has impressed the coaching staff with his blocking progress. That’s a lot of competition. The Bengals kept five tight ends in the latest post-preseason projection from Cincy Jungle, but that’s hardly guaranteed. Keeping five means sacrificing a roster spot somewhere else, and Cincinnati has plenty of other positions where players are making legitimate cases. Hudson’s veteran experience could ultimately win the day. But if the Bengals decide they can get enough receiving production from Gesicki and All while keeping Sample and Endries for their blocking and developmental value, Hudson could become expendable. And that would qualify as a pretty significant surprise considering how much he has contributed to Cincinnati in recent seasons. McKinnley Jackson Here’s the defensive name that might make some Bengals fans nervous. Jackson was a third-round…
