title: Lions try out 2 veteran guards, including former Detroit 1st-round pick
summary: According to the daily NFL transaction wire, the Detroit Lions tried out two veteran guards on Thursday: Will Hernandez and Laken Tomlinson. As of Thursday evening, neither player had signed with Detroit, but it is certainly notable that the team is looking at the guard position. It is likely no coincidence that the Lions are […]
full_text: Jul 23, 2025; Houston, TX, USA; Houston Texans guard Laken Tomlinson (75) during training camp at Houston Methodist Training Center. Mandatory Credit: Troy Taormina-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect According to the daily NFL transaction wire, the Detroit Lions tried out two veteran guards on Thursday: Will Hernandez and Laken Tomlinson. As of Thursday evening, neither player had signed with Detroit, but it is certainly notable that the team is looking at the guard position. It is likely no coincidence that the Lions are looking at guards on the same day that coach Dan Campbell announced that Ben Bartch—a veteran depth guard—is in concussion protocol and essentially out of the starting left guard competition for now. “It’s hard to say that (he can win the starting job),” Campbell said. “It’s real hard to say that over four (remaining) practices or whatever. Doesn’t mean it can’t, but that window is shrinking right now. So, the most important thing is for him to get to where he feels right again and to where he can go. He’s healthy, he feels good and he can start practicing and then we’ll see. But no, I mean, I think that window is closing quickly.” Beyond Bartch, the Lions don’t have much starting experience behind their projected starters in Christian Mahogany and Tate Ratledge. Mason Miller and Melvin Priestly have never appeared in an NFL game, while Michael Niese has never made a start in his 26 game appearances. Hernandez, on the other hand, is a former second-round pick with 98 starts under his belt. He also has extensive experience under new Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing, as he played with the Cardinals for the past four years, staring 42 games over that span. However, Hernandez has dealt with injuries the past two seasons. He suffered a torn ACL in 2024, and a hip and knee injury shortened his 2025 season to just seven games. Tomlinson, who was the Lions’ first-round pick all the way back in 2015, would also bring a boat-load of experience. He’s started 162 games, including seven starts with the Texans last year, but he was released by the team in December. At 34 years old, his best days are behind him, but he would still bring a veteran presence to a very young room. We’ll see if the Lions make a signing in the next few days.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Lions training camp observations: Jack Campbell dominates, OL struggles
summary: Observations are going to be relatively short from Thursday’s practice, because the Detroit Lions opted to finish this week of training camp by winding things down. Coach Dan Campbell thought the team had just finished a series of strong practices, including a long scrimmage on Sunday, so it was appropriate to pull back on Day […]
full_text: Aug 3, 2026; Allen Park, MI, USA; Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell (46) takes part in a linebacker drill during Detroit Lions training camp. Mandatory Credit: Paul Barnick-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Observations are going to be relatively short from Thursday’s practice, because the Detroit Lions opted to finish this week of training camp by winding things down. Coach Dan Campbell thought the team had just finished a series of strong practices, including a long scrimmage on Sunday, so it was appropriate to pull back on Day 16. “We’ve gotten a great week,” Campbell said. “The last three days that we’ve had padded practices, the day before that night practice, that day, the night practice, and then yesterday were outstanding. Just the work that we have got, the situations we have got, the amount of reps. They’re hard reps. They’re under stress. They get tired, have to work with each other. You have got to stay on top of your fundamentals. I just thought it was great work. So, I’m pleased—(we’ve) backed way off today.” This was the entirety of practice: walkthroughs, individual drills, four short drives, and one special teams set of drills. In total, it was less than a full hour, and it was an unpadded practice. Still, I’ll provide my brief thoughts. Jack Campbell completely disrupts the offense The first team offense and defense ran a total of nine plays during Thursday’s practice, and I had Jack Campbell making an impactful play on four of them. On his first impactful play, he blew through a blocking attempt from Jahmyr Gibbs for a sack—although they let the play run, and the pressure caused an inaccurate throw. The second came a play later, when Campbell dropped into a deep zone and got his fingertips on a floater downfield for Jameson Williams, knocking the ball out of harm’s way on third-and-long. On the next series, Campbell flashed his run-stopping abilities. He pursued Gibbs down the line for a gain of just 3 yards on first down. Then on a fresh set of downs, he shot the gap between Tate Ratledge and Juice Scruggs for a 3-yard tackle for loss. That’s Campbell literally contributing on all three phases of defense in just nine plays: pass rush, coverage, and run defense. Offensive line struggling with chemistry It appears the Lions have settled on a starting offensive line. While it’s not official, Detroit has been running with this line for the last few practices: LT: Penei Sewell LG: Christian Mahogany C: Juice Scruggs RG: Tate Ratledge RT: Blake Miller Campbell expressed some optimism before practice that things were starting to come together a bit, particularly with Scruggs. “I did think yesterday was better,” Campbell said of Scruggs. “And particularly in a lot of that situational work to where they got to be on the same page with some stuff. And the rest of the o-line, I think those only help.” Unfortunately, Thursday seemed like a step back for the unit. There were several missed assignments blocking in just those nine snaps for the first-team offense, and a false start—which have been a frustratingly common occurrence this camp. D.J. Reed was untouched on a corner blitz, resulting in a sack, although there were a few tight ends to that side that were likely responsible for a missed assignment. On Campbell’s 3-yard loss, Ratledge was late in getting off his double team to account for the blitzing linebacker. And on the final red-zone play for the offense, a screen pass to Jahmyr Gibbs never got off the ground because no one (Scruggs or Ratledge) put a hand on Alim McNeill, who forced Jared Goff to throw it at Gibbs’ feet. On the second team, there was another false start and zero success on two running plays. While it’s not yet time to panic, it’s clear Detroit’s offensive line needs all the reps they can get between now and the start of Week 1. Miscellaneous items Josh Dobbs played one entire team rep during practice: a 20-yard touchdown to a wide-open Jackson Meeks. This was the play when Ennis Rakestraw was injured . Because the Lions were doing these drills like a drive, the third-teamers were done after that one rep. Despite the low rep count in practice, Dobbs will apparently start in Saturday’s preseason game . Sione Vaki had the biggest play of practice, hauling in a swing pass into the blitzing side of the defense. He turned upfield with blockers and gained about 20 yards. Jake Bates was perfect on the day, making field goals from 41 and 42 yards, and he made his sole extra point. The starting kick returners were Tom Kennedy and Jacob Saylors. Ahmed Hassanein blew by Anthony Lucas on a punt pursuit drill, but Greg Dortch, the returner, juked him out of his shoes.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Detroit Lions injury update: Ennis Rakestraw leaves practice early
summary: The Detroit Lions were supposed to have a quick, non-padded practice as they prepare for preseason Game 2. Unfortunately, the game of football can be cruel even during the less intense practices. Lions cornerback Ennis Rakestraw suffered an injury toward the end of practice and did not return. Let’s get more into that injury and […]
full_text: Detroit Lions cornerback Ennis Rakestraw Jr. stretches after practice during OTAs at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Friday, May 30, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions were supposed to have a quick, non-padded practice as they prepare for preseason Game 2. Unfortunately, the game of football can be cruel even during the less intense practices. Lions cornerback Ennis Rakestraw suffered an injury toward the end of practice and did not return. Let’s get more into that injury and all the other Lions injury news from Day 16 of training camp. Injured during practice CB Ennis Rakestraw (lower leg) During a team drill, Rakestraw attempted to drop into coverage, but when changing directions, he immediately collapsed to the field. After a few moments on the ground, he picked himself up and gingerly walked to the sidelines, where he went back down to the ground and was evaluated for several minutes. Eventually, he walked slowly off the field under his own power. It’s another tough break for Rakestraw, but we don’t yet know the severity of it, so hopefully we get good news. The Lions are off until the preseason game on Saturday, so we won’t get an update from the team until Campbell’s post-game press conference. Working with trainer LB Jimmy Rolder (leg) Rolder continued to work with a trainer for most of Thursday’s practice, a good sign of his progress. However, before practice, Campbell cast doubt that the rookie linebacker would return by the end of training camp next week . “Probably unlikely,” Campbell said of his chances to practice this training camp. “He’s doing well. He is progressing well, but I think it’ll be hard-pressed to see him next week.” Still, it seems like he’s trending toward potentially avoiding injured reserve, unless the Lions want the roster spot initially. Not practicing: RB Isiah Pacheco (knee) OT Giovanni Manu (NFI) C Cade Mays (wrist) G Ben Bartch (concussion) TE Sam LaPorta (hip) EDGE Payton Turner (back) DT Mekhi Wingo (concussion?) LB Damone Clark (undisclosed) S Thomas Harper (undisclosed) S Kerby Joseph (PUP, knee) S Brian Branch (PUP, Achilles) Ben Bartch remains sidelined, and Campbell revealed he’s currently in concussion protocol. Unfortunately for Bartch, he has now missed almost all of training camp, and Campbell admitted that it’s unlikely he can challenge to win the starting left guard job before the start of the regular season. “That window is shrinking right now,” Campbell said. So, the most important thing is for him to get to where he feels right again and to where he can go. He’s healthy, he feels good, and he can start practicing, and then we’ll see. But no, I mean, I think that window is closing quickly.” We covered LaPorta’s injury more thoroughly here , but the main takeaway here is that a new hip injury is not considered serious. Still, it’s possible he could miss the start of the season. “I don’t know,” Campbell said. “I feel like we’ll be okay, but I don’t know.” Finally, there was no sign of Thomas Harper at practice on Thursday. No word yet from the Lions on his status.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Detroit Lions to start QB Josh Dobbs; select starters vs. Commanders
summary: The Detroit Lions will take on the Washington Commanders in their second game of the 2026 preseason on Saturday afternoon. With several position battles still unsettled and a lot of younger players added to the roster this offseason, the Lions are hoping to get some answers in this game. “You need to feel like things […]
full_text: Detroit Lions quarterback Josh Dobbs (6) practices with guard Mason Miller (63) during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Monday, August 10, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions will take on the Washington Commanders in their second game of the 2026 preseason on Saturday afternoon. With several position battles still unsettled and a lot of younger players added to the roster this offseason, the Lions are hoping to get some answers in this game. “You need to feel like things are cleaned up; you’re not making the same mistakes twice,” coach Dan Campbell said of his goals for the game. “Particularly these young guys. ‘Okay, what did you learn from the last game?’ That’s really what you’re looking for: their growth when the lights are on. In practice, you can see growth, guys getting better. You were under the lights on Thursday night at Cincinnati, but now where’s it at”? Previously, Campbell has stated that the plan is to play the Lions starters in this upcoming game , but with five practices in the last six days, including multiple padded and a full-team scrimmage , could those plans change? “I’m not quite there yet. I don’t see (Jared) Goff playing,” Campbell noted. With Goff not playing, the Lions will turn to rookie Luke Altmyer and recently signed Josh Dobbs to play quarterback in this game. Altmyer has been taking the majority of reps in practice, started the Lions’ first preseason game, and played all but one series with the reserves during the scrimmage, but Campbell insists that the battle for the reserve quarterback role is still very much a true competition. “Dobbs is a bright guy. He’s played in this league. But also (we’re) making sure we got him up to speed,” Campbell stated. “Also, Luke’s (Altmyer) a young player, but he’s promising, so we were trying to soak him with reps. But we plan to get a look at Dobbs and let him go.” Not only do the Lions plan to get a longer look at Dobbs in this game, but Campbell also revealed that he’ll get the start. “We’ll start Dobbs, but they’ll (Dobbs and Altmyer) play equal amounts. That’s the plan,” Campbell said. The Lions are also hoping to get some clarity with their starting offensive line. Christian Mahogany and Ben Bartch are battling for the starting left guard role, but Bartch has been bitten by the injury bug in camp, limiting his opportunities. He only recently got back on the field and is now in concussion protocol , which may put an end to this competition with only four practices remaining in camp. “That window is shrinking right now,” Campbell said of Bartch. “The most important thing is for him to get to where he feels right again and to where he can go.” With starting center Cade Mays out with a wrist injury, the Lions have been looking to solidify their starting center. Juice Scruggs is the favorite for the temporary starting role (Seth McLaughlin is his primary competition), but he also only recently returned from a soft tissue injury, and the Lions have been careful to limit his reps in practices, but plan to start him against the Commanders. “He just got back, and now he’s exclusively at center, and we’ve gotta kick some of the rust off. We’ve got to get that off and let those guys (the offensive line) work together,” Campbell said. “I did think yesterday (practice) was better, particularly in situational work where (the offensive line) needs to be on the same page. Juice has played center in real games; he’s suited for it, and it’s really about getting him up to speed with Goff and some of our calls, and being on the same page with the guards. Time on task, and we’ve got time to get there. I see Juice playing in this game with that OL, so this will be good work for them”.
author: Erik Schlitt

title: Sam LaPorta injury update: Lions unsure if TE will miss start to season
summary: On Thursday, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell offered an injury update on a couple of players, but none were more important than his star tight end, Sam LaPorta. Per Campbell, LaPorta suffered a hip injury in practice recently, and the team is holding him out to let it calm down. “He got hit in the […]
full_text: Detroit Lions tight end Sam Laporta (87), center, and tight end Tyler Conklin (72) practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Monday August 17, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co On Thursday, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell offered an injury update on a couple of players, but none were more important than his star tight end, Sam LaPorta. Per Campbell, LaPorta suffered a hip injury in practice recently, and the team is holding him out to let it calm down. “He got hit in the hip, and it just flared up a little bit. It’s aggravated, but we feel good long-term about him,” Campbell said. “We’re just—we’ll rest him for a little bit right here, letting it calm down.” But when asked if the injury could hold him out at the start of the regular season, Campbell was non-committal. “I don’t know,” Campbell said. “I feel like we’ll be okay, but I don’t know.” LaPorta spent the majority of his offseason recovering from back surgery after that injury caused him to miss the final eight games of the 2025 season. The Lions certainly felt his absence then, so it’ll be a tough blow if he misses any time to start the season. “He’s a stud,” quarterback Jared Goff said earlier this training camp. “He had a good play down the field today on third down, and he’s a stud. He’s the same guy every day and continues to get better like they all do and got to find ways to give him the ball.” Elsewhere, Campbell noted that reserve guard Ben Bartch is in concussion protocol, and his ability to contend for the starting left guard job is now in jeopardy. “That window is shrinking right now,” Campbell said. “The most important thing is for him to get to where he feels right again and to where he can go.” Finally, Campbell gave an update on rookie linebacker Jimmy Rolder. While the former Michigan Wolverine expressed optimism that he could practice as soon as next week from his hamstring injury , Campbell wasn’t quite as hopeful. “Probably unlikely,” Campbell said of his chances to practice this training camp. “He’s doing well. He is progressing well, but I think it’ll be hard-pressed to see him next week.” He did say, however, that he sees Rolder being available early in the season.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Lions LB Jack Campbell’s favorite play for 2025 is insane and awesome
summary: On Wednesday night, the Detroit Lions quietly dropped a short video entitled “Jack Campbell: Under the Lights.” It’s a profile on the Lions’ starting MIKE linebacker, and gives some insight into the position and what makes him so good at it. But what was profoundly amazing in the video is when Campbell talks about his […]
full_text: Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell (46) is called roughing the passer for a tackle against Minnesota Vikings quarterback J.J. McCarthy (9) during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, November 2, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co On Wednesday night, the Detroit Lions quietly dropped a short video entitled “Jack Campbell: Under the Lights.” It’s a profile on the Lions’ starting MIKE linebacker, and gives some insight into the position and what makes him so good at it. But what was profoundly amazing in the video is when Campbell talks about his favorite play from 2025. You’d think it would possibly be the fourth down stop he made on Lamar Jackson in their Monday night win in Baltimore , or maybe his impressive two-point conversion stop on Commanders running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt . Certainly it’s got to be one of his 176 tackles, 5.0 sacks, four passes defended, or three forced fumbles. Nope. Jack Campbell’s favorite play from last year won’t be found on his 2025 highlight reel. You won’t find it on any highlight reel of any game. In fact, you won’t even see the play recorded on a box score. Jack Campbell’s favorite play was when the Lions allowed a kick return touchdown against the Minnesota Vikings… but it was disallowed because of a penalty on the Vikes. Yes, you read that right. His favorite play was a touchdown scored by the Vikings that thankfully didn’t count. I’ll let Campbell explain: “I just remember the ball broke. There was a penalty flag, but I didn’t see it, and he ran it all the way back for a touchdown,” Campbell recalls. “I remember I gave my full effort to get him, and I didn’t get him. But, like, I just remember I just gave everything I got. Then, to have to go back out there on defense. Just something that I try to pride myself on. No matter what happens—even if the ball is on the other side of the field—I’m going to try and make the play.” That’s right. Jack Campbell’s favorite play of his from 2025 is a tackle he didn’t make on a play that didn’t count. If that’s not everything that Jack Campbell is about in a nutshell, I don’t know what is. He’s a full-out effort player who will do everything he can on every single down to help his team win. “This game really means a lot to him,” defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard said in the video. “He takes a lot of pride in it and he walks in (with) that purpose. I’m very fortunate to have a player like that as a guy that’s leading the defense.” And he’s pretty damn good, too.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Madden 27 simulation: Predicting the Detroit Lions’ 2026 season
summary: The 2025 Detroit Lions season was one to forget. Coming off a historic 2024 season, which was cannibalized by injuries and a disappointing NFC Divisional Round exit to the Washington Commanders, expectations were high. Unfortunately, the injuries returned, and the team couldn’t overcome them, finishing 9-8 and missing the playoffs entirely. For 2026, the expectations […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - AUGUST 13: A detailed view a Detroit Lions helmet in the game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2025 Detroit Lions season was one to forget. Coming off a historic 2024 season, which was cannibalized by injuries and a disappointing NFC Divisional Round exit to the Washington Commanders, expectations were high. Unfortunately, the injuries returned, and the team couldn’t overcome them, finishing 9-8 and missing the playoffs entirely. For 2026, the expectations have shifted a bit, but they are still high in the Motor City. One way to see how this season could play out is to simulate it in Madden NFL 27. The Lions have played only one preseason game, but what better way to get ready for the upcoming season than to see what the popular video game thinks? Last year, Madden predicted a similar ending from the 2024 season . It also made a bold Super Bowl prediction that this season’s simulation somewhat matches. Will Madden get it correct this year after failing again last year? Before reading, here’s how I laid out this Lions franchise: Difficulty: All-Madden Quarter Length: 15 minutes Pre-existing injuries: ON Final depth chart and roster were my predictions and close to what I believe the team will do First half (Weeks 1-11) For realism’s sake, I held out safeties Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch for the first four games, and center Cade Mays for the first five. Starting the season by losing to the New Orleans Saints at home would be a difficult start for the Lions, as fans would quickly question whether this team got worse than the year before. Luckily, the Lions proved it was a fluke and would go on to win four games in a row before the bye. A win over the Buffalo Bills would be nice, but struggling to beat the New York Jets, Carolina Panthers, and Arizona Cardinals would show that missing Branch, Joseph, and Mays had some impact. In the simulation, EDGE Aidan Hutchinson got hurt and missed Weeks 2-6, returning after the bye week. With the team at full strength, they defeated the Green Bay Packers before losing to the Minnesota Vikings. After the Vikings game, wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown suffered an injury and missed three weeks. The Lions then beat the Miami Dolphins before losing in Germany to the New England Patriots and returning home to beat the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. For the first 10 games, the Lions finished 7-3, taking advantage of having the easiest schedule in the NFL . Second half (Weeks 12-18) Things got a little rocky in the back half when rookie right tackle Blake Miller suffered an injury that knocked him out for six weeks (Week 12 to Week 17), but he returned for the season finale. This was thankfully the last major injury the team suffered, a much better instance than the previous edition. With that, the Lions lost back-to-back games to the Chicago Bears and Atlanta Falcons. They didn’t let that streak continue, blowing out the Tennessee Titans in their biggest win of the season. In the final month, the Lions got some big wins, dominating the Vikings and New York Giants while getting revenge against the Bears. In the season finale, they blew out the Packers in Green Bay, winning 41-21 to claim the NFC North crown once again and finish the year 12-5. Postseason Here is what Madden NFL 27 thinks the playoff field will look like this season. Once again, it believes the Lions are taking on the top seed, which could be possible with how easy the team’s schedule is. The shocking parts on the NFC side, though, are the Giants not just winning the NFC East, but claiming the No. 2 seed. Then you have the Falcons winning the NFC South and being the three seed over the defending Super Bowl champions, the Seattle Seahawks. Finally, the Saints proved that Week 1 wasn’t a fluke and sneaked into the playoffs as the seven seed. The Eagles and Packers took up the other Wild Card spots. For the AFC, we have just about one surprise: the Titans not only made the playoffs, but won the AFC South. The rest of the teams and order isn’t too surprising, as the Bills come out on top to start the postseason. The biggest shock of the playoffs is not seeing the current Super Bowl favorite, the Los Angeles Rams, even make it to the postseason. This time in the playoffs, the Lions didn’t lose their Divisional Round game, beating the Philadelphia Eagles 30-16—leading them to host the NFC Championship game against the Seahawks. In a close battle, the Lions came up short once again, losing 24-16. In the Super Bowl, the Los Angeles Chargers defeated the Seahawks 31-26, giving the Chargers their first Super Bowl title in franchise history. Final results and reaction Appearing back in the NFC Championship Game would be a big step in the right direction for the Lions in 2026. While it isn’t the ending everyone wanted, it would show their window is far from closed, and they’re still a threat in the NFL. Looking at the stats here, quarterback Jared Goff had a fantastic season, finishing 10th in the MVP race, throwing for 4,318 yards with 30 touchdowns and five interceptions. Running back Jahmyr Gibbs had a solid season, as well, rushing for 1,214 yards and 12 touchdowns. The biggest surprise on the offense came in the receiving room. Not only did Jameson Williams take over Amon-Ra St. Brown as the top target on the team, but also second-year receiver Isaac TeSlaa broke out in a huge way. Williams finished with 1,091 yards and 11 touchdowns. St. Brown tallied 1,032 yards with eight touchdowns, and TeSlaa finished the season with 969 yards and six touchdowns. I guess St. Brown’s injury pushed TeSlaa to step up, but man, oh man. Could you imagine if the Lions offense had three receivers with 1,000 yards? Tight end Sam LaPorta added 528 yards and three touchdowns of his own. For the defense, no player had a bigger impact than rookie EDGE Derrick Moore. Not only did Moore win Defensive Rookie of the Year in the simulation, but he also led the Lions in sacks with 13.5, beating out Hutchinson by a half-sack. Defensive tackle Alim McNeill had a big bounce-back season with 10.5 sacks, a career-high for him. Linebacker Jack Campbell led the team in tackles, to no surprise, with 114, and Branch wasn’t too far behind him with 101, despite missing four games. Finally, cornerback D.J. Reed led the team in interceptions with three. Overall, I would be happy with how this season played out if it’s true. Finishing the year as the top seed, with an appearance in the NFC title game is a big step forward for the franchise. While it’s not the storybook ending we all would like to see, it’s a bounce-back season this franchise desperately needs. Additionally, the team had √ery few injuries, which would be a huge relief for once. Would you be content with this type of season, or is it Super Bowl or bust for you?

title: 5 burning questions prior to the Detroit Lions’ 2026 season kicking off
summary: The Detroit Lions will kickoff their second game of the preseason, this time at home against the Washington Commanders on Saturday, and as the possibilities and promise of a summer’s training camp fade into the night, the rise of the midnight sun comes to sweat you in your bed. Here are five burning questions still […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - AUGUST 13: Detroit Lions quarterback Luke Altmyer (2) passes the ball during the game between the Detroit Lions and the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Cincinnati, OH. (Photo by Ian Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Detroit Lions will kickoff their second game of the preseason, this time at home against the Washington Commanders on Saturday, and as the possibilities and promise of a summer’s training camp fade into the night, the rise of the midnight sun comes to sweat you in your bed. Here are five burning questions still facing the Lions ahead of their penultimate preseason game. What’s Detroit’s plan along the interior of the offensive line? The Lions caught a bad break when they learned that center Cade Mays was going to miss anywhere from eight to 10 weeks with a wrist injury that will sideline him well into the start of their regular season. Truth be told, it’s been a stalled start for the interior of Detroit’s offensive line this summer. Juice Scruggs, part of the return for the offseason trade of David Montgomery to the Houston Texans, missed time with an undisclosed soft tissue injury earlier in training camp and is just now getting work with the first-team offense. Early returns have been a mixed bag, including botched snaps and tough sledding against a formidable group of interior defensive pressure from the likes of Alim McNeill and Tyleik Williams. Seth McLaughlin earned some praise for his preseason performance against one of the NFL’s best defensive tackles, Dexter Lawrence , and he’s played his way into a true competition for the starting center job in Detroit after Mays’ injury. But even after that encouraging start, the Lions, for a second year in a row, still gave second-year player Tate Ratledge another go at the center position earlier this week—and it lasted exactly one practice before the team returned to a rotation of Scruggs, McLaughlin, and Michael Niese. It at least seemed like part of the initiative to slide Ratledge into the center spot was to make room, finally, for veteran Ben Bartch to throw his hat into the ring for the competition at left guard. Christian Mahogany seems to still have pole position, but with so much still up in the air along the interior of Detroit’s offensive line, it’d be reassuring to see some of these pieces fall into place sooner rather than later. Week 1 of the 2025 season is firmly in the rearview, but hopefully the lessons learned about an offensive line in flux at season’s start are not lost on this regime. Who is Detroit’s slot cornerback when they go into their nickel defense? A spot once held down by Amik Robertson for the past couple of seasons has given way to a host of different players competing for the slot cornerback position in Detroit’s defense. Newcomers Christian Izien, Roger McCreary, and rookie Keith Abney II are vying for an all-important position to help Detroit reclaim their stout run defense, as outlined here by Anthony Balaj . Izien made his return off the non-football injury list just after the start of training camp, kicking the flu and getting cross-trained at safety and slot corner in Kelvin Sheppard’s defense. He appears to be the frontrunner for the job at the moment, but after some strong play from Abney and McCreary in Detroit’s first preseason game against the Bengals— especially in run defense —there’s some intrigue surrounding how things will shake out at this spot in the Lions secondary. Another name to consider is the much-maligned Ennis Rakestraw. His preseason debut unraveled about as badly as it could have, but after stringing together some strong showings in practice , where does Rakestraw fit into this secondary? His run defense was one of his strongest traits at Missouri, but his body has had trouble holding up in the NFL, so could some refinement and changes to his approach to tackling keep him on the field? Based on the conclusions to those questions, is he best served to play outside instead of the slot? What will Detroit prioritize in their depth at WR5/6? Typically, at the bottom of any given position’s depth chart, it’s critical those players provide special teams play. If they’re not seeing the field on offense or defense, special teams require special players in specific roles across a variety of phases, whether it’s kickoff, kick return, punt coverage, etc. As it stands, Greg Dortch is the team’s replacement for Kalif Raymond in a sense: he’s returning punts and one of the players back returning kicks alongside another returner—oftentimes it’s been running back Jacob Saylors. But when it comes to the wide receivers beyond Dortch, what exactly is Detroit looking for in those players? Dan Campbell said the wide receiver room is the best it’s been since he arrived in 2021, and there’s been plenty of play to justify the hype from Detroit’s head coach. Tay Martin impressed enough to earn first-team reps during Jameson Williams’ absence with a shoulder injury, Dominic Lovett has flashed some ability to separate and make plays, and Tarik Black hauled in Detroit’s lone touchdown reception on a smooth catch and run against the Bengals. However, there’s also the veteran Cedrick Wilson Jr., someone who earned early praise from the coaching staff during OTAs. He started in Detroit’s first preseason contest, played just 15 snaps on offense, but made an impressive, outstretched grab for 23 yards on the team’s first drive. Interestingly enough, there were three receivers who dressed that didn’t log a snap on special teams against the Bengals: Wilson, Isaac TeSlaa, and Tom Kennedy. While Wilson has 373 special teams snaps under his belt during his seven-year career—playing 138 of those snaps recently in 2024 with the New Orleans Saints—could Detroit be more interested in having a reliable receiver capable of lining up at the X, Y, and Z positions? Does that also speak to Tom Kennedy’s chances—another player with special teams experience—at locking down one of these—potentially—two spots available? Could Detroit choose to outsource some of their special teams snaps to players at other positions like running back and defensive back that would normally go to a receiver? Or does Wilson and Kennedy’s lack of involvement on special teams speak to Detroit’s comfort level in knowing what those guys are capable of on special teams, and at the same time, trying to figure out what some of those less experienced players bring to the table in those phases? What if Jimmy Rolder avoids getting put on injured reserve? In a surprising development, the Lions may be getting a player back from injury sooner than initially expected. During a recent podcast appearance, rookie linebacker Jimmy Rolder offered an optimistic outlook on when he could return to action . “Leg is getting better. We’re definitely making some strides,” Rolder told the “X’s and Bro’s” podcast on Aug. 18. “I’ll be back out there in a week—week or so. We’ll see.” Any good developments about an injury are obviously welcome news, but it could complicate things a bit. Instead of assuming Rolder would miss the first four weeks of the season and not count toward the initial 53-man roster, the Lions could find themselves having to make some tough decisions in the linebacker room. Devin White, who was signed after Rolder’s injury, has looked very competent on defense, fitting the run and bringing some juice as a blitzer. Damone Clark has missed time during training camp, as well as the first preseason game, so he and other veteran guys like Troy Reeder and Joe Bachie could end up missing out on a spot on the final roster should Rolder return in time to be counted on for special teams work. Which quarterback will earn the coaching staff’s trust—and then the backup job? The preseason opener in Cincinnati wasn’t the best opportunity to evaluate quarterback play. The inclement weather led to some sloppy play and execution on…
author: Ryan Mathews

title: Discussion: Which Detroit Lions position battle is the tightest?
summary: We’re past the halfway point of training camp, and we’re rapidly approaching cutdown date. The Detroit Lions’ personnel department has some tough decisions ahead, and with the amount of competition across the roster, it may be the hardest year to predict what they will end up doing. There are some easier positions to predict. For […]
full_text: Aug 3, 2026; Allen Park, MI, USA; Detroit Lions linebacker Erick Hunter (48) takes part in a linebacker drill during Detroit Lions training camp. Mandatory Credit: Paul Barnick-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect We’re past the halfway point of training camp, and we’re rapidly approaching cutdown date. The Detroit Lions’ personnel department has some tough decisions ahead, and with the amount of competition across the roster, it may be the hardest year to predict what they will end up doing. There are some easier positions to predict. For example, at running back, the top three players have been pretty well established with Jahmyr Gibbs, Isiah Pacheco, and special teams ace Sione Vaki. And when it comes to a possible fourth spot, Jacob Saylors has shown enough both on offense and special teams to be considered the favorite there. Offensive tackle seems similarly solidified with Penei Sewell, Blake Miller, and Larry Borom being the clear top three. But let’s talk about the other side of the coin. Which position battles remain tightly-contested? Today’s Question of the Day is: Which position battles are currently the tightest on the Lions roster? My answer: I’m looking at the linebacker group as a lot more complicated than it looks. While Detroit likely has their top four settled in Jack Campbell, Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, and Devin White, there is a huge competition brewing for the next two or three roster spots. Trevor Nowaske is likely the player I’d put in next, as he’s a four-core special teamer who also has the unique ability to back up the tricky SAM linebacker role. Then there’s Damone Clark, Troy Reeder, and Joe Bachie. All three are veteran linebackers with some defensive experience, but all three have an extensive history on special teams. Clark clearly led the pack amongst these three, but an injury has sidelined him for nearly two weeks, allowing the other two to gain ground. Beyond that, there are two rookies to consider. Fourth-round pick Jimmy Rolder would be a no-brainer to make the roster if he was healthy. Unfortunately, he suffered a hamstring injury early in camp and was expected to miss significant time. But now with the news that Rolder could return as soon as next week , he may avoid injured reserve completely, leaving one less spot available for the rest of the group. Then there’s Erick Hunter. The undrafted defender out of Morgan State has undoubtedly shined on special teams drills in training camp and has made the occasional defensive play, as well. But on Wednesday, special teams coordinator Dave Fipp warned of putting a player as raw and inexperienced as Hunter in a key role. “He’s definitely done something probably every practice where you’re like, ‘Wow, he did a great job there.’ Or he stood out, and that’s really what you’re looking for,” Fipp said. “Now, that being said, he’s also made some big mistakes, too. And it’s like, ‘Man, how much of that can you weather?’ Well, when you’re talking about the punt team, not a lot. So those guys have got to go out there and execute. They’ve got to protect the passer. It’s going to be a blitz most of the time that they’re picking up and they’ve got to be 100%. And you can’t have a sack or for us, a blocked punt.” Will the Lions be willing to risk some tough learning lessons early for the long-term potential of Hunter? That’s a tough question to answer right now. And on top of that, Fipp gave an unprompted compliment to recently added veteran linebacker Amen Ogbongbemiga, too. In essence, this is how I see the linebacker group right now: Locks: Jack Campbell, Derrick Barnes, Devin White, Malcolm Rodriguez Favorite for reserve spot: Trevor Nowaske In if he’s healthy enough: Jimmy Rolder Still very much in the hunt: Damone Clark, Troy Reeder, Joe Bachie, Amen Ogbongbemiga Wouldn’t surprise me: Erick Hunter That’s seven players who I think have a legitimate chance to make the roster fighting for 1-3 roster spots. I don’t think there’s any tighter position than that. What positions do you think are still very much up for grabs? Share your thoughts in the comment section at the bottom of this page. author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Jonathan Gannon’s 2023 Cardinals defense prioritized zone over everything else
summary: Preseason is in full swing and we’re getting our first glimpse into the defensive scheme of Jonathan Gannon. I’ll have more on that in the coming weeks but first, we still need to fill in the context of what his scheme is and where it went, and we’ll do that by diving into his first […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 30: Head coach Jonathan Gannon of the Arizona Cardinals stands on the field during an NFL football game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Raymond James Stadium on November 30, 2025 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Preseason is in full swing and we’re getting our first glimpse into the defensive scheme of Jonathan Gannon. I’ll have more on that in the coming weeks but first, we still need to fill in the context of what his scheme is and where it went, and we’ll do that by diving into his first season in Arizona as the head coach. No other season in Jonathan Gannon’s three-year sample in Arizona looks like 2023. As noted in the early down section, the Cardinals didn’t lean toward zone coverage in 2023 as they did in 2024 and 2025. In fact, the Cardinals’ 2023 defense, in Arizona, built their entire early down identity around playing in a zone shell. Early down rates: zone prioritized above everything else In looking at 839 early down plays (1st and 2nd down) in the three-year sample, we can see that in each year the Cardinals played a lot of zone. In 2023, early down snaps in zone were 76.88% (or 648/839), in man coverage they were 13.47% (or 114/839), and other schemes such as prevent, etc. were 9.65% (or 77/839) of plays. In sum, this is a defense that relies on the eyes of its players to complete assignments versus man coverage by cornerbacks. Thus, play calling on early downs was nearly 6-to-1 in zone versus man. This is the highest of the three years for early down plays. Of the various Cover structures that can be used to employ a zone defense, the structure of Cover 3 is by far and away the most basic to field. Here, the three corners all play in a three-deep format. We found that over 84% of all early down plays for the Cardinals in 2023 utilized a Cover 3, or similar, structure. Early down structure for the Cardinals in 2023 essentially equated to playing in a basic three-deep zone for the vast majority of plays called. Of course, such plays were frequently mixed in with plays that employed other Cover structures. The one place that this defense didn’t hold back was in their use of Cover 0 on early downs. The Cardinals played Cover 0 on 5.48% of their early downs in 2023, a number that was more than double the rate of both 2024 and 2025. Early down blitz rates were at their lowest in 2023 at 16.50%, however this was a defense that was extremely aggressive on first and second down, sending rushers in scenarios where the math favored such a move. This was in stark contrast to third down where the defense displayed a coverage discipline that was not on display during the rest of the season on early downs. Every Scheme, Side by Side: 2023 vs. 2024 vs. 2025 This graph shows the early down coverage in the three seasons, with all the schemes side by side. The big gap in coverage is not limited to a few schemes, but rather spans almost the entire call sheet. The four schemes that are ran at a higher rate in 2023 than in the two following seasons are Cover 3, Cover 4, Cover 2 and Cover 6. The one scheme that did not change as much is Cover 1, which was treated as a change-up package in 2023, and as a result, it was not changed as much as the other schemes in the following two seasons. This rarely saw the light of day, it was used primarily as a change-up package, and so this showed up very rarely throughout the sample of plays. For instance, early down, there were zero plays in 2023 for this coverage. This was used just once in 2024 for an early down play, and once in 2025 for a late down play. In sum, the use of this coverage was not typical of Gannon’s defense. Other schemes, aside from those previously discussed, made up the remaining 7.99% of the plays from 2023, while 2024 and 2025 saw use of these other schemes for late down plays in just 0.69% and 0.93% of all late down snaps, respectively. First Half to Second Half: A Real In-Season Adjustment For early downs in 2023, Gannon saw a defensive scheme morph over the course of the season in ways that he did not see in 2024 or 2025. Here, we see through the morphing of the defensive scheme in 2023 to find a clear pivot by the Cardinals away from three-deep zones and toward two-high safety structures. However, as the season went on the defense morphed into a totally different entity, morphing from 3 deep zones to two high safeties. Looking at the Cover 3 number for example, early in the season the Cards played a high number of Cover 3 plays at 36.58%, but as the season went on the number of Cover 3 plays decreased 16.6% to 30.50% as the team relied on other Cover types. While Cover 3 decreased drastically, the team’s use of Cover 4 and Cover 2 increased dramatically with the number of Cover 4 plays increasing 46.8% to 25.73% and the number of Cover 2 plays increasing 37.8% to 14.32%. Although the team’s use of zone increased throughout the season the defense changed to a two high safety look with two high safeties rather than three deep zones, or at least that is how it appeared. Third Down: zone-heavy but not too aggressive We look at third down in the same light as the rest of the early down plays. Here, too, the defense was an early down defense – heavily in zone. In 206 third down plays, they were in zone 68.93% of the time, the highest of the three years for early down plays, or roughly 80% higher than 2024 and 2025 for third down plays. Man coverage was used 21.84% of the time, or roughly the same amount as in 2024. This creates a very high zone-to-man ratio of 3.2-to-1, the highest in the sample for third down plays. However, as previously established, early down blitzed more frequently than third down. This year was no exception, and on third down found itself to be the least aggressive of the three years at 16.50%. That early down covered aggressively on first and second down, only to pull back into more standard coverage on third, resulted in third down proving to be the most ‘coverage disciplined’ of the down. Notice how the third down numbers for zone and man coverage create the most lopsided numbers in the entire chart for the 3.2 to 1 zone to man coverage ratio. Again these numbers are higher than the two subsequent years of 2024 and 2025 for both the 2.5 to 1 and 2.9 to 1 numbers respectively. Third down numbers for the season did change as the year progressed but in the opposite direction of early down numbers. Man coverage was used on 20.35% of third downs in the first nine weeks of the season and on 23.66% in the last nine weeks of the season. The number of blitzes increased to 17.20% from 15.93% in the first nine weeks of the season. Zone coverage was used on 68.14% of third downs in the first nine weeks and on 69.89% in the rest of the season, a rise of only 2.6%. The Bigger Picture: 2023 Was an Outlier, Not a Baseline Looking at all three years, it is clear that 2023 was an outlier year. Not only was the early down zone rate much higher than in 2024 and 2025 (77-88% higher), but the nature of the defense in terms of scheme and personnel usage was also different from the two subsequent years. What could account for this big of a change? In all likelihood, there are a few factors at play here, and none of them are necessarily mutually exclusive. For one, there was a significant amount of turnover in the secondary between 2023 and 2024, and it’s possible that the subsequent years featured a coaching staff that was employing more of a disguise-based, man-coverage-heavy approach to defending. On the other hand, it’s possible that the 2023 defense was simply a group of players that were fit to a particular scheme (in this case, a zone-heavy, early down identity), and that in subsequent years, that particular roster would evolve, and the subsequent years’ scheme would follow suit. Either way, though, what’s most impressive here is that the 2023 defense showed a real capacity for in-season adjustment. Key Takeaways An…

title: Isaiah Neyor is a truly interesting wide receiver prospect
summary: Both J. Michael Sturdivant and Isaiah Neyor flashed a few times at the back end of Green Bay Packers’ first preseason game in Pittsburgh. I’ve written a bit about Sturdivant before, and while he’s not my favorite wide receiver prospect, he is very toolsy, he fits a need on the team, and he has some […]
full_text: Both J. Michael Sturdivant and Isaiah Neyor flashed a few times at the back end of Green Bay Packers’ first preseason game in Pittsburgh. I’ve written a bit about Sturdivant before , and while he’s not my favorite wide receiver prospect, he is very toolsy, he fits a need on the team, and he has some special teams value. I get why the Packers picked him up, and if he makes the team, I won’t be surprised. But Isaiah Neyor is interesting in his own right , and I think he has more long-term upside if he can figure a few things out. The reason that Neyor remains interesting is because he hit on a few key criteria we use to project young receivers (with some caveats, which we’ll get to) while in college , and his relative lack of production near the end of his college career was likely caused by some ill-timed transfers while recovering from a torn ACL. It’s not a perfect profile, there are warts for sure, but there is a LOT of good here in context. In his 2021 season at Wyoming, Neyor had a legitimate breakout as a young 20-year-old (he turned 20 in June of 2021). He led the Cowboys with 44 receptions (17 more than second place Josh Cobbs), 878 yards (580 more than second place Ayden Eberhardt), and 12 TD catches (no other Cowboy had more than 2). He absolutely dominated the Wyoming passing game as the clear, best playmaker, and they leaned on him as a result. Breakout age is one of the better predictors for future success, and leading your team in all major receiving categories by far as a redshirt freshman is a great sign. Unfortunately, there are two major issues that call this performance into question. The first is the weirdness of the Covid years, which created many dominant performances that did not translate at the next level. Wyoming didn’t face a single quality opponent (Boise State was probably the best), and they got blanked by Fresno State and essentially blanked by New Mexico. It would have been nice to see Neyor face a random Big Ten or SEC team at some point, but it just didn’t happen, and so level of competition was a big question mark. The second is the fact that they just didn’t do that much passing in the first place. This is a problem that pops up with a lot of Big Ten schools, especially as you move further West. While Indiana and Ohio State throw plenty, a lot of schools (Iowa, Michigan, Wisconsin, etc.) don’t. When Nico Collins, now a star receiver for the Texans, played at Michigan, he never caught more than 38 balls in a season, though on a per play basis he was amazing. Volume is often an indicator of future success, as the ability to demand the ball will result in volume, but if an offense doesn’t pass much in the first place, those differences can sometimes just be noise. In a perfect world, Neyor would have parlayed that excellent season into a transfer to a higher volume school, or at least another dominant season at Wyoming, but instead a torn ACL robbed him over his entire 2022 season. He would then transfer twice, first to Texas where he did nothing in 2023 while recovering from injury, and in fact re-injured the same knee, losing most of the back half of the season. He then moved on to Nebraska for his final season, where he was likely still recovering, and was just okay. While at Nebraska, Neyor was out-targeted by possession receiver Jacory Barney and outside receiver Jahmal Banks, but he was still a dangerous deep threat, leading the Huskers in touchdowns with five. That said, while falling on the depth chart at Texas is excusable, 2024 was his best chance for a post injury breakout with limited talent for competition, and it just didn’t happen. Here’s why you should still care. First, that early breakout shows what’s possible. Neyor has some talent, and his lack of success comes with a good reason in that torn ACL. Second, any lingering concerns about his athletic profile were put to rest at the combine. Neyor posted a 9.90 RAS with elite testing in everything but agility drills, where he was merely good. His closest RAS comp is Brian Thomas Jr, with Alec Pierce and Bryce Lance also making appearances. He’s huge at 6-4, 218, and he’s back to full speed. And so, the problems with Neyor are mostly about the nuances of playing receiver. If you consult Dane Brugler’s 2025 version of The Beast , where he ranked Neyor 28 th among receivers with a sixth-round grade, he fawns over the athletic profile, his catch radius, and his body control. He even praises his blocking, which may be why he’s currently a Packer. The weaknesses are all defects that can be corrected. Brugler labels Neyor an “unseasoned route runner, slow to adjust at the top of routes.” While he praises Neyor’s blocking, he does call out his technique which resulted in two penalties in 2024. And he also points out that pressing corners can give him trouble. Importantly these are all teachable skills, and it’s worth remembering that because of his two knee injuries, Neyor lost a lot of development time in college where these things would normally be sorted out. You cannot practice route running when you cannot run. A year on the practice squad likely helped Neyor more than your average prospect. It’s difficult to perform technique work while on the active roster, where you are forced to prep for games, not refine technique. The practice squad is the perfect place for unrefined athletes, and it’s at least possible that some of that work is starting to pay off. Neyor looked good in limited work last week. He looked much more polished as a route-runner than he ever did on his college tape. His size and speed pop immediately as soon as he steps on the field. And importantly, even though he’s been through quite a lot at this point, he only just turned 25. The Packers have a pretty crowded receiver room between Christian Watson, Jayden Reed, Matthew Golden, Bo Melton, and Savion Williams, even though Romeo Doubs and Dontayvion Wicks are gone. But there is room for a tall burner, and it will be interesting to see if Neyor, or Sturdivant, or both, can continue to impress, and maybe even press Williams for a spot.
author: Paul Noonan

title: Which Packers players are most primed for success in 2026?
summary: The Green Bay Packers are heading into the 2026 season looking much different than they did last year. After parting ways during the offseason with players like receivers Romeo Doubs and Dontayvion Wicks, as well as kicker Brandon McManus and cornerback Nate Hobbs, plenty of doors have opened for younger and fresher faces to take […]
full_text: ASHWAUBENON, WISCONSIN - JULY 31: Matthew Golden #0 of the Green Bay Packers looks on during the Green Bay Packers training camp at Ray Nitschke Field on July 31, 2026 in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers are heading into the 2026 season looking much different than they did last year. After parting ways during the offseason with players like receivers Romeo Doubs and Dontayvion Wicks, as well as kicker Brandon McManus and cornerback Nate Hobbs, plenty of doors have opened for younger and fresher faces to take on more prominent roles. Who’s set up to make the most immediate impact? WR Matthew Golden I think this one is the most obvious. The Packers drafted Matthew Golden in the first round for a reason. He was always going to be a playmaker for the team; it was just a matter of when they’d unleash him. His rookie season left a lot to be desired, mostly due to a lack of opportunity in a very crowded WR room, something I did find puzzling at times. After this offseason’s moves, the team has shown that they’re committed to making Golden a huge part of their offense this year, and it looks like we’re starting to see it already in training camp. The Jordan Love and Matthew Golden connection is going feed families. #Packers pic.twitter.com/CvMysIf0jS — Kyle Malzhan (@KyleMalzhan) August 8, 2026 In 15 regular season and playoff games, Golden caught 33 of 49 targets (67%) for 445 yards (13.5 ypr) and 1 TD. Expect every single number in that last sentence to go up this season. If you took Golden’s stats from the team’s Wild Card game and stretched them over a 17-game season, he’d have 68 catches for 1,428 yards and 17 TDs. Sounds very realistic to me! I kid, I kid (no). CB Brandon Cisse Once upon a time, the phrase was actually “death, taxes, and the Green Bay Packers using a high draft pick on a defensive back”. The days of Josh Jackson, Damarious Randall, and Quentin Rollins, or as I like to call it: my personal Bubonic Plague. If Brandon Cisse plays his cards right (wrong?), he could be added to this list! So far, however, it’s looking like we may have gotten a good one. With the secondary dealing with a ton of injuries at the moment, Cisse has seen more first-team reps than I think we’d usually expect to see from a rookie at his position. The early reviews are…great! The rookie has been glued to whichever receiver he’s covered on any given day, he’s created a ton of PBUs, and he might just be the biggest lock to start Week 1 of all the CBs on the roster. What’s even better? He doesn’t have a history of major or long-term leg injuries. Almost seems like the Packers seek those out sometimes. With Week 1 coming against the Vikings, it’s very possible a matchup with Justin Jefferson will be Cisse’s “welcome to the NFL” moment, but if we can get that out of the way early, who’s to say he can’t play the rest of his career like the hall of famer he was destined to be? Rookie CB Brandon Cisse in 1-on-1s today: pic.twitter.com/PbpSA0Z0Tu — Kelly Hallinan (@kellyhals) August 4, 2026 K Trey Smack This last one could go very right. It could go very wrong too, but this article literally has “success” in the title, so let’s focus on that. In somewhat of a surprise move, the Packers traded up during the sixth round of the 2026 draft to select Trey Smack out of Florida. A short while after, they released veteran Brandon McManus, who was coming off of a brutal 2025 season in which he missed 6 FGs and 1 XP, and left another 7 points on the field in the team’s 4-point playoff loss. Training camp for Smack thus far has been hot and cold, which isn’t what anyone wants to hear, but it’s clear that he’s got a leg on him. In his first preseason game against the Pittsburgh Steelers, Smack was a perfect 3/3, including a 58-yarder (plus another 58-yarder that didn’t count due to a penalty on the Steelers). This is great news for the Packers, who had nightmares every time they had to send Brandon McManus out to attempt anything over 40 last year. If Smack can get his leg under control, we could see things go in the Packers’ favor a bit more this year. The team sees their next preseason action on Friday, August 21st, as they head to Denver to face off against the Broncos. Be there or be square.
author: Sam Kallien

title: Packers Film Room, Preseason Week 1: Isaiah Neyor & J. Michael Sturdivant
summary: The Packers’ first preseason game is slowly drifting further into the rear view mirror, but I still have some clips so I’m gonna write about them. Today, we’ve got a mini film room and we’re looking at Isaiah Neyor and J. Michael Sturdivant. Isaiah Neyor Neyor was an undrafted free agent pick-up by the 49ers […]
full_text: Green Bay Packers wide receiver Isaiah Neyor (80) participates in a drill during the sixth day of training camp on Aug. 4, 2026, at Ray Nitschke Field in Ashwaubenon, Wis. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Packers’ first preseason game is slowly drifting further into the rear view mirror, but I still have some clips so I’m gonna write about them. Today, we’ve got a mini film room and we’re looking at Isaiah Neyor and J. Michael Sturdivant. Isaiah Neyor Neyor was an undrafted free agent pick-up by the 49ers in 2025, but spent the regular season on the Packers’ practice squad, getting 3 snaps with the team all year (in the Wild Card game against the Bears). At 6’4”, 218 lbs & running a 4.43 40, Neyor has the measurables you’d expect to see out of a Packers WR. His 9.97 RAS score certainly backs that up. Isaiah Neyor is a WR prospect in the 2025 draft class. He scored an unofficial 9.97 #RAS out of a possible 10.00. This ranked 11 out of 3408 WR from 1987 to 2025. Splits projected, times unofficial. https://t.co/TmcbybAh18 pic.twitter.com/s3I00O62Et — RAS.football (@MathBomb) March 1, 2025 How did he look in the first preseason game? If you care about preseason stats, he was the Packers leading receiver on the day, grabbing all 4 of his targets for 34 yards. He looked like a natural receiver to me. He certainly struggled with some things – and he didn’t really show off that 4.43 time – but he looked like a professional possession receiver. In our Jordan Love post we talked about the out-breakers we’re likely going to see in this offense this year. How showed the ability to threaten vertically, cut off sharply and make a catch while going to the sideline. Is that fairly basic stuff? Sure! But there’s an ease in how he operates as a receiver that shows up there. You can also see some of the suddenness in his route running on this quick slant. Again, nothing too crazy here, but that’s a nice, crisp route exactly where it’s supposed to be. I also like seeing what he does when the ball is in the air. On this route, he does a nice job of working back to the ball instead of waiting for it to come to him. His big body suggests that he could work in the blocking game. While he shows a willingness in that part of his game, his technique could still use some work. When blocking from out wide, he has a tendency to get his arms wide and wrap around his target. While he may get away with it from time to time, that kind of action is the exact type of motion that will draw holding. He had a couple reps as an insert blocker. Again, with his size, this seems like something he could be good at. It didn’t go well. Another rep as an insert blocker went better, but he was tentative and got moved back into the pile (and also has an initial reaction of opening his arms to his target). As a receiver, I really like him. He shows a good understanding of what his role is on a play, and he moves like a receiver. If he can clean up his blocking, you can color me intrigued. J. Michael Sturdivant Where Neyor is starting year 2 in the Packers organization, Sturdivant is brand new. He was a UDFA out of Florida this year. As you might expect, he is also a RAS all-star, posting a score of 9.96. He comes in at 6’3”, 207 lbs, with a 40 yard dash time of 4.40. Sturdivant posted elite scores in his 10 yard & 20 yard times, as well as in his explosion grade. J. Michael Sturdivant is a WR prospect in the 2026 draft class. He scored an unofficial 9.96 RAS out of a possible 10.00. This ranked 17 out of 3844 WR from 1987 to 2026. Pending bench and agilities, splits projected. https://t.co/7rz888iu7Z pic.twitter.com/g7He5z6Kql — RAS.football (@MathBomb) March 1, 2026 That’s truly what stands out: explosion. I mentioned earlier how I didn’t really see Neyor’s speed show up in the first game. The same was not true of Sturdivant. You can see the explosion out of the blocks. The speed is immediate. He looks like a true speed freak down the field. There were a couple other flashes he showed (we’ll get to those shortly), but, if you’re looking for the trait that will have the biggest impact as to whether he makes the team or not, it’s the speed. Like I said, there were a few other things that showed up. He showed a good understanding of coverage and was able to throttle down and find room in the middle of the field for his QB. He also showed nice adjustment to a ball thrown outside of his frame. (There’s a chance that he ran the wrong route and was supposed to cut to the sideline, but we don’t currently have a way to know that.) There’s also a bit of nastiness to his game as a blocker. He has shown that he is up for the fight. The problem is that, while he may be up for the fight, he still is far from a polished blocker. He doesn’t show a great ability to adjust after he hits his spot, which leads to reps in space like this, where he looks to overrun his block. Or this, where it looks like he’s pulling up short, but he’s really just waiting for the defender to react, but is then unable to adjust to that reaction. There’s more, but you get the idea. He has the size and willingness that would profile as a good blocker, but he has a lot to work in that part of his game, from both an understanding an adjustment/movement perspective. That being said, his combination of size and speed is intriguing. If he can show some value on special teams, he could carve out a nice role on this team as the honorary Charles De Mar “Go that way really fast” player. Get a few snaps a game on the outside as a straight line speed guy to give some other guys a breather or open up some underneath opportunities for some other guys. Much like Neyor, I’ll be keeping an eye on Sturdivant’s blocking as the preseason rolls on. Sturdivant has further to go in that regard, but if he can even get a small amount better, he starts to become an extremely interesting player. The most likely scenario is that it isn’t until 2027 when we see him truly carving out a role for himself, but improving a tick as a blocker would go a long way to seeing him running fast in a straight line a few times this year. title: Green Bay Packers News: Kamal Hadden does the safety dance in the slot
summary: Xavier McKinney and Evan Williams make a pretty darn good tandem, and the safety group has quickly gone from a massive hole to a massive strength for the Green Bay Packers over a very brief period. With those two players locking down the back end and Javon Bullard taking a big step forward in the […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 13: Kamal Hadden #36 of the Green Bay Packers warms up before the game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Justin K. Aller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Xavier McKinney and Evan Williams make a pretty darn good tandem, and the safety group has quickly gone from a massive hole to a massive strength for the Green Bay Packers over a very brief period. With those two players locking down the back end and Javon Bullard taking a big step forward in the slot last season, the Packers have a trio of safeties as good as any in the NFL. Expect them to all be on the field for most of the team’s defensive snaps this season, as well. This week, we learned that new defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon is very particular about the slot position in his defense, specifically in that he wants safeties at that position instead of a more traditional smaller cornerback. That should help explain why Packers fans have not seen players like Keisean Nixon or Carrington Valentine in the slot this summer. The team is looking for a different approach at that position, one that seems to be better filled by Kamal Hadden when the team looks for a cornerback to contribute there. Hadden has been getting more and more reps in the slot with Bullard recovering from an ankle issue, and Wednesday was his best performance to date. Let’s look at why he appears to be a good fit at that spot in this defense in today’s Cheese CUrds. Packers defensive coordinator Gannon wants slot corners to be safeties | Packersnews.com ($) Gannon appears to be a firm believer that safeties, not corners, have the better body type and playing style to fit in the slot in his scheme. This is a good look into why that is from the players who have been lining up there for much of training camp, and it should help explain why Kitan Oladapo has been the next man up after Bullard. 5 things learned at Packers training camp – Aug. 19 | Packers.com Kamal Hadden is pushing hard for the backup slot job, however, and he has been impressing when rotating in with the 1s. Though he has mostly played perimeter cornerback, Hadden has just a little bit of slot and safety background and he has good size, making the transition a bit easier. Nickel, Dime: Play and Player of Day From Practice 14 of Packers Training Camp | SI.com Hadden gets some praise in this writeup as well, as he picked off a pass from Kyle McCord on Wednesday, but McCord got his own big play with a beautiful rainbow to J. Michael Sturdivant for a big gain. Packers rookie Dani Dennis-Sutton returns to field after heat-related illness | Packers Wire Fans old enough to remember when Vikings lineman Korey Stringer died of heat stroke during training camp should appreciate that the NFL appears to have robust protocols in place for addressing players who show similar signs. Seahawks sign CB Trevon Diggs as Terrion Arnold deal remains in limbo | NFL.com The one-time (briefly) Packer lands with a new team. Cannabis facility goes up in smoke near High River | CBC Does the High River flow into Munchies Bay? Green Bay Packers News in the Feed This cutup of locker room interviews shows the leadership that McKinney has with this team, as he has been taking the rookie kicker under his wing a bit. title: Texans Postgame: Texans Lose to Raiders
summary: Well, just like last week, Houston had a very deflating finish to this preseason game, losing to the Las Vegas Raiders 22-20, dropping to 0-2 this preseason. Despite the loss, however, this game was a much more satisfying showing from the Texans roster than last week’s loss against the Los Angeles Chargers. Tonight, the Houston […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - AUGUST 20: Davis Mills #10 of the Houston Texans throws a pass in the first half against the Las Vegas Raiders during a preseason game at Reliant Stadium on August 20, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Well, just like last week, Houston had a very deflating finish to this preseason game, losing to the Las Vegas Raiders 22-20, dropping to 0-2 this preseason. Despite the loss, however, this game was a much more satisfying showing from the Texans roster than last week’s loss against the Los Angeles Chargers. Tonight, the Houston Texans faced first overall pick QB Fernando Mendoza, hoping to get some positive action from their roster following the devastating news of WR Jayden Higgins’ injury yesterday. They got exactly what they were looking for on the first two drives of the game: a methodical, run-heavy drive from the first-stringers that ended in a 20-yard Woody Marks touchdown run, and then a pick-six on Mendoza by rookie LB Wade Woodaz! TEXANS PICK-6 ALERT 🚨 LVvsHOU on ESPN Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/li2QM4hEah — NFL (@NFL) August 21, 2026 For a moment, you might’ve mistaken this game to be a pivotal late-season matchup with the amount of cheering from the fans following Woodaz’s interception. Then, on the next Raiders’ drive, DE Jadeveon Clowney announced his return to Houston with a deflection against Mendoza on third down! Seeing that #90 screaming off the edge for Houston’s defensive line again after seven years away is a very welcome sight, especially considering the state the Texans’ franchise is in now compared to the chaotic state it was in during the Bill O’Brien era. Clowney makes for an excellent depth piece on the edge, and if the preseason is any indication, Houston may be leaning on its defensive line a lot once again in 2026. Following the three-and-out by the Raiders, Texans backup QB Davis Mills entered the game along with many second and third-string players. He targeted backup TE Foster Moreau and Noah Whittington on this drive, and he even got a nice completion to undrafted rookie Daniel Sobkowicz on third down. Just barely not enough for a new set of downs, though, so Houston settles for a field goal, making it 17-0 with a little over 3 minutes left in the first quarter. The Raiders answered that drive with a field goal drive of their own, led by some impressive runs from rookie RB Mike Washington – who’s too fast for Texans LB Jake Hummel – and FB/TE Connor Hayward. Texans rookie DT Kayden McDonald put an end to the string of positive plays for the Raiders, sacking Mendoza for an eleven yard loss and reminding everyone what this Texans d-line is capable of. The Raiders settle for a field goal, and then both teams trade punts, and Houston nabs a field goal shortly before halftime. KMAC WITH THE SACK 😮‍💨 📺: @nflonespn pic.twitter.com/kOks1uMcrW — Houston Texans (@HoustonTexans) August 21, 2026 Texans rookie WR Lewis Bond made an impressive reception on 3rd & 8, and RB Noah Whittington had a few nice runs in the second quarter, but the run-blocking from Houston’s backup offensive lineman still leaves much to be desired. Blake Fisher still doesn’t look the part of a second-round pick, and Braden Smith wasn’t particularly impressive, either. Thankfully, it appears they may have found a star in rookie TE Marlin Klein, who had a 17-yard reception that showcased his ability to track a bad pass, reel it in while in motion, and crank up the speed as he approached the sideline. Klein has made a few plays in each of the preseason games thus far, making you wonder if he’s going to win the TE3 job over the likes of Cade Stover and Brevin Jordan. Both Brevin and Texans RB Jawhar Jordan remain injured and were inactive for this game, putting them in dire straits entering the final ten days before cut day on August 30th. Marlin Klein is going to be a stud man Feel like I will be tweeting that a lot this szn — Nick Schwager (@nick__schwager) August 21, 2026 Entering the second half, the goal for the Texans (at least to me) was to not crumble on defense like they did last week, and to determine who their best depth pieces are at CB, LB, WR, and O-Line. Wade Woodaz made a very impressive tackle on Raiders TE Albert Okwuegbunam, solidifying his spot in my head as a reliable sideline-to-line MLB. For the Raiders, it would be QB Aiden O’Connell and RB Dylan Laube to start the second half, and they would find a similar amount of success as Chargers’ QB D.J. Uiagalelei and RB Jaret Patterson did last week. There’s clearly some air in Houston’s defense left by backup CBs Stephen Hall and Brandon Codrington. Codrington, S Jaylen Reed, and DT Kyonte Hamilton all made a few plays in the second half, but it wasn’t enough to stop O’Connell and Laube from taking over the game and scoring a touchdown in the third quarter, making the score 20-10 Houston. Newly signed QB Brett Rypien would make his first appearance in a Texans uniform this quarter, replacing Graham Mertz following his season-ending injury, and his performance was just about as forgettable as this sentence. In the fourth quarter, Raiders rookie RB Roman Hemby and former Texans RB Dare Ogunbowale would lead another touchdown run, making the score 20-16 Houston. Now, the fading nature of this defense was really starting to remind you of last week, and the worrying thoughts about what might happen to this team if several starters get hurt start to crop up, again. But, in my opinion, Ogunbowale should have surrendered himself at the one-yard line considering his former team allowed him to kick a field goal in 2023. Dare Ogunbowale touchdown 🫡 pic.twitter.com/QkRYANUXQ6 — Houston Stressans (@TexansCommenter) August 21, 2026 Now, this Raiders team was running all over Houston, and the third-string d-lineman and linebackers didn’t have an answer for Las Vegas’s rushers. Following three more punts between the two teams (with the only notable play being a 9-yard run by RB Owen Wright), the Raiders would lead a 8-play, 96-yard game-winning touchdown drive at the end of the game, highlighted by some pristine passes from Aiden O’Connell and some more poor coverage from CB Stephen Hall and newly-signed Texans CB Bryce Hall. Great…just, great. It’s just the preseason, it’s just the preseason, it’s just the… Brett Rypien throws one of the worst interceptions I've ever seen. pic.twitter.com/roS7vd56LT — SM Highlights (@SMHighlights1) August 21, 2026 ….the preseason… This loss felt almost inevitable on that last drive considering how poorly Houston’s players were performing, as if they were helpless as the Raiders meteor descended upon them. It was a better showing than last week, but Houston will need to show more in their preseason finale vs. the Carolina Panthers on Friday, August 28th if they want to placate their fans before September. The stars of this game were certainly LB Wade Woodaz and TE Marlin Klein, and maybe there’s enough room for RB Noah Whittington. Hopefully next week, we’ll get to talk more about a rebound performance from the defensive backfield. What did you think of the Texans performance tonight, though? Were the Texans able to excite you for the upcoming regular season, or have they made you more nervous? Do you think they’ve found their answer to replacing Jayden Higgins, or is the jury still out? Let us know your thoughts down in the comments below! Go Texans!
