title: Replacing Higgins: Sign or Trade?
summary: Yesterday’s news about the ACL injury to 2nd year receiver Jayden Higgins was a significant blow to the Houston Texans hopes for 2026. Most considered Higgins as the lock for WR2. And while the Texans have a solid receiver room, none of the players behind him look like viable replacements. Next man up is a […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 12: Jayden Higgins #81 of the Houston Texans runs the ball during the third quarter of the AFC Wild Card playoff game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on January 12, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images Yesterday’s news about the ACL injury to 2nd year receiver Jayden Higgins was a significant blow to the Houston Texans hopes for 2026. Most considered Higgins as the lock for WR2. And while the Texans have a solid receiver room, none of the players behind him look like viable replacements. Next man up is a thing, for sure, but Higgins was the best compliment to WR1 Nico Collins on the roster. And, in what seems to be a make or break year for embattled franchise quarterback C.J. Stroud, losing a solid target is not helpful. At all. Many may point to the hopeful return of Tank Dell as an insurance policy. But, Dell and Higgins are different blades in the Swiss Army knife of Houston’s receiving corps. Xavier Hutchinson might stand a better chance, but Hutch has had a lot of chances already to grab the brass ring and has yet to wrap his fingers around it fully. Jared Wayne is catching a lot more than passes this off-season, as the latest “camp star” pass catcher in Houston lore. But, we’ve all seen the Devier Posey’s come and go, year after year. All this adds up to general manager Nick Caserio having to roll up his sleeves and bring in a new face. Then hope that face fronts a mind that can grasp Nick Calley’s offense quickly, and a skillset that not only replicates Higgins’, but can do so from week 1 deep into the playoffs. The 1st name that many are bringing up is former H-Town receiving superstar DeAndre Hopkins. 🚨DeAndre Hopkins posted a picture today with him in a #Texans uniform DHop might be back in Houston soon pic.twitter.com/ewQGhC4mmT — NFL Rumors (@nflrums) August 20, 2026 While this makes for great sports bar discussion around a pitcher of draft, the reality is Hopkins is currently a coach, no longer employed as an NFL wideout. With the number of teams out there who could use a former pro bowler, the fact that Nuk is on the sidelines speaks volumes to his ability to step into a WR2 role. Odds are we’d all love to see the 2nd best receiver in Texans history run it back in 2026. Paired with Collins and Dell, a prime D-Hop would be glorious. Unfortunately, he’s clearly past that juncture. Another interesting idea floated on X is trading with the Arizona Cardinals for Marvin Harrison Jr. , who provides a near 1-to-1 match for Higgins’ skills. Check out Houston Stressans’ comparison: Marvin Harrison Jr. would be about as close to a one for one replacement for what Jayden Higgins was expected to give you this year as you could find. If production is a concern: he was more productive as a rookie than Higgins was, and more productive again in Year 2. If Higgins… pic.twitter.com/UTK35zq1QB — Houston Stressans (@TexansCommenter) August 19, 2026 A potential trade package was also floated by a prominent Texans X’er, AyooNoah: Arizona Cardinals get : future 3rd & 5th 🤝 Houston Texans get : Marvin Harrison Jr Who says No ??? pic.twitter.com/m0lq3F8LHs — AyooNoah (@AyooTexanNation) August 19, 2026 Not sure a 3rd and 5th gets it done if the Cardinals smell blood in the water, but Caserio is definitely in a win-now mode, so trading future picks for a shot at this year’s Super Bowl makes a lot of sense. After Will Anderson Jr.’s recent comments on the mission for this team, it seems even more plausible that Caserio and crew get a deal done with another team to bring in a starter instead of sifting through the Free Agent pile. Men on a mission 🏆 pic.twitter.com/LsLAcOzmB0 — Sports Illustrated (@SInow) August 20, 2026 Sharp Football Analysis dropped this list of best available NFL receivers yesterday. That’s about as fresh as it gets in light of the Higgins news. Best 2026 NFL Free Agent Wide Receivers Tyreek Hill JuJu Smith-Schuster Brandin Cooks Curtis Samuel Josh Reynolds Deandre Carter Zay Jones D’Wayne Eskridge Hunter Renfrow Allen Lazard Michael Gallup Gabe Davis Malik Heath D.J. Turner Kristian Wilkerson River Cracraft None of those names jump out as a plug and play replacement. Which makes me think Caserio, the draft day wheeler dealer, is likely on the phone right now trying to trade for a starter. That player will need to fit the system bring Higgins-like qualities have the right personality to add to the locker room culture currently occupy a roster spot on a team thinking they’re better off building for 2027 and beyond than playing catch with him in 2026. Seems that Marvin Harrison Jr. ticks all those boxes. And he’d make a great addition to the Houston Texans depth chart. Who do you want? Nuk or Harrison? Have someone else in mind? Bring your ideas and let’s have the sports bar debate in the comments section.

title: Keenan Allen makes debut as Colts close Grand Park era with second joint-practice against Falcons
summary: WESTFIELD, Ind. — The final whistle blew 40 minutes earlier than expected as eight summers of Indianapolis Colts training camp at Droplight Grand Park Sports Campus had officially come to an abrupt end. For the Colts, the Grand Park chapter began in 2018 when the team originally announced a 10-year partnership, with the first camp […]
full_text: Indianapolis Colts receivers (from left to right): Alec Pierce #14, Josh Downs #2, and Keenan Allen #10 talk on the sidelines after a team session during Thursday’s training camp practice at Droplight Grand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, Ind. — Aug. 20, 2026. | Thomas Butler-Guerrero WESTFIELD, Ind. — The final whistle blew 40 minutes earlier than expected as eight summers of Indianapolis Colts training camp at Droplight Grand Park Sports Campus had officially come to an abrupt end. For the Colts, the Grand Park chapter began in 2018 when the team originally announced a 10-year partnership, with the first camp opening July 25, 2018. The Colts were forced back to their Indianapolis headquarters in 2020 because of the NFL’s COVID-19 protocols, then returned back to Grand Park in 2021. Beginning next summer, training camp will return to the Indiana Farm Bureau Football Center on West 56th Street. Operationally, the move makes sense because the coaches will have their offices, meeting rooms and practices all at one facility. It allows the organization to take advantage of the technology and infrastructure already installed at its headquarters. But there is something that cannot be measured by better WiFi, because Grand Park gave fans a different kind of exposure. For eight summers, families packed the grandstands, walked through Colts City and watched the stampede in blue prepare for another season from only a few yards away. Today, there were families who traveled four hours in a car or caught a flight that left devastated after the announcement that there would be no post-practice autographs. It was a crummy buzzkill to what felt like a special annual event for the community. Children who might not have had the opportunity to attend a Colts game at Lucas Oil Stadium in downtown Indy could see their favorite player like Jonathan Taylor (or Bijan Robinson) break through a runway, watch quarterbacks launch deep passes or try to collect a signature from an athlete they had only seen on television. While Grand Park is just one mile away, it became part of the rhythm to the end of summer for me as each practice still offered plenty to evaluate while covering the Colts. For starters, Keenan Allen waited until the very last day to give Colts fans their first glimpse of Indy’s newest receiver in full pads. The 14-year veteran, who signed a one-year contract worth up to $8.32 million in incentives, participated in two one-on-one battles before getting a series of reps in an 11-on-11 team period. Allen won his first 1-on-1 battle on a short slant route, but then he essentially had to play defensive back on his second rep and used his length to knock away a bad pass thrown toward the back corner of the end zone. The six-time pro bowler did not receive a target during team drills, but Allen’s presence offered an encouraging live-action look. The 34-year-old spent seven seasons with head coach Shane Steichen in their time with the Los Angeles Chargers, giving Allen a familiarity with the system that could accelerate his transition to Indianapolis. #Colts WR Keenan Allen during 1-on-1s. 🎥: @TBGofficial_ https://t.co/C6rrEBeYTm pic.twitter.com/cfw2uh6ABJ — Noah Compton (@nerlens_) August 20, 2026 The Colts spent much of the final practice aiming to confront an issue that Steichen mentioned he wants to see more consistency from, the rushing attack. There was no way to sugarcoat the struggles in both joint practices as Jonathan Taylor’s first five carries produced fewer than 10 yards. The Falcons repeatedly stuffed the Colts’ tailbacks at the line of scrimmage, including another stuffed run by rookie defensive tackle Carlos Allen Jr. against fellow Colts’ rookie Seth McGowan. Even a low-red-zone period designed to emphasize the battle in the trenches produced little rhythm for the Colts touted offensive line. For all the offensive frustration though, the Colts quarterbacks offered way more encouraging moments than the Falcons QBs did. Riley Leonard flourished in his final practice of camp, throwing four touchdown passes during the low red zone period to four different pass catchers, including Nick Westbrook-Ikhine, Deion Burks, Will Mallory and Tyler Moore. Anthony Richardson Sr. completed 5-of-7 passes in Thursday’s joint-practice, but his best moment came during the final one-minute drill while leading the second unit. Both teams were faced with a scenario where the offense was trailing by one point with just 1:05 remaining on the game clock. For four straight series, the Colts emerged victorious. Jones ignited the final drive with a short hitch to Josh Downs, then followed with a deep shot for Downs down the near sideline as a defensive pass interference penalty gifted the Colts an advantage from the opposing 40-yard-line. Rather than risk a turnover, Steichen chose to drain the clock like he did in the Denver Broncos game last season and fed McGowan for an inside run instead of airing it out. Shrader delivered a 48-yard field goal before time expired. Richardson also needed just two plays to moonwalk into Falcons territory as he connected with Westbrook-Ikhine over the middle, then found Burks wide open on a drag route for another chunk gain. Despite bobbling a couple high snaps in opposing territory, Richardson was still able to hit Burks on a slant before finding Coleman Owen on a quick out route. Steichen again settled for Shrader to try from 50 yards out and he drilled it, with enough distance to strike the left upright on the opposite practice field. Four straight competitive periods. Four Colts victories between Wednesday and Thursday’s practices. Next summer, there won’t be a grandstand filled with fans waiting to greet Colts players walking out from the Field 0f Dreams’ practice facility in Westfield. The Grand Park era is over. There was no grand finale. No fireworks. No post-practice autographs. Just one last practice. Perhaps that was a bittersweet ending. Training camp has never really been about the last practice. It has been about the work that comes during it. The sweat from the 90 August heat. The competition to make the team and earn their place on the field. There was uncertainty from injuries like most NFL teams. Some were answered like Daniel Jones full participation, while others were left unanswered like Alec Pierce and Charvarius Ward. The backup quarterback competition remains unresolved. Leonard will get his opportunity to start inside Lucas Oil Stadium for Saturday’s preseason game against the Falcons.

title: Colts adding Keenan Allen provides solidifying veteran presence to depleted receiving corps
summary: The Indianapolis Colts made national headlines earlier this week after signing six-time former Pro Bowl veteran wideout Keenan Allen to a one-year, $8.32 million deal to boost their seemingly depleted wide receiver corps. While the Colts had been in talks with Allen and his representation for months this offseason, the 13-year veteran and Indianapolis were […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, INDIANA - AUGUST 19: Keenan Allen looks on during the joint practice against the Atlanta Falcons at Grand Park Sports Campus on August 19, 2026 in Westfield, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts made national headlines earlier this week after signing six-time former Pro Bowl veteran wideout Keenan Allen to a one-year, $8.32 million deal to boost their seemingly depleted wide receiver corps . While the Colts had been in talks with Allen and his representation for months this offseason, the 13-year veteran and Indianapolis were finally able to strike a deal with the regular season rapidly approaching. Fortunately for Allen, he’s expected to have a starting role within the Colts offense, once he gets up to speed of course, without having had to go through the summer and heated rigors of NFL training camp. Even though Allen will not be replacing Alec Pierce’s deep threat role by any means, should the latter miss initial regular season time still recovering from an ankle/heel injury, I can’t help but think that Pierce’s potential pending absence still played a part in this much needed signing finally getting done. “Deadlines spur action,” and right now, we’re just a few weeks away from the Colts regular season opener, and Pierce has yet to even practice. One would have to think that there’d even be a ramp up period for conditioning once he debuts in practice. Any Pierce absence that carries over into the regular season clearly decimates the Colts wide receiver corps. While whoever played outside WR2 opposite Pierce was less relevant, whether it was Ashton Dulin or Nick Westbrook-Ikhine, when Pierce, Josh Downs, and Tyler Warren are all fully healthy from a target sense. Right now, Pierce isn’t fully healthy, and both Downs and Warren have had recent injury scares themselves. When you’re WR1 is out, suddenly the rest of your wide receiver corps gets elevated a spot. It’s no different than when Aaron Judge misses time for the New York Yankees, and suddenly Cody Bellinger is now hitting in the 2-hole. That lineup gets far less imposing and is easier for pitchers to get through the lineup. Dulin or Westbrook-Ikhine isn’t as meaningful when either is the 3rd or 4th option out there, but with Pierce out, a Colts receiver corps of Downs, Dulin, and Westbrook-Ikhine otherwise looks a whole lot less formidable, and a lot easier to cover for opposing secondaries. Allen isn’t realistically the same guy he once was, but his reputation, experience, and recent production clearly carry weight—as does his complete body of work in the NFL. I think the Colts had enough time to see what Dulin and Westbrook-Ikhine could do out there throughout training camp, and while the two could be a serviceable platoon by deploying them to their clear strengths, neither player was going to be nearly as complete of a wideout as the departed Michael Pittman Jr. on the field. The Colts reasonably knew that going in, but were still looking at evaluating their potential options. Although he was understatedly effective last year, I’m not sure a 34-year-old Keenan Allen will be a complete Pittman Jr. replacement either (particularly from a perimeter blocking sense), but at 6,‘2”, 211 pounds, he can work a lot of the underneath routes and occasional intermediate routes that the Colts recently utilized Pittman Jr. for—while providing lost veteran leadership in their wide receiver room. I remember asking Reggie a year or two ago which wideout compared favorably with Michael Pittman Jr. He said Kennan Allen. Now, Allen steps into void created when Colts traded Pitt to Pitt. https://t.co/SvUUiBwvsF — Mike Chappell (@mchappell51) August 18, 2026 Also interesting. 2025: *Keenan Allen – 122 tar., 81 rec., 777 yds, 4 TDs *Michael Pittman – 111 tar., 80 rec., 784 yds, 7 TDs — Mike Chappell (@mchappell51) August 18, 2026 On ‘The Pat McAfee Show,’ it was interesting that Allen actually led the league in 3rd down catches last year, having 34 such catches for 355 total receiving yards, showcasing that he can still effectively move the sticks as a sure-handed, reliable possession target. He doesn’t separate as well as he used to, but he can still get consistently open and make contested catches. The hope has to be that he still has a good amount of juice left to help an AFC playoff hopeful close the gap, as the Colts were previously burned by the veteran free agent signing of future Hall of Famer Andre Johnson, who was also 34-years-old back in 2015, and lasted just that sole season in Indianapolis after an underwhelming, 41 receptions for 503 total receiving yards and 4 touchdown receptions during 16 games (14 starts), even with franchise quarterback Andrew Luck passing to him behind center. Allen has some momentum, given the productive season he had last year returning to the Chargers. That being said, expectations have to be tempered a bit, as he’s closer to being a complementary piece for the Colts offense than the perennial Pro Bowler of years past—think more of a WR3/4 than a WR1/2, and that’s all Indy realistically needs.
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Daniel Jones shows out, drops dimes in Colts-Falcons joint practices
summary: Would he or wouldn’t he? That was a question most had just a few months ago pondering Daniel Jones’ health and availability for training camp and even the start of the season. Tearing his Achilles doesn’t appear to be more than a blip at this point as Jones is back in full swing. He has […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, INDIANA - AUGUST 19: Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts throws a pass during the joint practice against the Atlanta Falcons at Grand Park Sports Campus on August 19, 2026 in Westfield, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images Would he or wouldn’t he? That was a question most had just a few months ago pondering Daniel Jones’ health and availability for training camp and even the start of the season. Tearing his Achilles doesn’t appear to be more than a blip at this point as Jones is back in full swing. He has picked up right where he left off as the leader of the Indianapolis Colts, and he flexed his muscles over the Atlanta Falcons in joint practice on Wednesday. The Falcons and Colts don’t officially meet in the preseason until Saturday afternoon, but as has become tradition, two teams mix it up in joint practices before meeting on the gridiron. It’s a welcomed sight to get more work in from the starters and see how they stack up against another NFL unit. Sure, not everyone is out there, but it’s a heck of a lot more complete than what we saw against New England. The last time these teams met, they produced a thriller in Berlin with the Colts taking the win in overtime. It would mark their last win in 2025. Perhaps facing the Falcons in the preseason will propel them in the opposite direction. If that is going to happen, it will be because of Jones. Although the offensive line wasn’t perfect, Jones was slinging it, going a perfect 15-15. That type of stat line sounds like something we experienced from the Colts last year to start. Jones won’t have to be that perfect, but reaching a new level will be imperative. Seeing him go 15-15, even in something as basic as joint practice is a great sign. Daniel Jones, along with just a few others, holds the keys to what this season will look like at its completion. If we get the lost looking Jones from the late stages in New York, the second year of the contract won’t come to pass. If we get Danny Dimes, like we saw in practice, Jones will prove to be the absolute best choice for this franchise and save a lot of jobs. It’s just one practice, but add up enough dimes, and you’ll have a wealth of success.

title: Jaguars activate OL Cole Van Lanen from PUP list
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars have activated Cole Van Lanen from the Active/Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list. Hell yeah. Originally selected by the Green Bay Packers in Round 6 of the 2021 NFL Draft, the Jaguars traded for Van Lanen in August 2022. He played 33 total games (3 starts) in his first three seasons in […]
full_text: Jacksonville Jaguars offensive tackle Cole van Lanen (70) runs on the field before an NFL football matchup at EverBank Stadium, Sunday, Jan. 4, 2026, in Jacksonville, Fla. The Jaguars defeated the Titans 41-7, capturing the AFC South title. [Corey Perrine/Florida Times-Union] | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Jacksonville Jaguars have activated Cole Van Lanen from the Active/Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list. Hell yeah. Originally selected by the Green Bay Packers in Round 6 of the 2021 NFL Draft, the Jaguars traded for Van Lanen in August 2022. He played 33 total games (3 starts) in his first three seasons in Jacksonville before starting 10 of 16 games last year. Van Lanen emerged as a breakout player, finishing 12th among 109 AFC offensive linemen with a 78.7 PFF grade despite playing 40+ snaps at four different positions. The Jaguars inked him to a three-year, $51 contract extension just a few days before the final game of the regular season — when Van Lanen sustained a right knee injury that required offseason surgery. Fortunately, with Van Lanen now activated from the PUP list, he’s expected to be on track to start in the season opener. He and Anton Harrison will occupy the tackle positions as the Jaguars continue to mix up their interior lineup following surgery for Patrick Mekari and a trade for Daniel Faalele . Beyond Van Lanen and Mekari, the offensive line has also dealt with injuries to Walker Little, Chuma Edoga, Emmanuel Pregnon, and Wyatt Milum. Jags fans, let us know your thoughts in the comments below!

title: Can the Jaguars carry over their redzone performance from last year?
summary: Trevor Lawrence and the Jacksonville Jaguars’ first-team offense were surgical in the red zone on Thursday. Competing against the Carolina Panthers in a joint practice, Lawrence completed all three of his redzone attempts for touchdowns. The second-team offense had several spikes as well. Lawrence’s first score came against former teammate Devin Lloyd, who was moved […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - AUGUST 19: Trevor Lawrence #16 of the Jacksonville Jaguars practices during joint training camp with Jacksonville Jaguars at Miller Electric Center on August 19, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Dustin Markland/Getty Images) | Getty Images Trevor Lawrence and the Jacksonville Jaguars’ first-team offense were surgical in the red zone on Thursday . Competing against the Carolina Panthers in a joint practice, Lawrence completed all three of his redzone attempts for touchdowns. The second-team offense had several spikes as well. Lawrence’s first score came against former teammate Devin Lloyd, who was moved out of the picture by Lawrence’s eyes as Brenton Strange used his physicality to shake off a defensive back and pop wide open. The second score was a tight-window dart between two defenders to Nate Boerkircher, and the third score was a quick-hitting in-breaker to Jakobi Meyers. The veteran wideout showcased his concentration by snatching the ball cleanly despite a tip at the line of scrimmage. There were no easy completions. If you go back and watch each clip, even the fastball to Meyers required some post-snap processing from Lawrence. Head coach Liam Coen didn’t seem surprised by the outing, which followed a strong redzone performance against the New Orleans Saints in last week’s joint practice. “I mean, I thought we were pretty good the back half of the year in the red zone. I think we finished in the top five in the NFL.” According to NFL Pro, Jacksonville ranked fourth in touchdowns (43) and yards per play (3.3) in the red zone last season. Pretty impressive, considering they also ranked 25th in rushing success rate and 31st in average target separation. “It also helps when the quarterback can run,” said Coen. “That, obviously, you don’t necessarily see in this setting. But he did scramble, right? He made a couple of off-schedule throws, and that’s what I would attribute a lot of it to, to be honest.” “When we got better in the red zone last year was when Trevor started using his legs. And we saw that again today. It’s so hard to scheme wide-open or open receivers in the red zone. It’s so much tighter. There’s less vertical grass. And especially versus a three-man, four-man rush, it’s challenging. And so, you watch around the league of the top red-zone touchdowns every week, and 90 percent of them are off schedule. They’re just, ‘Hey man, you got to buy a little time. Find a window. Somebody’s got to make a little move and boom, touchdown.’ And it’s not exactly how you draw it up, but it’s football.” Most Rushing TDs by QB since 2021: 60- Jalen Hurts 54- Josh Allen 23- Trevor Lawrence 23- Justin Fields 17- Daniel Jones 17- Kyler Murray 16- Lamar Jackson pic.twitter.com/jPBvjQVq3G — Daniel Griffis (@DanDGriffis) May 7, 2026 Jags fans, let us know your thoughts in the comments below!

title: Fantasy football 2026: Parker Washington and 5 other league-winners
summary: I had a pretty typical summer this year. Did a bit of traveling, saw some extended family. Read a book. Went to the beach. Poured a concerning number of hours into NFL preview guides, team projections, film breakdowns, and any other viable resource that would help me obliterate my closest friends in the absurd competition […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - AUGUST 3: Parker Washington #11 of the Jacksonville Jaguars practices during training camp at Miller Electric Center on August 3, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) | Getty Images I had a pretty typical summer this year. Did a bit of traveling, saw some extended family. Read a book. Went to the beach. Poured a concerning number of hours into NFL preview guides, team projections, film breakdowns, and any other viable resource that would help me obliterate my closest friends in the absurd competition that is fantasy football. You know how it goes. With my home league draft in the books, now’s the time to release some takes into the wild. Here are my top targets in fantasy football this year. Average Draft Position (ADP) consensus rankings via footballguys.com on Aug. 18 Bijan Robinson RB | Atlanta Falcons | ADP: 2 I’m taking this opportunity to call my shot that Bijan Robinson will have an Offensive Player of the Year/Madden cover athlete/all-time-productive season. Robinson has over 400 more yards from scrimmage than any NFL player since he was drafted eighth overall in 2023. The former Longhorn paces his position in targets (261), receptions (198), and receiving yards (1,738) in that span. Now, he’ll be playing with a passer in Tua Tagovailoa who’s accustomed to force-feeding running backs through the air. After the Falcons substituted Brian Robinson Jr. for Tyler Allgeier at RB2, there’s also a path to elite redzone usage. And I’d consider Kevin Stefanski — who’s bringing along renowned OL coach Bill Callahan — to be an upgrade at playcaller over Zac Robinson. Atlanta’s offensive stability may not be that of the Detroit Lions, but that can be offset by Robinson’s frame (5’ 11”, 215 lbs) compared to Jahmyr Gibbs (5’ 9”, 202 lbs). Are we really expecting the latter to see 350-plus touches in a season? From what I gather, Gibbs is the consensus top pick in fantasy drafts this year because his Lions project to score more points than Robinson’s Falcons. That’s a fair assumption to make, but should it really sway your pick? Both backs have sick skill sets, but Robinson is a more complete player with a true bellcow build. That’s a trump card worthy of winning the entire pot. With Allgeier out, plus Tagovailoa and Stefanski in, Robinson has the runway to prove that he’s one of the single best players in the league on his way to an RB1 overall finish. A.J. Brown WR | New England Patriots | ADP: 20 After emerging as one of the league’s elite offensive players in his first few years in the league, A.J. Brown is coming off consecutive “down years” of 1,000 yards and 7 touchdowns. The recently-turned-29-year-old missed five games in 2024 and another two in 2025 while dealing with a lingering hamstring injury. Anyone who watched a Philadelphia Eagles game in recent years could tell you that Brown seemed a bit disconnected from the offense and unsatisfied with his role. Did the New England Patriots trade a first-round pick for a fading star? In my studied opinion, no. I’m buying into a bounce-back from Brown. Without Jalen Hurts and Saquon Barkley dominating touches on the ground, it’s easy to see a world where Brown’s target volume spikes back up. Furthermore, I don’t think it’s silly to expect a more motivated version of the former All-Pro. He’s expecting a larger workload, reuniting with his former head coach, and not only is he playing with the best quarterback of his life in Drake Maye, but he’s also providing Maye with the best pass-catcher he’s ever had. Is it that outlandish to suggest Maye and Brown could be one of the NFL’s scariest duos of 2026? To me, the upside of a top-five QB/top-five WR pairing outweighs the risks associated with Brown’s availability and attitude. If Robinson is my top bet to become the undisputed champion of his respective position, Brown is my pick to remind the league that he’s still in the ring. Let’s not overthink “elite player goes to better situation” the way we did when Barkley was a second-round fantasy pick after joining Philly in 2024. For the record, I’ve always been a fan of Romeo Doubs (ADP: 124), so I am happy to target him at the end of fantasy drafts whenever I take a running back or Brock Bowers (ADP: 18) in the second round instead of Brown. David Montgomery RB | Houston Texans | ADP: 47 Houston’s defense is equipped to be as formidable as ever under DeMeco Ryans. If Nico Collins can stay healthy and C.J. Stroud can perform as he did in the 2025 regular season (92.9 passer rating) as opposed to his abysmal playoff performance (51.8 passer rating), the Texans should be a true title contender. After the Seattle Seahawks won Super Bowl LX with an elite WR and good-but-certainly-not-great talent at QB/RB/TE/OL, the path for Houston is seemingly there. Jaxson Smith-Njigba won OPOY due (in small part) to a run-first attack that forced defenses to load the box with bodies and play basic coverage structures. Last season, Houston’s rushing offense finished bottom-four in yards per play, first downs, touchdowns, Expected Points Added per play, and success rate. So how do they fix the problem? By trading an offensive lineman and two Day 3 picks for David Montgomery. There’s hope that continuity within the scheme and tweaking along the O-line will provide a boost as well, but really, there’s pressure on Montgomery specifically to elevate the run game. I think he’s capable of rising to the challenge. He and Houston’s offense alike may not be explosive enough to reach RB1 fantasy numbers, but that’s okay. Not every hit has to be a home run. This is as safe a pick as you can make in the “running back dead zone.” David Montgomery lost his goalline carries to Jamhyr Gibbs, so he decided to do this instead: 75 yards to the house. Beast. pic.twitter.com/MBKEsmcRaE — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) November 12, 2023 Some of my other favorite mid-round targets include Breece Hall (ADP: 31), Jaylen Waddle (ADP: 44), DJ Moore (ADP: 51), Mike Evans (ADP: 58), and anyone projected to play the majority of snaps for the Chicago Bears’ offense. Parker Washington WR | Jacksonville Jaguars | ADP: 65 One of the hottest players in fantasy football this summer is Parker Washington. A third-year pro who’s been thoroughly impressive in every offseason of his career — including this year — Washington finally emerged as an offensive contributor in 2025. He led the Jaguars across the board with 72 targets, 48 receptions, and 747 receiving yards after their Week 8 bye (including playoffs). On a per-game basis over that stretch, Washington averaged 7.2 targets, 4.8 catches, 74.7 yards, 0.5 touchdowns, and 15.8 fantasy points in PPR formats. For context, Davante Adams finished as fantasy’s WR9 last season with 15.9 PPR points per game. During that 10-game sample size to close last season, Washington ranked second among 113 wide receivers in yards per route run (2.69) and PFF receiving grade (90.8). He was also top-12 in first downs per route run (0.12), contested catch rate (75%), and passer rating when targeted (124.3). He. Was. Good. Yet he ranked 101st in route rate (92.1%). It’s hardly a guarantee that a player will continue to yield efficient results with a rise in volume. In Washington’s case, though, it feels like a bet worth making. He’s not just a scrappy competitor who’s the first guy in the building each day . He also happens to be a young playmaker who’s improved year after year, has more chemistry and experience with Trevor Lawrence than any other Jaguars wideout, and will play in an offense that has drawn some incredible fantasy numbers from its slot receiver. Washington’s relatively small stature (5’ 10”, 204 lbs) may inhibit him from being a do-it-all, ultra-productive slot receiver like Cooper Kupp and Chris Godwin were under Liam Coen. As this offseason has progressed, though, the drumbeat has grown louder and louder that “PDub” is the team’s top receiver. “I get the opportunity…

title: Chiefs fans are worried about the defensive line
summary: On Monday afternoon, Kansas City Chiefs fans of the Arrowhead Pride community were asked to vote on a poll in The Feed, answering a question about which hampered position is most worrisome at this point. Of the three positions listed, wide receiver was the choice for nearly half of those who voted. However, the comment […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - AUGUST 15: Kansas City Chiefs defensive tackle Chris Jones (95) talks with Kansas City Chiefs defensive end George Karlaftis (56) prior to the game against the Los Angeles Rams on August 15th at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by William Purnell/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images On Monday afternoon, Kansas City Chiefs fans of the Arrowhead Pride community were asked to vote on a poll in The Feed , answering a question about which hampered position is most worrisome at this point. Of the three positions listed, wide receiver was the choice for nearly half of those who voted. However, the comment section correctly called me out for leaving off the defensive line as an option. That only became a stronger point of emphasis with the news today that defensive end Ashton Gillotte ruptured his plantar fascia . Here are the concerns shared by our Arrowhead Pride users: Chiefsdodgerslakers2415 answer is definitely just DE for me. Pretty surprising it isn’t listed as an option. RamX21 None of them worry me da’Monk D. None of the above. How is it possible that DL is not on this list? We, currently, have Jones and Tonga as DT. ONL is on the PUP list and Peter Woods is, seemingly, hobbled up right now, too. Who else do we have? To call this a non-worrisome unit seems to be…..off. MajikDad How is DE not on here? That’s gotta be concern #1. I actually really like R Mason but it feels like we’re 1 steady starter off here. Even if EO regains some form (welcome back!) it feels lackluster RoyalsFanBill How about D line, how did you not make that a choice? title: Chiefs roster 2026: Nohl Williams, Alohi Gilman, and Cyrus Allen are underrated
summary: The thing about sports dynasties is that they always come to an end. The Kansas City Chiefs were as good and as compelling as any NFL team ever has been from 2018-2024, when they sported a 90-26 regular season record and a .776 win percentage — by far the NFL’s best; the Baltimore Ravens ranked […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - AUGUST 15: Wide receiver Cyrus Allen #13 of the Kansas City Chiefs catches a second quarter pass over linebacker Nikhai Hill-Green #54 of the Los Angeles Rams during an NFL preseason game at Arrowhead Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images The thing about sports dynasties is that they always come to an end. The Kansas City Chiefs were as good and as compelling as any NFL team ever has been from 2018-2024, when they sported a 90-26 regular season record and a .776 win percentage — by far the NFL’s best; the Baltimore Ravens ranked second in that time with a 78-38 record and a .672 win percentage. They appeared in four Super Bowls, winning three in five seasons from 2019-2023, they never finished a season with a lower result than an AFC Championship game loss, and they put Kansas City on the map as a championship town as it had never been before. 2025’s 6-11 relative faceplant told us a lot about the future of the Chiefs franchise. Primarily that if there’s to be another Chiefs dynasty soon, it will look markedly different than the one before. Yes, GM Brett Veach, head coach Andy Reid, defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo, and that Patrick Mahomes guy are still in place, but so much has changed around them. Trent McDuffie, Jaylen Watson, Bryan Cook, Leo Chenal, Marquise Brown, Jawaan Taylor, Charles Omenihu, Isiah Pacheco, Derrick Nnadi, and Michael Danna are among the veterans of import, starters or not, who walked out the door via trade or free agency this offseason. Travis Kelce is heading into his 14th NFL season, and Mahomes is heading into his 10th, believe it or not. So, any new Chiefs dynasty will need to be done with a lot of different names and faces. That will be true not only of the new stars, but the guys whose names have not caught up in terms of national recognition to what they can accomplish on the field. To that end, I’ve identified three Hidden Gems for the 2026 Chiefs — one underrated veteran, one underrated free agent and one underrated draft pick. Underrated veteran: CB Nohl Williams Losing McDuffie and Watson to the Rams via trade and free agency, respectively, were two big hits to a Chiefs defense that ranked 16th in DVOA in 2025 — down from 12th in 2024, and seventh in 2023 A few years ago, as that defense was being built, Spags told me that he had never coached a defense with so many young players who had so much on the ball. Now, it’ll be up to Spags to bring the thing together similarly with different guys. One 2025 rookie who stood out was Cal cornerback Nohl Williams, and that one was relatively easy to predict from a schematic perspective. Throughout his time as the Chiefs’ DC, which goes back to the 2019 season, Spags has always called the NFL’s highest rate of plays in which at least one of his cornerbacks were in press coverage. It happened again last season — the Chiefs had no cornerbacks in press coverage on just 13% of their snaps per Pro Football Focus; the Chicago Bears ranked second with 24%. Enter Nohl Williams, the 2025 third-round pick out of Cal. Last season in 458 total snaps and 272 coverage reps, Williams allowed 19 catches on 35 targets for 223 yards, one touchdown, no interceptions, eight pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 83.4. But when he was targeted in press coverage, Williams allowed just 17 catches on 33 targets for 108 yards, seven of those eight pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 58.7. . @Chiefs CB Nohl Williams in 2025 and 2026. Nobody calls more press coverage from year to year than Spags, so watch out for this guy. pic.twitter.com/ZMgc1Sjh5X — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 17, 2026 If you saw Williams’ college tape before he was drafted, this would come as no surprise. The Chiefs had at least one cornerback in press coverage last season on 88% of their snaps. Nohl Williams is a brilliant fit from Day 1. https://t.co/uRWIpRetAz — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) April 26, 2025 Now, with McDuffie and Watson gone, it will be up to Williams and first-round pick Mansoor Delane (who allowed a 0.0 opponent passer rating when in man coverage last season for LSU) to take the reins. Even the quarterback has noticed Williams’ improvement in moving from Year 1 to Year 2. “I think Nohl Williams kind of is the first one in my mind,” Mahomes said on August 8, when asked which of the rookies and second-year guys have shown the most improvement. “I knew how talented he is, but you can tell when the guy starts to get it, starts to figure out formations, figure out motions and know where to put himself at to make it easier on himself. So, he’s someone that’s kind of been big.” Well, he’ll need to be. Underrated free agent: Safety Alohi Gilman It’s not just McDuffie and Watson that the Chiefs are replacing from their 2025 secondary — there’s also safety Bryan Cook, who signed a three-year, $40.25 million contract with the Cincinnati Bengals. To replace Cook, the Chiefs signed former Los Angeles Chargers and Baltimore Ravens safety Alohi Gilman to a three-year, $24 million contract with $14.5 million guaranteed. Last season for both the Ravens and Chargers — he was traded from L.A. to Baltimore for edge-rusher Odafe Oweh on October 7 — the 5’10”, 201-pound Gilman allowed 27 catches on 41 targets for 403 yards, 225 yards after the catch, one touchdown, no interceptions, eight pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 114.2. He also had 61 solo tackles, 17 stops, one tackle for loss, one forced fumble, and two quarterback pressures in 11 pass-rushing reps. Gilman had at least 100 snaps last season in the slot, the box, and the deep third, and as he’s heading into his seventh NFL season, he brings experience to a younger secondary, and a safety duo alongside Chamarri Conner. “Obviously a lot of respect for Spags, and what he’s been able to do in his career,” Gilman said in May, when asked how he’s adjusting to what Spagnuolo does. “I think just the amount of layers that he’s had over the long career, and the depth and the way that’s he’s able to put together his scheme is probably the biggest adjustment. A lot of different little nuances. Whether its preference or scheme, stuff that he’s been able to put together throughout the years. I would say more just the depth of it. I’ve seen pretty much a lot of different – most of the coverages since I’ve been in the league. But just the depth and the detail is definitely the biggest adjustment, and it makes it fun for me.” Gilman can handle the depth and detail. New @Chiefs safety Alohi Gilman with the Chargers and Ravens last season. For some reason, I kept thinking of Greg Kihn's "The Breakup Song" when watching Gilman in coverage. pic.twitter.com/zbQhbfEKQg — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 17, 2026 Underrated draft pick: WR Cyrus Allen The Chiefs’ receiver room is… well, what it is. Xavier Worthy, Rashee Rice, and Tyquan Thornton are the projected top three starters, but clearly the guy to watch is Cincinnati’s Cyrus Allen, who the Chiefs took with the 176th pick in the fifth round. Why the 5’11”, 183-pound Allen lasted as long as he did in the draft after a 2025 season in which he had 51 catches, 674 yards, and 13 touchdowns last season is best left to the vagaries of time, but safe to say that the Chiefs are already pretty happy with that particular bargain. Since he arrived in KC, Allen has done everything possible to validate the idea that he’s worth much more to his new team. Just got to Cincinnati receiver Cyrus Allen in my process, and me likey. We talk a lot about traits with receivers, but one really important trait is the ability to get open over and over with an understanding of the nuances of the position. Allen has it. pic.twitter.com/xdX0jYA1ZD — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) March 19, 2026 As he showed in the Chiefs’ preseason opener against the Los Angeles Rams last Saturday, it isn’t taking long for Allen to get…

title: Latest Chiefs injury update includes Ashton Gillotte rupturing his plantar fascia
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs finished training camp at Missouri Western State at St. Joe on Thursday morning with a light practice ahead of preseason Week 2. Head coach Andy Reid met with local media after practice, providing a status update ahead of the road exhibition against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers that kicks off at 6:30 […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - AUGUST 15: Defensive end Ashton Gillotte #97 of the Kansas City Chiefs talks with teammates on the team bench during the fourth quarter of an NFL preseason game against the Los Angeles Rams at Arrowhead Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs finished training camp at Missouri Western State at St. Joe on Thursday morning with a light practice ahead of preseason Week 2. Head coach Andy Reid met with local media after practice, providing a status update ahead of the road exhibition against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers that kicks off at 6:30 p.m. on Saturday evening. Chiefs Kingdom will have to wait at least another week to see star quarterback Patrick Mahomes. Reid revealed that Justin Fields would start again on Saturday, then shared the schedule for backup quarterbacks Garrett Nussmeier and Chris Oladokun. “The way the quarterbacks will play this week,” Reid began. “We’ll go a quarter and a half with Justin, a quarter and a half with Garrett and Chris will take the fourth quarter. It will be somewhere in that area, don’t hold me to the play on that. That’s a rough itinerary, and the rest of the guys will follow that schedule.” When asked if there was a possibility of Mahomes playing in the preseason Week 3 game against the Seattle Seahawks, Reid jabbed ESPN’s Nate Taylor with a joke before kicking that can down the road. “We’ll see how it goes,” Reid said. “We’ll see.” Injury update Reid shared the status of a handful of Chiefs injuries during his press conference, with one note about defensive end Ashton Gillotte standing out above all. “Gillotte has a plantar fascia that ruptured,” Reid said nonchalantly. “He won’t play.” In their initial evaluation, the Chiefs are optimistic that Ashton Gillotte, who ruptured his plantar fascia, could return in about 3 weeks. If his rehab goes well, Gillotte would have a chance to be available Sept. 14 to play on opening night against the Broncos. — Nate Taylor (@ByNateTaylor) August 20, 2026 During the 2015 NFL season, Denver Broncos quarterback Peyton Manning partially tore plantar fascia in his left foot. That was revealed after an all-time bad performance from the Hall of Fame quarterback against the Chiefs: Kansas City nabbed four interceptions in a 29-13 win. Manning had battled a plantar fasciitis injury for weeks, but aggravated it before the matchup with Kansas City. Reportedly, he had difficulty walking, although ESPN’s report from that situation says a partial tear is more painful to play with than a complete tear. That sounds like a severe injury for a defensive lineman, although there are still over three weeks until the Week 1 game. Reid has not made any injury — including starting right guard Trey Smith’s hip issue — out to be a serious problem. “These aren’t extended injuries; they’ll be back,” Reid said later in his press conference. “Just nicks-and-bruises type things. They’re working through them and back going.” Other injury notes Reid said that veteran linebacker Jack Cochrane and safety Chamarri Conner tried to practice on Thursday, but the team backed off; neither will be available for Saturday’s preseason game. The head coach also revealed that starting left tackle Josh Simmons (Back) and Trey Smith (Hip) will not suit up for Saturday’s game. Reid again said Smith has been “making progress.” Rookie, undrafted wide receiver Jeff Caldwell hyperextended his knee in practice this week and will not play on Saturday. Wide receiver Jimmy Holiday will not play either; he has not practiced in over a week.

summary: On Thursday morning, the Kansas City Chiefs released one backup offensive lineman to sign another. Offensive tackle Matt Waletzko was waived with an injury designation, making room for an offensive lineman who was most recently in the United Football League (UFL). According to Mike Garafolo of NFL Network, the Chiefs have signed offensive lineman Kellen […]
full_text: LOUISVILLE, KENTUCKY - MAY 16: Kellen Diesch #74 of the Louisville Kings looks on prior to a UFL football game against the DC Defenders at Lynn Family Stadium on May 16, 2026 in Louisville, Kentucky. (Photo by Jeff Dean/UFL/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Thursday morning, the Kansas City Chiefs released one backup offensive lineman to sign another. Offensive tackle Matt Waletzko was waived with an injury designation, making room for an offensive lineman who was most recently in the United Football League (UFL). We have waived T Matt Waletzko with an injury designation. We have signed Free Agent T Kellen Diesch. pic.twitter.com/Iil2up7gEn — Kansas City Chiefs (@Chiefs) August 20, 2026 According to Mike Garafolo of NFL Network, the Chiefs have signed offensive lineman Kellen Diesch. He is 28 years old and listed at 6 feet 7 inches tall and 303 pounds in his UFL player bio, which lists him as a tackle. After playing five years of college football between Texas A&M and Arizona State, Diesch was invited to the 2022 NFL Scouting Combine and posted impressive results in his athletic tests. 40-yard dash: 4.89 seconds (97th percentile) 10-yard dash: 1.7 seconds (94th percentile) Vertical jump: 32 1/2 inches (90th percentile) 20-yard shuttle: 4.43 seconds (95th percentile) Diesch was an undrafted free agent following that year’s draft and signed with the Miami Dolphins . He was placed on the Chicago Bears ’ practice squad after he didn’t make it through Miami’s cutdown day and made a few other NFL stops, but never took a regular-season snap. He has played for three teams in the UFL over the 2025 and 2026 seasons, which take place in the spring. This past season, Diesch played 130 snaps at left tackle, 14 snaps at left guard, 66 snaps at right guard, and 64 snaps at right tackle, according to Pro Football Focus . Diesch will be looked upon to fill a role on the third-team offensive line after Waletzko’s injury left the position group thin; starting left tackle Josh Simmons ran with the third team the other day before popping up on the injury report with a back designation. Chiefs have signed OT Kellen Diesch, one of two tackles they had in for a tryout Wednesday. He’s wearing No. 74. title: The Chiefs have plans to create salary cap space if needed
summary: As training camp breaks and the Kansas City Chiefs begin eyeing the regular-season opener against the Denver Broncos on September 14, the team finds itself in the familiar position of being tight against the NFL’s salary cap. At Arrowhead Pride, we estimate that Kansas City is currently about $4.1 million under the limit. However, most of that cushion will […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - JUNE 08: A detail view of the Kansas City Chiefs logo on a helmet on set during a production shoot at The University of Kansas Health System Training Complex on June 08, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images) | Getty Images As training camp breaks and the Kansas City Chiefs begin eyeing the regular-season opener against the Denver Broncos on September 14, the team finds itself in the familiar position of being tight against the NFL’s salary cap. At Arrowhead Pride , we estimate that Kansas City is currently about $4.1 million under the limit. However, most of that cushion will disappear after the roster is finalized on August 30. At that point, the team will need to account for all 53 active-roster salaries, as well as any players who open the season on injury lists. Speaking after the penultimate training camp practice at Missouri Western State University, Chiefs assistant general manager Chris Shea seemed unconcerned about the team’s finances. Shea is widely considered the front office’s cap guru. He believes he is on the same page about cap management and player acquisition with team Chairman and CEO Clark Hunt, general manager Brett Veach and head coach Andy Reid. “We feel good about where we’re at,” remarked Shea. “Obviously, the rules change a little bit when the season starts. Certain things come onto the cap that aren’t there now. We have a plan to create ample space for us to be able to operate with those charges that come on and create some flexibility. We have lots of avenues to create more flexibility and more cap space. We may take advantage of some or all in the next few weeks, but we certainly have the ability and likely will create some cap space to get us into the regular season.” As teams trim their rosters in less than two weeks, that cap room could be needed to pursue surprising players who become available. Every year, Shea finds himself surprised by some of the players who do not make other teams. “Having done this for a long time, I think more than you’d think,” he confirmed. “So, retaining flexibility to be able to entertain the unforeseen is an important aspect of how we try to structure our cap management philosophy. We really want to present Coach and Brett with the flexibility to entertain smart roster moves that are independent of cap constraints that we may have. “We certainly have some of them, but we don’t have a perfect crystal ball — none of us in the front office — and opportunities present themselves that are unforeseen. So, we plan to be flexible. There are limits to that given that we have a lot of good players under contract, but we try to present Brett and Coach with opportunities through our cap management.” For the foreseeable future, Shea knows he will be working around quarterback Patrick Mahomes’ record-setting new contract. In June, Mahomes and the Chiefs agreed to an extension that will pay him over a half billion dollars through 2033. The eye-popping numbers come with the territory of having the league’s best quarterback. The contract already being in place will also help the front office plan future moves. “I think as Clark and Coach and Brett alluded to when we did the contract extension in June,” Shea explained, “he’s an elite player and an even better person. We were delighted to be able to, once again, extend him here, and we have a special relationship with him. Obviously, he is the highest-paid player in the league. He’s earned that, and we have a plan to manage around it. The fact that we have certainty around the quarterback allows us to plan how to allocate the rest of our resources in a way that gives us a lot of stability and ability to predict how we can move in the future.” The Chiefs opened the offseason with a surprising contract structure for veteran tight end Travis Kelce. Kelce will make about $13.4 million in his 14th — and expected final — season. The bulk of that will come from a $10.7 million signing bonus, likely split between the 2027 and 2028 salary caps. Kelce will play with a 2027 cap number of under $5 million. However, he will likely leave behind dead money charges of about $3.6 million in each of the next two seasons. While teams like the Philadelphia Eagles have made similar contract structures almost routine in personnel signings, expect the Chiefs to treat Kelce’s effective void years as a unique situation to accommodate a franchise great. “Different teams have different philosophies about how to structure contracts,” Shea added, “and generally we’ve been a team that has pretty simple, straightforward deals. In Travis’s case — with him wanting to come back and we’re delighted that he did — we used some tools that are in the toolbox that maybe we don’t dust off very often to be able to spread his cap hits over multiple years. And Clark Hunt was allowing us to do that in this special instance with his special legacy and role on the team. Any time that you spread cap hits out into the future years, you’re kind of borrowing [like] using a credit card. So, we don’t do a lot of that, but, with Travis [and] with him wanting to come back, we used some things that we wouldn’t normally otherwise think about.”

title: Chiefs News: It’s the final day of this year’s training camp in St. Joe
summary: The latest On Thursday, the Kansas City Chiefs will practice on the grass fields at Missouri Western State University in St. Joe for the 18th and final time of the 2026 preseason. At the end of Thursday’s session, the team will pack up and head to Tampa, Florida, for a Preseason Week 2 matchup with […]
full_text: ST JOSEPH, MISSOURI - JULY 26: Quarterbacks Garrett Nussmeier #14, Chris Oladokun #19, Patrick Mahomes #15 and Justin Fields #6 participate during Kansas City Chiefs Training Camp at Missouri Western State University on July 25, 2026 in St Joseph, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images The latest On Thursday, the Kansas City Chiefs will practice on the grass fields at Missouri Western State University in St. Joe for the 18th and final time of the 2026 preseason. At the end of Thursday’s session, the team will pack up and head to Tampa, Florida, for a Preseason Week 2 matchup with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Saturday at 6:30 p.m. Next week, the team will practice at its facility in Kansas City, awaiting the season opener on September 14th. Five Observations from Wednesday’s Practice | Chiefs Training Camp 8/19 | The Mothership 5. Here’s a look at Wednesday’s injury report. Offensive tackle Josh Simmons (back), offensive guard Trey Smith (hip), offensive tackle Matt Waletzko (knee), linebacker Jack Cochrane (knee), wide receiver Jimmy Holiday (groin), defensive end Ashton Gillotte (foot) and wide receiver Jeff Weimer (hamstring) didn’t practice for the Chiefs on Wednesday. Wide receiver Jeff Caldwell (knee) left early. Defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott (knee) remains on the “Physically Unable to Perform” list (PUP) and did not participate in Wednesday’s practice, either. 5 observations from Day 17 of Chiefs camp: Cyrus Allen’s latest highlight catch | The Kansas City Star The play of the day likely came on one-on-ones, with Allen making a one-handed catch to beat Delane despite close coverage. “I think Cyrus has come in and he’s taken the coaching,” receivers coach Chad O’Shea said. “He’s done a great job of working extremely hard and trying to concentrate on the things that we’ve asked him to do.” Kansas City Chiefs host three players for tryouts at training camp on Wednesday, including two offensive linemen | A to Z Sports Chiefs host offensive linemen John Campbell and Kellen Diesch for tryouts The two players the Chiefs hosted suggest there might be bad news about Matt Waletzko’s knee injury. John Campbell and Kellen Diesch each have experience playing tackle, but the flexibility to play inside. They fit that similar mold as Waletzko. Campbell could help extend the UFL-to-NFL pipeline. He played college football at Miami and Tennessee. The 6-foot-5 and 309-pound tackle played 43 games with 27 career starts in college. His final season at Tennessee saw him play the right tackle position. He went undrafted in 2025 and didn’t catch on with an NFL club. However, he found his spot in the UFL. In 2026, he won a UFL title with the Louisville Kings after defeating the DC Defenders 27-20 in the United Bowl. Chiefs’ Travis Kelce Welcomes Special Guest on Final Day of Training Camp | Heavy Sports “Listen, I think Jason’s great,” Chiefs DC Steve Spagnuolo said after practice. “He and I talk a lot about the, you know, coordinator/center battle when we used to go against each other, and he’s great. He’s into it.” “I remember that one. He did this. I said, I remember when he got us on that one,” Spagnuolo continued, recalling a time when Kelce got the better of his defense. “I’m a big fan. He lives out there outside of Philadelphia, and we go back there a lot. I had a chance to play golf with him this summer, and I look forward to maybe doing that again sometime. They’re just good people, those Kelces, right? How can you not want to be around them?” Chiefs finally have a losing season advantage they can actually use | Arrowhead Addict Chiefs assistant general manager Mike Bradway spoke to reporters on Wednesday from St. Joseph and opened up about the new perch from which the Chiefs can claim players. He said the team’s evaluative process is already in place, but there are benefits to sitting at No. 9 for once. “I don’t think it’s going to change the process itself, so to speak, I think we’re still going to go about it the way we do in terms of watching as many bubble guys as we can, talking to teams, getting as much information as we can,” said Bradway. Around the NFL Colts TE Tyler Warren injures groin in practice | ESPN Indianapolis Colts star tight end Tyler Warren sustained a groin injury in Wednesday’s joint practice with the Atlanta Falcons and did not return, adding another injury question within the team’s group of pass catchers. The Colts have already been navigating practices without top wide receiver Alec Pierce, still sidelined after undergoing offseason ankle surgery. Now, they might be without their most targeted pass catcher from a season ago, when Warren caught 76 passes as a rookie. Texans WR Jayden Higgins {Torn ACL) Out for 2026 season | NFL.com Jayden Higgins suffered a torn ACL in Tuesday’s joint practice with the Las Vegas Raiders, NFL Network Insider Ian Rapoport reported on Wednesday, per sources. The second-year wideout will miss the 2026 season. The No. 34 overall pick of the 2025 NFL Draft, Higgins caught 41 passes for 525 yards and six touchdowns as a rookie, finding himself in an elevated role following Tank Dell’s season-ending injury suffered late in the 2024 campaign. Bucs, veteran DT Vita Vea agree to 1-year contract extension: Source | The Athletic The Tampa Bay Buccaneers have agreed to a one-year contract extension with defensive tackle Vita Vea, a team source told The Athletic . The deal is worth $30 million, with $6 million applied to this season, the source said on condition of anonymity because they aren’t authorized to reveal the terms of the contract. With the agreement, Vea is tied to Tampa Bay through the 2027 season and is slated to make $24 million both this season and next. title: Chargers-49ers Game Recap: Niners throttle Bolts 41-17
summary: The Chargers may have dominated the 49ers during Tuesday’s joint practice, but that was far from the case when both teams took the field Thursday night. After building up the excitement to watch Justin Herbert inside SoFi Stadium during the month of August, all we got was a quick three-and-out before the starters bowed out. […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 20: Trey Lance #5 of the Los Angeles Chargers throws a pass against the San Francisco 49ers during the second quarter in a preseason game at SoFi Stadium on August 20, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chargers may have dominated the 49ers during Tuesday’s joint practice, but that was far from the case when both teams took the field Thursday night. After building up the excitement to watch Justin Herbert inside SoFi Stadium during the month of August, all we got was a quick three-and-out before the starters bowed out. From there, things did not get much more exciting. The Chargers looked undisciplined, and unmotivated, for most of the night. The offense was plagued with numerous procedural penalties, half of which erased some of the team’s best plays of the game. Running the ball seemed like the world’s tallest task against the Niners, as well. At one point, the Chargers running backs had three net rushing yards on 10 total carries in the third quarter. All night, defenders were shooting through gaps before any back could manage to cut north and south. It wasn’t much different for the defense who all but vanished in the third quarter, as well. Allowing 40+ points in the preseason should be a difficult task, but it looked far too easy for the 49ers. The Bolts ultimately fell 41-17 in a game that they’ll have to watch and stomach in order to see just how the entire operation fell apart. That also includes special teams which allowed an 83-yard punt return for a score. The Chargers are back in SoFi Stadium as the away team against the Rams next Thursday. Kickoff is scheduled for 7:00 p.m. PST. First Quarter The Chargers won the toss and chose to receive. Justin Herbert and Co. was up first. On first down, Omarion Hampton received a sweep to the right but tight end David Njoku was beat to the outside and it resulted in a one-yard loss. The next play, Herbert found another tight end in Charlie Kolar for a gain of nine to bring up third-and-two. Herbert faked a handoff on third down before firing left to Ladd McConkey but he was covered well and the ball fell incomplete. The 49ers offense led by Brock Purdy saw a bit more success on their opening drive. Purdy found rookie De’Zhaun Stribling several times for first down receptions and rookie back Kaelon Black ran hard enough to move the chains early, as well. The Chargers defense clamped down a bit near midfield and ultimately forced a punt that bounced into the end zone. Unfortunately, when Jim Harbaugh said that the starters would only have one series in the game, that was the truth. Despite going a quick three-and-out to begin the game, Herbert was taken out for Trey Lance who managed to move the chains once with a short throw to running back Keaton Mitchell. Overallthe offense went 26 yards in six plays before punting back to San Francisco. Second Quarter After going 56 yards in 10 plays to close out the first quarter, the Niners began the second period with a successful 48-yard field goal by Eddy Piniero. Both teams combined for four punts through the early portion of the quarter. The Chargers were the first to finally break the short stalemate as Lance broke off a 37-yard run to get the offense to the Niners six-yard line. Unfortunately that’s where the excitement ended as Lance could only muster a two-yard completion to Scott Matlock over the next three plays before Cameron Dicker came on to tie the game 3-3 with a 21-yard kick. The Niners offense got their biggest play of the day with a 37-yard run by Sincere McCormick. After an illegal shift penalty, McCormick bowled over three Chargers defenders and into the end zone from seven yards out to give the Niners a 10-3 lead. Los Angeles went three-and-out once again on their next drive before allowing an 83-yard punt return for a touchdown by wideout Jacob Cowing. That special teams score pushed their lead to 17-3 with a little over three minutes remaining in the half. Just before the break, quarterback Mac Jones brought the Niners into field goal range with a 20-yard pass over the middle to receiver KhaDarel Hodge. A seven yard completion to Cowing three plays later set them up at the LA 27 where Piniero was good from 45 yards out as time expired. Third Quarter The Chargers started strong out of halftime as they forced a three-and-out after Adrian Martinez took over for quarterback for the 49ers. D.J. Uiagalelei took over for Lance to start the second half and he wasted no time in finding Oronde Gadsden II for a 16-yard gain to move the chains. However, that play was followed by a pair of incompletions and a run for a one-yard loss which led to another punt. On the second play of the ensuing Niners drive, Martinez was pressured by Nadame Tucker who burst untouched through the line. The pressure forced Martinez to get the ball out quick but he ended up throwing it right into the arms of linebacker Junior Colson who returned it untouched for a touchdown. Martinez and the 49ers offense finally shook off their slow start to the half to put together a lengthy 14-play,74-yard touchdown drive aided by a defensive holding flag in the end zone by the Chargers. Following what looked like a turnover on downs in the red zone by the Bolts defense, Avery Smith was flagged and the Niners scored on the very next play on a two-yard run by Khalil Herbert. Fourth Quarter Martinez ran it in himself to cap off a 30-yard drive after the Niners forced a turnover on downs inside Chargers territory. A Devonte Ross fumble on the ensuing kickoff once again set up San Francisco with great field position and Martinez found wideout Jordan Watkins for a 17-yard score two plays later. The Chargers punted two more times before making their first splash play in some time with an interception off Martinez by rookie defensive back Devin Grant. Just before regulation ticked away, Uiagalelei found UDFA tight end Jerand Bradley wide open up the left sideline for a big gain. However, the 49ers never touched him down and he managed to find his feet and trot into the end zone for a score. Tight end Evan Svoboda caught a two-point conversion to make the final score of 41-17.

title: Who are the most clutch players in Super Bowl history?
summary: Winning a Super Bowl does not automatically make a player “clutch.” Some players have won multiple championships without producing particularly memorable performances on the biggest stage, while others have delivered extraordinary numbers, game-winning plays and fourth-quarter performances that changed Super Bowl history. To identify the 15 most clutch players in Super Bowl history, the emphasis […]
full_text: Winning a Super Bowl does not automatically make a player “clutch.” Some players have won multiple championships without producing particularly memorable performances on the biggest stage, while others have delivered extraordinary numbers, game-winning plays and fourth-quarter performances that changed Super Bowl history. To identify the 15 most clutch players in Super Bowl history , the emphasis here is on what actually happened inside the Super Bowl: late-game production, efficiency, touchdowns, yards, turnovers, game-winning scores, record-setting performances and performances under extreme pressure. This is not simply a list of players with the most rings. 1. Tom Brady — QB Brady is the obvious starting point, but the statistical case goes well beyond his seven championships. He owns Super Bowl records for passing yards (3,039), completions (277), attempts (432) and touchdown passes (21). He also owns the single-game Super Bowl passing record with 505 yards in Super Bowl LII and threw for 466 yards during the Patriots’ historic comeback in Super Bowl LI. His Super Bowl LI performance may be the ultimate definition of clutch: Brady completed 26 of 33 passes for 284 yards and two touchdowns during New England’s five possessions from the middle of the third quarter through the winning touchdown. 2. Joe Montana — QB Montana’s Super Bowl résumé is almost impossible to match for efficiency. In four Super Bowls, he completed 83 of 122 passes for 1,142 yards, 11 touchdowns and zero interceptions, producing a 127.8 passer rating. His 9.02% touchdown rate and 0.00% interception rate are remarkable over that many attempts. 3. Patrick Mahomes — QB Mahomes has already established himself as one of the greatest pressure performers in Super Bowl history. Even though he has lost two of five Super Bowls and has some statistical flaws, he has led comebacks in the fourth quarter or overtime in all three of his wins. His back-to-back Super Bowl MVP performances in LVII and LVIII included a combined 515 passing yards and five touchdowns. Kevin Harlan's call of Patrick Mahomes' game-winning touchdown pass to Mecole Hardman to win the Super Bowl. Fantastic. pic.twitter.com/wdYlgxPmtY — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) February 13, 2024 4. Jerry Rice — WR Rice is the greatest Super Bowl receiver statistically. He owns the career records for 33 receptions, 589 receiving yards and eight touchdown receptions. His 48 Super Bowl points are also a record. That combination of volume and scoring production makes Rice arguably the greatest non-quarterback clutch performer in Super Bowl history. 5. Eli Manning — QB Manning’s career Super Bowl statistics are excellent: 49-of-74 passing for 551 yards, three touchdowns and one interception across two appearances. But the numbers become even more impressive when considering the quality of the opponents. Manning defeated Tom Brady and the Patriots twice, including a 2011 performance in which he threw the game-winning touchdown with just over a minute remaining. 6. Adam Vinatieri — K If “clutch” means delivering when the game is literally on the line, Vinatieri deserves to be near the top. He made seven Super Bowl field goals, tied for the career record through 2019, and twice kicked game-winning field goals for New England. Super Bowl XXXVIII Patriots 32 / Panthers 29 Adam Vinatieri kicks a 41-yard FG with 4 seconds left to give the Patriots their 2nd Super Bowl win in 3 years pic.twitter.com/TN7yrWMAZG — Rose (@UnknownModeX) February 12, 2023 7. David Tyree — WR Tyree’s helmet catch is arguably the greatest catch in Super Bowl history…right alongside player player #8 on this list. Tyree didn’t have the statistical volume but his clutch moment helped the Giants capture their 2007 championship. The iconic David Tyree helmet catch 🤯 pic.twitter.com/xY29IdCgE8 https://t.co/mTTCpdTR80 — Nosebleed Baseball (@Baseball_NBS) January 20, 2026 8. Julian Edelman — WR Edelman produced 24 career Super Bowl receptions for 337 yards, including 10 catches for 141 yards in Super Bowl LIII, when he won MVP. His defining clutch moment, however, came in Super Bowl LI when his improbable fourth-quarter catch kept the Patriots’ comeback alive. The Julian Edelman catch Patriots fans will NEVER forget😳🔥 pic.twitter.com/zjwqvH11S1 — PFF (@PFF) April 12, 2021 9. Terry Bradshaw — QB Bradshaw’s four Super Bowls produced 932 passing yards and nine touchdowns. His 112.8 career Super Bowl passer rating ranks among the best quarterbacks with significant Super Bowl volume. His four-touchdown performance in Super Bowl XIII remains one of the most impressive quarterback displays in championship-game history. 10. Kurt Warner — QB Warner threw for 1,156 yards and six touchdowns in three Super Bowls. His 73-yard touchdown pass in the final two minutes against Tennessee is one of the most famous late-game scoring moments in Super Bowl history. Warner only delivered 1 championship in his 3 trips to the big game but Warner is known for racking up 414, 365, and 377 passing yards in each game he played. 11. James Harrison — LB Harrison’s Super Bowl XLIII performance remains one of the greatest defensive plays in NFL history. He returned an interception 100 yards for a touchdown at the end of the first half, giving Pittsburgh a crucial 17-7 lead. When James Harrison returned an interception 100 yards for a touchdown against the Cardinals in Super Bowl XLIII. (Video: @BackThenFB ) pic.twitter.com/qqMYnppYm8 — Kalshi Football (@KalshiFB) July 17, 2026 12. Malcolm Butler — CB Butler played only one Super Bowl in a starring role, but what a role it was. His interception of Russell Wilson at the goal line with Seattle threatening to score ended Super Bowl XLIX and preserved New England’s 28-24 victory. It is difficult to construct a more literal definition of a clutch defensive play. Has to be done 👀 @Patriots vs @Seahawks calls for one thing… THAT Malcolm Butler interception. Legendary. pic.twitter.com/OBvUY88M5u — NFL UK & Ireland (@NFLUKIRE) September 20, 2020 13. Von Miller — LB Miller dominated Super Bowl 50, recording 2.5 sacks, six tackles and a forced fumble while winning MVP. Miller also helped bring a championship to Los Angeles; registering 2.0 sacks as the Rams defense suffocated Joe Burrow and the Bengals in the second half. 14. Cooper Kupp — WR Kupp’s Super Bowl résumé consists of one game, but his Super Bowl LVI performance was outstanding: eight catches, 92 yards and two touchdowns, including the game-winning touchdown with less than two minutes remaining. He was named Super Bowl 56 MVP. Matthew Stafford really threw a no-look pass on the game-winning drive in the Super Bowl. Cooper Kupp: “That was probably the best no-looker of his life. I saw the lane and he fit it right in there.” So gutsy and so awesome. pic.twitter.com/lRVGgAvyzk — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) February 14, 2022 On the Rams final drive, everyone knew the ball was going to Cooper Kupp. And there was nothing the Bengals could do to stop him. 15. Terry Bradshaw, QB Terry Bradshaw belongs among the most clutch Super Bowl performers in NFL history because his production consistently rose on the biggest stage. In four Super Bowl victories, Bradshaw threw for 932 yards and nine touchdowns. He was named Super Bowl MVP twice, including after throwing for 318 yards and four touchdowns in Pittsburgh’s 35-31 victory over Dallas in Super Bowl XIII. Bradshaw’s ability to make explosive plays and deliver in championship moments helped establish the Steelers as the NFL’s dynasty of the 1970s.
