title: Eagles News: Lane Johnson says Philadelphia could see 2024 Saquon Barkley in 2026
summary: Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Eagles’ Lane Johnson on Barkley: ‘We’ll see the Saquon from two years ago’ – NFL.comLane Johnson sees Sean Mannion’s offense getting Saquon Barkley back to his explosive ways. Speaking Wednesday from joint practice with the New England Patriots, the star right tackle gushed about how […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JULY 30: Saquon Barkley #26 of the Philadelphia Eagles smiles during training camp at Jefferson Health Training Complex on July 30, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Eagles’ Lane Johnson on Barkley: ‘We’ll see the Saquon from two years ago’ – NFL.com Lane Johnson sees Sean Mannion’s offense getting Saquon Barkley back to his explosive ways. Speaking Wednesday from joint practice with the New England Patriots, the star right tackle gushed about how the wide run plays will fit Barkley’s ability. Johnson also noted that the Eagles will find more ways to get the RB the ball. “The more productive we are in the run game and stuff feeds off that, we’ll see the Saquon from two years ago,” Johnson said, via Zach Berman of The Athletic . “We’ll see the big plays, we’ll see him flex wide at wide receiver, we’ll see him in the screen game.” Will Saquon Barkley become a receiving threat in 2026? It may finally happen – NBCSP Seems like every summer we talk about how this is the year the Eagles are finally going to start throwing to the backs. And every year they don’t. The Eagles have never had a running back with 300 receiving yards in a season under Nick Sirianni. Their last 300-yard receiving back was Miles Sanders with 509 yards back in 2019, and along with the Rams they’re one of just two NFL teams without a 300-yard receiving back since 2021. But they’ve spent a lot of time working on the passing game with the backs this summer, and on Day 1 of joint practices with the Patriots outside Gillette Stadium, the Eagles spent a good chunk of the day working on the running game with Saquon Barkley and getting Barkley and the other backs involved in the passing game. “The more productive we are in the run game, stuff feeds off of that,” Lane Johnson said after practice. “We’ll see the big plays, we’ll see (Saquon) flex out at wide receiver, we’ll see him in the screen game. So we saw just a little bit of it today.” Barkley has quietly enjoyed a strong training camp as the Eagles transition to an outside zone running scheme that should help him get back to his Offensive Player of the Year form of 2024. Eagles-Patriots Joint Training Camp Practice Notes: Day 1 – BGN OVERALL PERFORMANCE: The Pats looked like the better team in the first of these two joint training camp practices. They started strong before the Eagles made up some ground … only for New England to pick it back up and finish on top. It wasn’t like the Birds got thoroughly dominated, though. What’s the biggest worry for your team entering this season? – SB Nation The NFC East Mixtape Feed is here! It’s a spot for fans of the Giants, Commanders, Cowboys and Eagles to gather and talk ball (and a little smack for good measure, as well). I have more info about this new Feed community in a formal intro , but, for now, let’s get the football discussion going! I asked each site manager from the four NFC East sites a question to kick off a series of roundtable discussions we’ll have on here… Patriots training camp recap: Drake Maye shreds Eagles defense in first joint practice – Pats Pulpit Dominant Drake: The Eagles’ top defense stood no chance against Drake Maye and the Patriots passing attack. Maye completed his first 13 passes across four periods including several downfield completions to A.J. Brown, Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas, and Kayshon Boutte. Maye then ended his day with 1:05 on the clock and the ball around the 20-yard line. After a first-down drop by Doubs, completions to Douglas and Mack Hollins got New England across midfield. A short pass to Hunter Henry then got the unit in field goal range which Andy Borregales knocked through from 52 yards out. Eagles/Patriots Day 1 Reactions: AJ Brown Beats The Eagles – Go Birds! Podcast Eliot Shorr-Parks is joined by Brandon Lee Gowton to recap everything that happened on Tuesday during the first day of the Eagles and Patriots joint practices. Later, Dave Uram stops by to tell us everything he saw from AJ Brown on an impressive day for the former Eagles receiver. Eagles 2026 training camp notes, Day 13: Eagles-Patriots joint practices, Part I – PhillyVoice That’s six of the Eagles’ top seven linemen with a clean sweep on their reps. The only loss was Landon Dickerson, to Milton Williams. (I originally thought Dickerson narrowly won that rep, but a few other Eagles beats with a better angle on that one vehemently disagreed, so I’ll concede.) I would have also given Willie Lampkin a 2-1 record on his three reps. The Eagles’ other backups in 1-on-1’s? Yuck. Myles Hinton in particular got torn up. I had him down for 0 wins, 4 losses, and some of the losses were bad. Eagles-Pats Roundup Day 1 – Iggles Blitz The Eagles focused on running the ball today and had a lot of success. Some of that was good blocking, some was Saquon Barkley doing Saquon things. He’s had a great summer. As for Hurts and the passing game, it was a mixed bag. They didn’t have DeVonta Smith in team drills, which didn’t help. The passing game is just erratic right now. The deep ball to Moore was great. But there were also off-target throws that should have been made. The coaches and players will study the tape to see what went right and what went wrong. Having good tape to study is invaluable when discussing problems and coming up with solutions. The offense struggled at the end of practice when in a 2-minute-drill. The Pats were able to score, the Eagles weren’t. Bowen: A.J. Brown stuff is great fun, but Vic Fangio said something at Eagles-Pats joint practice that might actually matter – PHLY In a month or so, I don’t think anyone will still care what A.J. Brown said or did during these joint training camp practices between the Eagles and the Patriots. I doubt anyone will still be referencing anything Jalen Hurts or Devonta Smith had to say about Brown, on an August day in Foxborough, Mass. Someone did say something Wednesday that might matter in a month, though. It was Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio. He was asked about Jonathan Greenard, the former Vikings edge rusher the Eagles traded for this offseason, then signed to a $98 million contract extension. Greenard was the Eagles’ biggest offseason move, the reason many fans and observers felt good about an edge rush that wasn’t nearly as good in 2025 as it had been a year earlier. Greenard had shoulder surgery early in the offseason. Then, on the first day of training camp, the Eagles told us he had suffered a pec strain, and wouldn’t be ready to practice. General manager Howie Roseman told reporters he wasn’t worried. “When you have a guy like that who prepares the way he does, who has the experience in the NFL the way he does, you know he’s going to be ready to play when we start the season,” Roseman said. That was on July 29th. Wednesday was three weeks later, to the day. Here is what Fangio said in Foxboro: “I don’t know when Greenard will be back. That injury he got in our weight room is going to take some time to heal.” Quinyon Mitchell-A.J. Brown battle highlights Eagles’ joint practice vs. Patriots – The Athletic Let’s start with A.J. Brown because he was the biggest story. Eagles fans might not like hearing it, but Brown was outstanding in this practice. He caught seven passes in seven-on-seven drills and team drills in different spots on the field — coming back to the ball, in stride on crossers, over his shoulder. Brown faced Quinyon Mitchell and Riq Woolen. It seemed most of the plays came when he was on Woolen’s side. Brown was a force in this practice, as he often was in Eagles practices. The Eagles know as much. But if you were of the view that the Eagles traded a declining player to New England … it didn’t look like that Wednesday. Biggest concern for every NFL team entering the 2026 season – PFF Philadelphia Eagles: Replacing A.J. Brown. Trading A.J. Brown made long-term sense for…

title: Eagles-Ravens Film Review: Defense edition
summary: IMPORTANT DISCLAIMER: It’s preseason! The Ravens finished with 440 yards, completed 30 of 37 passes, and possessed the ball for more than 41 minutes, but the Eagles rested almost every established starter and ran an extremely basic version of their defense. The Eagles’ inability to sustain drives on offense also left the defense on the […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - AUGUST 15: Ty Robinson #95 of the Philadelphia Eagles celebrates during an NFL preseason football game against the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images IMPORTANT DISCLAIMER: It’s preseason! The Ravens finished with 440 yards, completed 30 of 37 passes, and possessed the ball for more than 41 minutes, but the Eagles rested almost every established starter and ran an extremely basic version of their defense. The Eagles’ inability to sustain drives on offense also left the defense on the field for 76 plays. That provided plenty of evaluation material, but it created a game that bore almost no resemblance to what the regular-season defense will look like. Defense A.J. Epenesa’s debut looked exactly as I expected. He played 20 defensive snaps, recorded three tackles, and consistently handled the less glamorous parts of the position. He set a firm edge against the run, tackled the back on a screen, and correctly handled a Zone Read later in the game. There was not much pass-rush production, but his overall performance was dependable. I liked Epenesa when I watched him, and I think he’s a solid rotational option. The Eagles also dropped him into coverage more frequently than I anticipated. He was beaten early on in the game, but I was impressed by his ability to stay relatively close to a tight end running vertically. Epenesa is a big defensive end, so he is never going to look entirely natural carrying players downfield. However, he moved better than expected and did not appear completely out of place. This rep demonstrates the reliability that stood out. Epenesa is too physical for the tight end at the point of attack and blows up the run. Quick Eagles' Defense All22 Thread vs Ravens (preseason). 1) It was good to see AJ Epenesa out there, even if he was in coverage a lot! He played well, as I expected. He's too big and physical for tight ends, but also showed good hustle on a screen pass and tackled the back on a… pic.twitter.com/aGenLbVi5R — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) August 18, 2026 Nothing makes me happier than watching Jeremiah Trotter Jr. play linebacker. He doesn’t have elite size or athleticism, but he processes the game so quickly that those limitations rarely keep him from making plays. Trotter consistently identifies blocking schemes, anticipates where the running lane will develop, and triggers downhill without hesitation. Many young linebackers wait until the picture becomes completely clear before committing, but Trotter trusts his eyes. That decisiveness allows him to beat blockers to their landmarks and make plays before the running back can build momentum. I am almost certain that he could start for several teams. Jihaad Campbell also looked sharp during his limited action, especially in coverage. The contrast with Smael Mondon Jr. was noticeable. I thought he was far too hesitant fitting the run. The physical tools are appealing, especially as a pass rusher, but he did not play with the same decisiveness as Trotter or Campbell. I would not consider him a certainty to make the roster as the fourth linebacker. 2) Ah, nothing makes me happier than watching Jeremiah Trotter play football. He just gets it. His mental processing is awesome; he gets downhill so quickly and makes so many plays against the run. He would start for a lot of teams, even if he isn't the biggest or the fastest.… pic.twitter.com/RL4bnEFUWt — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) August 18, 2026 Trotter’s mental processing also translates to his work as a blitzer. This is an outstanding rush for so many reasons. He times the snap well, attacks the protection before the running back can become set, and then avoids the block without losing sight of the quarterback. The finish is also impressive, as Tyler Huntley is a mobile quarterback. Trotter still needs to improve in coverage, particularly when he is asked to carry more athletic players through space. However, his ability against the run and as a blitzer make me feel very confident in him as the 3rd linebacker on this team. Remember when this team did not have a single good linebacker? What a luxury we have… 3) Trotter can blitz too! What a fantastic rush. He shows excellent snap timing, avoids the RB, and still keeps his eyes on the QB at all times before tripping him up. Great stuff. Remember when we didn't have a single good linebacker? pic.twitter.com/RnZ2a1PaLN — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) August 18, 2026 Mac McWilliams had a busy evening. He played 65 defensive snaps (!), and whilst there were some encouraging moments, his performance was inconsistent. The Ravens repeatedly tested the Eagles’ inexperienced secondary, and McWilliams did not always process route combinations quickly enough. This rep is a good example. McWilliams is slow to recognize the switch release and lets himself get caught in the traffic created by the two receivers. Once he loses his positioning, the route breaks open downfield. Luckily for McWilliams, Ty Robinson produces one of his best plays of the game. Robinson needed an encouraging performance after an underwhelming rookie season, and there were some positive signs. He recorded two tackles and a sack while showing some good athleticism and effort. His motor was noticeable throughout the game, even when he did not make the final play. Robinson’s hand usage is the key to this rep. He catches the guard’s initial strike, knocks the hands away, and immediately transitions into a swim move. It is encouraging to see him using both hands together rather than attempting to win purely with his one-arm club move, which he relied on last year. The guard’s technique is terrible, which must be acknowledged, but Robinson still executes the move correctly and finishes the rush. No other defensive tackle consistently flashed, so Robinson’s disruption stood out. He did commit a slightly stupid roughing-the-passer penalty on third down late in the fourth quarter, but I thought he looked OK overall. I’m still worried about defensive tackle depth against the run (outside of the big 3), as I don’t think Bryon Young or Gabe Hall looked great. 4) Mac McWilliams owes Ty Robinson. McWilliams was up and down, but this was a poor rep where he struggled to spot the switch release and ended up getting picked. Luckily, Ty Robinson has a fantastic rep. He catches the guard's strike, swats it away, and then swims past him. It's… pic.twitter.com/jGVPLwSWQL — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) August 18, 2026 I didn’t need to include another clip of Trotter making a tackle, but why not? He diagnoses the run immediately, stays clean by avoiding the guard, and arrives at the football under control. This is what dependable linebacker play looks like. The more interesting part of the clip is Michael Carter coming downhill from safety. I watched Carter closely because his transition from cornerback is one of the more intriguing defensive experiments this preseason. His movement skills looked comfortable enough in space, and he did not appear restricted when changing direction or playing from depth. The bigger concern was his willingness to attack the running game. Carter looked hesitant coming downhill for much of the game. That is understandable for a player learning a new position, because a safety has to process the run fit, route distribution, and potential play-action threat before committing. However, Fangio’s safeties cannot consistently wait for the play to reach them. They must be willing to close space and deliver contact from depth. This is one of Carter’s better reps. He reads the play, accelerates downhill, and strikes the runner rather than arriving passively. I would still like to see him trigger earlier and play with more conviction throughout the game, but the improvement on this rep was a positive sign. 5) Did I need to post another rep of Trotter making a tackle? No. Did I anyway? Yes. I also posted this because it…

title: Vic Fangio is concerned that Jonathan Greenard won’t be available for Week 1
summary: The Eagles are up in New England for joint practices ahead of their second preseason game. Defensive coordinator Vic Fangio spoke to reporters before taking the field, and he gave some insights into players performance in the first preseason game, and also gave an unfortunate update regarding Jonathan Greenard’s return from injury. Here’s what else […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - MAY 27: Jonathan Greenard #52 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on during OTA offseason workouts at Jefferson Health Training Complex on May 27, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Eagles are up in New England for joint practices ahead of their second preseason game. Defensive coordinator Vic Fangio spoke to reporters before taking the field, and he gave some insights into players performance in the first preseason game, and also gave an unfortunate update regarding Jonathan Greenard’s return from injury. Here’s what else the DC had to say: On Greenard and the EDGE group When asked if there was concern that Greenard’s pec injury could keep him sidelined to start the regular season, he admitted that was a possibility. “ I don’t know when Greenard will be back. That injury he got in our weight room is going to take some time to heal.” In the meantime, though, Fangio said he’s been happy with Jalyx Hunt and Nolan Smith, and also mentioned Arnold Ebiketie has been coming along. The DC said they are really looking for the third and fourth guy on the depth chart to solidify himself while they wait for Greenard to get back. Fangio also showed support, again, for DE A.J. Epenesa and his effort to learn how to drop back into coverage. “Yeah, [Epenesa’s] been doing good and he played good in the preseason game. He had a great learning experience on that pass he got beat on. I’m really happy that happened because it was a preseason game. But not only for him, but all the outside backers/EDGE players. It’s a great learning experience on how to play that play, and he’s doing good. He’s picking up– We dropped those guys a little bit, not a lot. He’s really done well with it and I think he’ll continue to improve.” On joint practices “I love doing these things. I think these things are great. I wish we would do another one. It’s great to go against a new team, new schemes, new players. You learn things. You’re going to get unscouted looks and plays, and you see how people react. These things are tremendous.“ Fangio later talked about how the Patriots have been a team to utilize a fullback, which isn’t something they get a chance to see much in Philly. He also pointed out that New England’s offense is more spread out compared to the Eagles, so everything they do this week will be valuable. On Ty Robinson’s performance “Yeah, [Ty Robinson] came to life. He’s been on life support since he’s been here, but he came to life and hopefully that will continue.” On other specific players Fangio explained that they played Jihaad Campbell because his snap count went down when Nakobe Dean came back last year, and the DC felt Campbell needed extra reps — a decision he felt was justified by the OLB’s uneven performance. As for Marcus Epps not playing in the first preseason game, Fangio said they wanted to see Michael Carter get a lot of reps at safety. He noted that Epps has played his whole career at safety, so this was a good opportunity to get Carter more reps there and totally evaluated. “[Michael Carter] did fine. Mike’s had a good camp. I think it was [the Ravens] first touchdown pass in the game, he should have played better. But to me, it’s more just his newness on the job, particularly when he’s in a deep zone, it’s all new to him. We need to get him as many reps doing that as we can.” The DC was very complimentary of LB Jeremiah Trotter Jr. and his development. He said Trotter was reaping the benefits of being in the system for three years, and he’s matured over their time together. “[Jeremiah Trotter] always knew what to do, but his processing is a whole lot faster and quicker. I mean, the most important quality you can have as an inside backer is instincts, play recognition. His is really showing more in this camp than it had before.” Fangio called DT Uar Bernard and OLB Joshua Weru their “exchange dudes,” and said the pair is doing fine but they’ve got a long way to go. The DC admitted that Kelee Ringo has been the focus of criticism, but Fangio gets a sense that Ringo could be coming into a stride. He also emphasized how big these next few days are for the third-year cornerback He said that S Maximus Pulley and CB Kapena Gushiken came alive in the first preseason game, and did some good things. Fangio said they are two good young prospects. The DC said that their ILB position is probably the deepest group on defense – he called Trotter and Smael Mondon two good quality players. Chance Campbell has been hurt for awhile but finally returned to practice on Wednesday.

title: Teams interested in Joey Porter Jr. trade
summary: In what has become an increasingly common chapter in high-profile NFL contract negotiation sagas, Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr. is now the subject of trade rumors, according to insider Jordan Schultz. “Joey Porter Jr. is a name multiple teams around the NFL have wondered about as a potential trade target, per source,” Schultz posted late […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PA - JANUARY 12: Joey Porter Jr. #24 of the Pittsburgh Steelers defends in coverage during an NFL wild card playoff football game against the Houston Texans at Acrisure Stadium on January 12, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images In what has become an increasingly common chapter in high-profile NFL contract negotiation sagas, Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr. is now the subject of trade rumors, according to insider Jordan Schultz. #Steelers CB Joey Porter Jr. is a name multiple teams around the NFL have wondered about as a potential trade target, per sources. JPJ is in the final year of his rookie contract, and with where the CB market is, teams have wondered if Pittsburgh could ultimately be open to a… pic.twitter.com/0t1CX9laOQ — Jordan Schultz (@Schultz_Report) August 21, 2026 “Joey Porter Jr. is a name multiple teams around the NFL have wondered about as a potential trade target, per source,” Schultz posted late Thursday. “(Porter) is in the final year of his rookie contract, and with where the CB market is, teams have wondered if Pittsburgh could ultimately be open to a move with the Pro Bowl caliber corner.” The Steelers have completed contract extensions with three members of the team’s 2023 draft class already this offseason with Nick Herbig, Darnell Washington and most recently Keeanu Benton landing new deals. And with the top of the cornerback market now solidly over $30 million per year on average — the Seahawks’ Devon Witherspoon recently signed a four-year, $132 million extension — Porter’s asking price is expected to be well above what his teammates received. Porter remains under contract in 2026, but started camp on the physically unable to perform list with a reported back injury. Schultz’s wording is vague in the report, not mentioning if the Steelers have any interest in trading the 26-year-old defensive back, and it doesn’t seem to mention that any team has reached out to Pittsburgh, either. Steelers beat writers such as Steelers Now’s Alan Saunder s have responded to the report saying it would be a surprise if Pittsburgh moved on from Porter this year.

title: Andy Weidl emphasizes importance of building the trenches
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers have made it clear in recent years that building in the trenches remains a priority. Few people are more responsible for that philosophy than assistant general manager Andy Weidl, who has played a significant role in Pittsburgh’s scouting and draft process alongside general manager Omar Khan. Since Weidl arrived in Pittsburgh, the […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 13: Gennings Dunker #73 of the Pittsburgh Steelers in action during the game against the Green Bay Packers at Acrisure Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers have made it clear in recent years that building in the trenches remains a priority. Few people are more responsible for that philosophy than assistant general manager Andy Weidl, who has played a significant role in Pittsburgh’s scouting and draft process alongside general manager Omar Khan. Since Weidl arrived in Pittsburgh, the Steelers have consistently invested significant draft capital in both their offensive and defensive lines. That approach continued in the 2026 NFL Draft, when Pittsburgh used its first-round pick on Arizona State offensive tackle Max Iheanachor before adding Iowa offensive lineman Gennings Dunker in the third round and Notre Dame defensive lineman Gabriel Rubio in the sixth. For Weidl, however, the philosophy is about more than simply winning the line of scrimmage on Sundays. It is about making sure the team still has enough in the tank when the season reaches its most important stretch. “It’s nice to have that,” Weidl said via Chris Adamski . “It keeps your guys fresh, so when you get to December and January football, you’re able to surge. That’s why we invest there.” That mindset is particularly evident on the defensive line, where the Steelers have aggressively built depth around veterans such as Cameron Heyward and younger players including Keeanu Benton, Derrick Harmon and Yahya Black. Pittsburgh also added veteran Sebastian Joseph-Day and drafted Rubio this offseason. Weidl has seen the benefits of that strategy firsthand. Before joining the Steelers, he was part of Philadelphia’s front office during the Eagles’ Super Bowl-winning era, an organization known for emphasizing the trenches and maintaining waves of defensive linemen. “Two waves” of players can keep a defensive front fresh, Weidl has explained, allowing the unit to maintain its physicality deep into the season. That philosophy could become particularly important under new defensive coordinator Patrick Graham, whose scheme emphasizes versatility and interchangeable pieces along the defensive front. The Steelers have also invested heavily in their offensive line, selecting Broderick Jones, Troy Fautanu, Zach Frazier and Iheanachor with significant draft capital in recent years. The objective is similar: establish depth, competition and enough quality up front to withstand the inevitable injuries and attrition of an NFL season. Weidl’s philosophy isn’t complicated – Build the trenches. Build depth. Keep players fresh. Then, when December and January arrive and the stakes rise, Pittsburgh wants to be the team still capable of playing its best football. For a Steelers team trying to end a seven-game playoff losing streak and make a deeper postseason run in 2026, that investment could ultimately prove more important in January than it appears in August. Let us know what you think in the comments . Be sure to bookmark Behind the Steel Curtain for all the latest news, breakdowns, and more! The report provides a significant dose of optimism after both veterans have been sidelined for roughly a week and a half with injuries. Steelers WR DK Metcalf and Michael Pittman Jr. are both expected to be ready for Week 1, per @FarabaughFB pic.twitter.com/UQ1ajb4cB8 — SleeperNFL (@SleeperNFL) August 19, 2026 Metcalf is dealing with an undisclosed injury, while Pittman has been battling a minor hamstring issue. Neither player has indicated that the injuries are expected to become long-term concerns, with both anticipating that they will be available when the regular season begins Sept. 13. That is particularly important for a Steelers offense entering its second season with Aaron Rodgers at quarterback and a revamped receiving corps. Pittsburgh made a significant investment in its wide receiver room this offseason, adding Pittman to a group that already featured Metcalf while also drafting Alabama wide receiver Germie Bernard in the second round. The Steelers have been cautious with their two veteran starters during the preseason. Head coach Mike McCarthy indicated that neither Metcalf nor Pittman was expected to practice this week, meaning both are likely to miss Friday’s preseason matchup against the New York Jets. While their absence limits the opportunities for Rodgers to develop further chemistry with his new-look receiving corps, the bigger picture is clearly focused on having both players healthy when the games count. The early returns from the rest of the receiver room have also been encouraging. Bernard, Roman Wilson and others have received additional opportunities while Metcalf and Pittman have been sidelined, giving Pittsburgh a chance to evaluate its depth heading into the regular season. For the Steelers, however, the biggest takeaway is simple: If Metcalf and Pittman remain on track, Pittsburgh should have its projected top two receivers available for Rodgers when the Falcons arrive at Acrisure Stadium. title: Make-or-break position battles to watch in Steelers’ preseason game against the Jets
summary: The games still don’t count, but the Steelers are looking to maintain positive momentum in Week 2 of the NFL preseason. Last week, the team had an impressive if imperfect 28-9 victory over the Green Bay Packers. Not many of Pittsburgh’s expected starters suited up for that tilt, though the members of the offensive line […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 13: Will Howard #18 of the Pittsburgh Steelers rushes against the Green Bay Packers in the first half at Acrisure Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Justin K. Aller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The games still don’t count, but the Steelers are looking to maintain positive momentum in Week 2 of the NFL preseason. Last week, the team had an impressive if imperfect 28-9 victory over the Green Bay Packers. Not many of Pittsburgh’s expected starters suited up for that tilt, though the members of the offensive line that did were arguably the biggest cause for concern. Mike McCarthy will undoubtedly be looking for progress from that unit, as well as a cleaner game after the Steelers were flagged 11 times for 134 total penalty yards in their first showing. Earlier this summer, we here at Read & React outlined many of the various position battles on offense and on defense as the team prepared to head into training camp. Now, as we head into the second preseason contest, it feels like the perfect time to reexamine those battles. With the third and final preseason game typically not bearing as much weight for NFL clubs, this might be the last real chance for certain players to cement their roles and, in some cases, a place on the 53-man roster. Put another way, which players have the most to gain or lose from the game with the Jets? Let’s explore. Quarterbacks RP : On Wednesday, McCarthy gave us a definitive answer on what the team is planning to do at quarterback against the Jets. Mike McCarthy announces that Mason Rudolph and Aaron Rodgers will not play against the New York Jets. It will instead be Will Howard and Drew Allar, with Howard getting the start. McCarthy adds he 'saw what I needed to see' from Rudolph. pic.twitter.com/qu8jP2iq7e — Nick Farabaugh (@FarabaughFB) August 19, 2026 What the Steelers do at quarterback behind Aaron Rodgers has been one of the main intrigues surrounding the team since drafting Drew Allar in the third round this spring. By now, you should be well-versed in the Steelers’ dilemma. The team has four quarterbacks in camp and will be forced to make a difficult choice once roster cuts must be made. No team carries four quarterbacks on its active roster; it just isn’t a reality in the NFL. With just 53 jobs available, a team can’t afford to carry three players it hopes never have to take a snap. So the Steelers’ conundrum is this: as a team that has clearly indicated it wants to compete for the playoffs this season, can it afford to have two inexperienced and developmental passers behind Rodgers? This is a source of much debate among the fanbase. Some, like myself, would posit that the Steelers are well familiar with Mason Rudolph at this point, and the idea that he will keep them playoff-competitive should Rodgers miss time is a silly notion. If Rodgers misses time, the season is likely a wash, and it would be better to find out what they have in their young passers against real competition, because hardly anyone should believe Rudolph is a future starter for this team, not after seven years in the league, including a one-year stint on another team. But others would argue that NFL teams don’t think that way. They pay deference to veterans, and trusting two incredibly green signal callers to back up Rodgers is not the move a team like the Steelers would make. I might disagree with the philosophy, but it’s impossible to know how the Steelers truly feel. We’re not mind readers, after all. For now, there is no clear consensus on what the team will do, even here at BTSC. Devil's advocate, you know what you have in Rudolph. Years of tape, familiarity in the building, etc. If this is genuinely a competition it makes sense to put more on the young guys' plates. Rudolph would do nothing in PRE2 to sway what the org thinks of him, in either direction https://t.co/zRHplKXN2Z — Ryan Parish (@ArmchairScout21) August 19, 2026 We can pretty safely say that both Rodgers and the rookie Allar are making this team. Rodgers is the starter in his final year; of course, he is making the team. Allar, meanwhile, is too high-profile of a rookie to stash on a practice squad. If Pittsburgh were to be reckless enough to try that, you can count on another quarterback-desperate franchise claiming him immediately. If we can accept those sentiments as truths, then this has always been a case of choosing Howard or Rudolph. As for my money, I know which player looked more impressive last week. If this is a true competition, and the team hasn’t already decided to keep Rudolph, then I don’t see how his inactive status could be considered an endorsement. In fact, if this was truly a competition, I would interpret this as the Steelers having seven years of knowledge and tape on Rudolph while only having one preseason game on Howard. I’m not saying Howard should be considered to be holding a lead in this competition, but I think the Steelers have more to gain by giving him an extended look. Rudolph won’t show you anything you don’t already know about him. Howard has a chance to either rise to the occasion or wilt under the pressure. Likewise, I see getting Allar more reps as a better benefit to the team than giving those reps to Rudolph at this stage in his career. All that’s to say, the two players who might have the most riding on this game are Howard and Rudolph. One of them has a chance to make a big statement that he belongs. The other will be forced to watch from the sidelines. Running back RB : Based off of last Thursday’s Packers matchup, Travis Homer emerged as the sudden favorite for the Steelers’ RB3 spot, starting the game for the resting Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle. Frankly, Homer didn’t have a memorable day on offense. He averaged just two yards per carry on what was admittedly a rough outing for the offensive line, and was steamrolled in pass protection on a rep that resulted in one of the two sacks Mason Rudolph took during the game. Sack allowed on first drive of Steelers v Packers pic.twitter.com/xsL5iT6pU9 — Ryan Parish (@ArmchairScout21) August 14, 2026 Still, Homer showed some solid traits for a prospective No. 3 back, seeing extensive snaps on special teams — including as the personal protector on the punt unit — and recording two catches in the dump-off passing game. Honestly, his day in pass protection was just fine outside of a rep where he showed good effort and recognition but just got overpowered. Also in the running back battle, Lew Nichols and Eli Heidenreich both showed more juice as runners, with Nichols looking the best on offense of the group (the only one to break three yards per carry). It’s worth noting Heidenreich saw some snaps as a kick returner, although it was fellow rookie Kaden Wetjen who caught the ball on each rep. Then there’s 2025 third-rounder Kaleb Johnson, who looked fine during his eight snaps in the game — but the thing is, it was just eight snaps: less offensive reps, carries, and special teams reps than the other contenders in the battle for RB3. Despite a fresh start under a new coaching staff in 2026, it appears Johnson has still struggled to stand out from the rest of the team’s depth at the position, and he didn’t get many chances to prove otherwise against the Packers. The rest of the preseason might be essential for Johnson’s chances at salvaging his career in Pittsburgh. And while Homer’s 53-man roster odds have increased in the past week, he certainly hasn’t run away with the RB3 job just yet. I’ll add that I only expect there to be one running back spot available behind Dowdle and Warren. It appears Robert Tonyan has established himself as a clear favorite for the TE3 job, which may have contributed to Riley Nowakowski taking on a more fullback-heavy role — and there’s no need to keep four running backs and a fullback. title: New Seahawks cornerback Trevon Diggs discusses signing, fit with team
summary: The Seattle Seahawks are in desperate search of more cornerback depth, at least judging by their recent free agency moves. Seattle still intends to sign troubled ex-Detroit Lions starter Terrion Arnold, but in the meantime they’ve turned their sights to former Dallas Cowboys corner and two-time Pro Bowler Trevon Diggs. The Seahawks signed Diggs on […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 28: Trevon Diggs #7 of the Dallas Cowboys warms up against the Green Bay Packers before the game at AT&T Stadium on September 28, 2025 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks are in desperate search of more cornerback depth, at least judging by their recent free agency moves. Seattle still intends to sign troubled ex-Detroit Lions starter Terrion Arnold , but in the meantime they’ve turned their sights to former Dallas Cowboys corner and two-time Pro Bowler Trevon Diggs. The Seahawks signed Diggs on Wednesday , and on that same day the 27-year-old corner spoke to the media about his health and decision to sign with Seattle. “This is the first offseason I’ve been able to not rehab and do offseason training,” Diggs said, confirming that he is 100% healthy. “A lot of trainers help me put the work in to help me get to where I’m at today, I’m truly thankful for that. It’s a blessing from God honestly, to be able to come out here again.” While Diggs is new to the Seahawks, he’s joining some familiar faces. Diggs played with edge rushers DeMarcus Lawrence and Dante Fowler Jr. and was coached by Seahawks defensive coordinator Ande Durde during his time in Dallas. Diggs said having those faces he can turn to ask questions is incredibly valuable, and he sees similarities to the family-esque bonds his Cowboy defenses had. “That’s very important with a football team just being together, being one and making sure your locker room is straight,” Diggs said. “I see a lot of similarities there.” Diggs also played alongside Seahawks starting corner Josh Jobe during his time at Alabama. In his introductory presser, Diggs said Jobe has already offered to help him understand head coach Mike Macdonald’s defense. “He’s saying he’ll help me out, get the playbook down. I’ll be in my playbook every day to get the whole defense down,” Diggs said of Jobe. “Being able to give myself a chance, give myself an opportunity to come out here and compete and help win.” Speaking of Macdonald’s defense, Diggs said that it looks amazing. “They get to the quarterback. They create turnovers. They do all the right things,” Diggs said. “I’m excited to hopefully be a part of it and just try to help this team win.” The Alabama product said he has experience playing in the slot and outside and that he prides himself on his ball skills as a corner. That makes sense considering he has 20 career interceptions, with a whopping 11 of them in one season, 2021, when he was named to a first-team All-Pro. Despite his production, Diggs has struggled to stay healthy recently and struggled with concussion symptoms after a TV mounting incident last season. The Cowboys cut Diggs just 10 days after reactivating him from injured reserve, and though he found a new home with the Green Bay Packers, they would also waive him on January 20. Diggs discussed the ordeal, saying he leaned on his family a lot during that time. However, now fully healthy, Diggs said he’s ready to put that behind him. “I love football. I love to play it. This has been a part of football. It’s part of my job, it’s a part of your job,” Diggs said. “You’re going to get hurt. You’re going to have things that’ll happen. You’re going to get traded, you’re going to get cut. Things happen, but you have to keep going.” Diggs was unsure if he’d be ready to play by Sunday, when the Seahawks take on the Tennessee Titans, but said he’d be looking forward to getting to know the team better on their road trip. “I just want to get in with the guys, vibe, get familiar with them and get familiar with new faces, and go out there and help,” Diggs said.

title: Seahawks sale unanimously approved by pair of key NFL committees
summary: The Seattle Seahawks opened their 2026 preseason with a showing that was disappointing to many, especially on the heels of a 2025 season that ended with the Hawks hoisting a Lombardi trophy on the home field of a key division rival. Regardless of how the preseason turns out, however, the upcoming sale of the Seahawks […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 08: Jody Allen of the Seattle Seahawks celebrates with the Vince Lombardi Trophy after winning Super Bowl LX against the New England Patriots at Levi's Stadium on February 08, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. The Seattle Seahawks defeated the New England Patriots 29-13. (Photo by Ronald Martinez/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks opened their 2026 preseason with a showing that was disappointing to many , especially on the heels of a 2025 season that ended with the Hawks hoisting a Lombardi trophy on the home field of a key division rival . Regardless of how the preseason turns out, however, the upcoming sale of the Seahawks has been a key story not just during this past offseason, but for most of the nearly eight years since Paul Allen died, leaving control of the team to his sister, Jody Allen, by virtue of her role as the trustee for his estate. With a $9.612B price tag having been agreed to between the estate and future owner Vinod Khosla , the official sale of the team became largely a matter of time and getting the correct approvals from the league and the other owners. According to a report Wednesday from Mark Maske of Front Office Sports, two of those approvals have arrived, with the NFL finance and ownership policy committees voting to unanimously to approve the sale. NEWS: The NFL notified teams today that members of the league's finance committee and ownership policy committee voted unanimously Wednesday to recommend approval of the $9.612 billion sale of the Seahawks from the Paul G. Allen estate to a group led by the family of venture… — Mark Maske (@MarkMaske) August 20, 2026 As Maske notes, the approval from these two committees sets the table for the sale to be officially approved by league owners next week, setting the expectation that the transaction to close in September . Assuming the sale is indeed approved by owners on Wednesday, August 26, there would be two weeks remaining until the Seahawks open the regular season at Lumen Field against the New England Patriots on September 9. It is possible that it could get done by then, but such a tight window would seem to make it unlikely. Thus, the report that the sale is expected to close in September combined with the fact that the season opener is the only game Seattle is scheduled to play at home during the month would appear to set the table for the final home game of the Allen family ownership era to fittingly end in a nationally televised, season opening game celebrating the Seahawks victory in Super Bowl LX.

title: Early-season Seahawks opponents suffer major offensive line injuries
summary: Two of the Seattle Seahawks’ first four opponents are dealing with big injury problems on their respective offensive lines. Earlier this month, Washington Commanders left tackle Laremy Tunsil suffered torn triceps during a 1-on-1 rep in training camp. He’s since undergone surgery and will bare minimum miss a majority of the regular season. Tunsil is […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 02: Laremy Tunsil #78 of the Washington Commanders drops back to block during an NFL football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Northwest Stadium on November 2, 2025 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Two of the Seattle Seahawks’ first four opponents are dealing with big injury problems on their respective offensive lines. Earlier this month, Washington Commanders left tackle Laremy Tunsil suffered torn triceps during a 1-on-1 rep in training camp. He’s since undergone surgery and will bare minimum miss a majority of the regular season . Tunsil is in his second season with the Commanders after he was traded by the Houston Texans, with whom he was a five-time Pro Bowl selection. According to Commanders head coach Dan Quinn, Brandon Coleman will fill in for Tunsil at left tackle. Coleman was the team’s starting left guard, but he was drafted as a tackle out of TCU and made 12 starts at LT as a rookie in the 2024 season. More recently, the Los Angeles Chargers made a significant free agent investment in former Commanders center Tyler Biadasz, who signed a three-year, $30 million contract to join a line that’s getting back a healthy Joe Alt and Rashawn Slater. Well, after a joint practice with the San Francisco 49ers, Biadasz is probably not going to make his Chargers debut any time soon. Speechless pic.twitter.com/L9pWmxF7Cg — Tino ⚡️ (@TinoFromTheQ) August 18, 2026 After 49ers defensive tackle Sebastian Valdez was thrown into Biadasz, he can be seen immediately grabbing his knee. As of this writing, we don’t know if it’s a season-ending injury, but the extent of his injuries indicates he will be out for a long time. Chargers center Tyler Biadasz is out indefinitely after suffering damage to his ACL and additional injuries to his left knee during Tuesday’s joint practice against the 49ers, per @rapsheet and me. Biadasz will meet with more doctors to try to get more clarity. pic.twitter.com/0cyNFBmUdY — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) August 19, 2026 At the moment, the would-be Chargers starting center is second-round rookie Jake Slaughter, a former first-team All-American out of Florida. Seattle hosts the Chargers in Week 4, so in all likelihood Slaughter’s second road start will involve lining up against Byron Murphy II, Leonard Williams, and Jarran Reed. It’s a really unfortunate set of circumstances for the Commanders and Chargers. The hope is that the Seahawks can continue going through their own preseason relatively unscathed, particularly at the top of the depth chart. When the regular season comes around, Seattle’s defense will look to capitalize on two teams who already know they won’t be at full strength on the offensive line.

title: Film review: Rylie Mills is no longer just a redshirt project for the Seahawks
summary: When the Seattle Seahawks selected Rylie Mills in the fifth round of the 2026 NFL Draft, they weren’t betting on production—they were betting on traits. Mills entered the draft with a higher grade than where he was ultimately selected, but a knee injury suffered during Notre Dame’s College Football Playoff run dramatically altered his stock. […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 08: Rylie Mills #98 of the Seattle Seahawks reacts to a sack against the New England Patriots during the first half of Super Bowl LX at Levi's Stadium on February 08, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images When the Seattle Seahawks selected Rylie Mills in the fifth round of the 2026 NFL Draft , they weren’t betting on production—they were betting on traits. Mills entered the draft with a higher grade than where he was ultimately selected, but a knee injury suffered during Notre Dame’s College Football Playoff run dramatically altered his stock. Knowing he would miss a significant portion of his rookie season, Seattle was able to capitalize on a player who likely would have come off the board much earlier had he been healthy. Even before the injury, however, there were questions about how his physical profile would translate to the NFL. His lack of ideal arm length and only average play strength projected to limit his ceiling, particularly against the run. Because of that combination of injury and developmental concerns, the expectation entering his rookie year was straightforward: treat it as a redshirt season. That script largely played out. After spending much of the year recovering, Mills finally began seeing the field late in the season—making his NFL debut against the Indianapolis Colts—and although the snap count remained modest, those reps carried more value than the box score could ever capture. Development doesn’t happen on the sideline; it happens between the whistles. Every defensive snap, even in rotational duty or late-game situations, provides experience that simply can’t be replicated in practice. Whether it’s recognizing blocking schemes, adjusting to NFL speed, or learning how opponents attack protections, those live repetitions accelerate a young player’s growth far more than another afternoon spent watching from the bench. His rookie film isn’t extensive, but there is enough to evaluate what Seattle has today—and perhaps more importantly, what it can reasonably expect moving forward. What stood out on Rylie Mills’ tape Quickness off the ball translated immediately One of the reasons Seattle was so intrigued by Mills throughout the draft process was his first-step explosiveness. Rylie Mills, DL, #98The Seahawks emphasized get-off metrics, and Mills consistently graded among the best. That burst shows on NFL tape, allowing him to stress blockers before they establish their sets despite lacking elite length or overwhelming power. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-20T02:21:18.570Z The Seahawks placed significant emphasis on get-off metrics during their evaluation process, and Mills consistently graded among the top performers in that area. That burst shows up on NFL film just as it did at Notre Dame. Even in limited opportunities, he routinely threatened blockers before they could fully establish their pass sets, allowing him to create immediate stress despite lacking elite length or overwhelming power. Rylie Mills, DL, #98 Rather than winning with overwhelming physical tools, Mills wins by forcing offensive linemen to react early. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-20T02:21:41.646Z Rather than winning with overwhelming physical tools, Mills wins by forcing offensive linemen to react early. Rylie Mills, DL, #98 That first step gives him a chance to stay competitive against NFL-caliber athletes and should remain the foundation of his pass-rush game. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-20T02:22:01.764Z That first step gives him a chance to stay competitive against NFL-caliber athletes and should remain the foundation of his pass-rush game. Finishing the season with a statement Football often leaves lasting impressions. For Mills, the final one couldn’t have been much better. Rylie Mills, DL, #98 This is one of Mills's first snaps in the NFL. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-20T02:22:20.436Z This is one of Mills’s first snaps in the NFL… Rylie Mills, DL, #98 His sack in the Super Bowl—driving through the blocker before bringing down the quarterback—provided perhaps his most encouraging individual rep of the season. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-20T02:22:47.618Z His sack in the Super Bowl—driving through Jared Wilson before bringing down Drake Maye—provided perhaps his most encouraging individual rep of the season. One play shouldn’t outweigh months of evaluation. At the same time, it demonstrated exactly why Seattle remained excited about his long-term fit. The burst, leverage and relentless effort all came together on a stage where mistakes are rarely forgiven. It wasn’t proof that Mills had arrived. It was proof that his best traits can translate against NFL competition. Areas for improvement Play strength remains the biggest concern The same physical limitations that appeared during the pre-draft process were still visible on rookie tape. Rylie Mills, DL, #98 Mills' rookie tape showed the same concerns from the pre-draft process. He lacks the power and length to consistently control blocks, limiting his ability to set edges or disengage vs. the run. Technique can improve, but physical limitations may cap his ceiling. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-20T02:23:37.323Z Mills doesn’t consistently generate enough power to control blocks against the run, particularly when offensive linemen are able to engage him squarely. Without ideal arm length, he also has less margin for error when trying to create separation at the point of attack. Those issues occasionally prevented him from setting firm edges or disengaging quickly enough to finish running plays. They’re not unexpected weaknesses; they’re largely the same concerns evaluators had entering the draft. Improvement is certainly possible through NFL strength training and continued technique refinement, but there are natural physical limitations that likely cap how much those areas can develop. Rylie Mills, DL, #98 Mills shows a good pass-rush plan here, using a bull rush into a double-swipe. But the OL resets and drives him back with relative ease. The technique is there; now he needs to add more power to consistently finish these reps in Year 2. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-20T02:24:31.074Z This can also be seen on pass-rush snaps. He has a good plan, using a bull rush that transitions into a sort of double-swipe; however, the offensive lineman is able to push him back with relative ease, even after losing the initial exchange. This is one area where I hope Mills improves in Year 2. Rylie Mills’ future outlook Rylie Mills, DL, #98 The biggest reason for optimism with Riley Mills is simple: he's healthy. A full offseason in Macdonald's system, plus NFL experience, should help him play closer to his profile. Don't expect a breakout—expect more consistent rotational impact. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-20T02:24:58.947Z Perhaps the biggest reason for optimism has little to do with what happened on the field last season. Mills is healthy entering his second season. A full offseason allows him to participate in every phase of the defensive installation rather than splitting attention between rehabilitation and football. That continuity matters, particularly for a player who essentially experienced a delayed rookie season. Training camp already offered encouraging signs, including reps as a gunner on special teams—a role that further highlights the explosiveness Seattle valued throughout the draft process. Expecting a dramatic breakout may be unrealistic. Instead, the more reasonable projection is a player who is already close to his long-term profile, but now has the health, familiarity with the scheme and valuable NFL experience to play that role more consistently. title: Seahawks Football 101: What is the difference between edge and defensive end?
summary: Defensive line players, as well as offensive line players, can be described as the “meat and potatoes” positions in the NFL. They put their hands in the dirt and fight in the trenches. Then, they hopefully are able to help players coming off the edge to rush the quarterback, whether its a defensive end or […]
full_text: Tennessee quarterback Cam Ward (1) eludes the pressure of Seattle defensive end DeMarcus Lawrence (0) during their game at Nissan Stadium Sunday, Nov. 23, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Defensive line players, as well as offensive line players, can be described as the “meat and potatoes” positions in the NFL. They put their hands in the dirt and fight in the trenches. Then, they hopefully are able to help players coming off the edge to rush the quarterback, whether its a defensive end or edge player. The question is: What’s the difference between a defensive end and an edge? That is the very question we are tackling today on this edition of Seahawks Football 101. Let’s dive in and use some Seattle Seahawks examples along the way! Edge players: DeMarcus Lawrence/Uchenna Nwosu The edge position is a hybrid position, where it can be either a 4-3 defensive end or a 3-4 outside linebacker. It is a bit like the nickel position for the front seven. Their main goal is to generate quarterback pressure, sacks, and stopping the outside run no matter their official position. Their primary goal, though, is to be a pass rusher and apply pressure to the quarterback. The current Seahawks tandem DeMarcus Lawrence and Uchenna Nwosu are two of the better examples of this hybrid position on the front seven position for the Super Bowl champions. DEMARCUS LAWRENCE WITH HIS 2ND SCOOP-N-SCORE! AZvsSEA on CBS/Paramount+ https://t.co/HkKw7uXVnt pic.twitter.com/rdrh4DKds9 — NFL (@NFL) November 9, 2025 Defensive End Players: Michael Bennett/Mike Morris The defensive end position is a traditional defensive lineman who lines up on the line of scrimmage next to defensive tackles and across from the offensive lineman. Their main duties are a mix of heavy run defense (aka “setting the edge”) with crashing the pocket through the offensive line. They also try to absorb the initial blocks to free up the linebackers to go after the quarterback. It all depends on whether it is a 3-4 scheme (three defensive lineman and four linebackers) or a 4-3 scheme (four defensive lineman and three linebackers). If it is a 3-4 scheme, their job is to block the opposing lineman to allow the linebackers to pressure the quarterback. If it is a 4-3 scheme, the defensive end is the primary pass rusher. Michael Bennett and Mike Morris are examples of defensive ends for the Seahawks. Dwight Freeney gets a sack on a speed rush from the outside! Michael Bennett forced Cousins backwards making it easier. #Seahawks #SEAvsWAS pic.twitter.com/jg62yaKOjw — Samuel Gold (@SamuelRGold) November 5, 2017 The two positions are similar. While a defensive end can be an edge, not all edges are defensive ends. The Seahawks have had a lot of great run defenders and pocket infiltrators. Who are some of your favorites? summary: Cooper Kupp has won multiple Super Bowl titles, including one with his home state Seattle Seahawks in 2025. Now, he’s taking on a new challenge by opening a coffee shop. That Kupp is into coffee isn’t surprising considering his ties to the Seattle area. The fact that the coffee shop will be in Fayetteville, Arkansas, […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 8: Cooper Kupp #10 of the Seattle Seahawks arrives to the stadium prior to the NFL Super Bowl LX football game against the New England Patriots at Levi's Stadium on February 08, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Cooper Kupp has won multiple Super Bowl titles, including one with his home state Seattle Seahawks in 2025 . Now, he’s taking on a new challenge by opening a coffee shop . That Kupp is into coffee isn’t surprising considering his ties to the Seattle area. The fact that the coffee shop will be in Fayetteville, Arkansas, may elicit some surprise, however. Kupp and his wife, along with other family members, started Dodo Coffee in 2024. After selling coffee out of a small building in Arkansas, they ran into problems and lost the building in 2025. This new location was built specifically for the Dodo Coffee location, and Kupp couldn’t be more excited. “We shared what we were about, who we are. And he just built us, designed for us basically this building that was going to fit all the things, all the intentional things, that we’re about and try and make them a physical place to come drink coffee,” Kupp said. Dodo Coffee is a passion project for Kupp, and they go to great lengths to source the beans and syrups used in their shop. “There’s an intention all the way through to be like how can we also just make sure that you’re getting the very best. That you are going to, by the time you’re enjoying the coffee, that you’re having it the way you’re supposed to,” Kupp said. Kupp is still a force to be reckoned with on the field, receiving rave reviews in training camp so far this year. This new endeavor could be his second act in retirement from the NFL. Maybe there will be a Dodo Coffee in Seattle some day? ( H/T UltrasonicsII for bringing this up on The Feed )

title: 49ers drop 40 on the Chargers in a lopsided blowout
summary: We saw Brock Purdy throw six passes, but once Kyle Shanahan saw him scramble, that would be the end of the night for the San Francisco 49ers’ franchise quarterback. Still, there was plenty of action in the first half. Deebo Samuel was the first punt returner up, but Jacob Cowing showed why he should be […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 20: Sincere McCormick #35 of the San Francisco 49ers runs the ball against the Los Angeles Chargers during the second quarter in a preseason game at SoFi Stadium on August 20, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images We saw Brock Purdy throw six passes, but once Kyle Shanahan saw him scramble, that would be the end of the night for the San Francisco 49ers’ franchise quarterback. Still, there was plenty of action in the first half. Deebo Samuel was the first punt returner up, but Jacob Cowing showed why he should be the starter come Week 1: JACOB COWING WITH THE 83-YARD PUNT RETURN TD 🏠 SFvsLAC on @nflnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/BUV9YE8LyF — NFL (@NFL) August 21, 2026 Cowing needed to atone for an earlier drop on a pass that happened right in front of his head coach. Cowing could’ve caught a first down, but Mac Jones sailed a throw to him. Cowing had an eventful half. It also was for De’Zhaun Stribling, who caught four passes for 46 yards, including a 21-yarder on third down. Stribling dropped a would-be touchdown after beating a Chargers defensive back on a double move. The pass from Jones was perfect, but Stribling couldn’t haul it in. Otherwise, he lined up at multiple spots and had a reception on four different routes. He was not the most impressive rookie. That goes to Kaelon Black. He had eight carries for 33 yards with a long of nine. But one of those should’ve been a loss of four. Black fought his way back to the line of scrimmage, which helped set up Stribling’s third-down conversion. Black was decisive, and that paid off, leading to multiple positive gains. Sticking with the rookie theme, Carver Willis started at left guard. That wasn’t a surprise. Austen Plesants was up next. That qualifies as a surprise. We didn’t see Robert Jones at all in the first half, as Connor Colby played every snap at right guard. That might say more about Colby and Jones than it does about Pleasants. Regardless, it still seems like Willis’s job to lose. Colby ended up playing left guard in the fourth quarter. The 49ers had a commanding 20-3 lead at the half, thanks to some impressive blocking that sprung Sincere McCormick for a 37-yard gain. McCormick found the end zone on the same drive. Adrian Martinez took over in the second half. Plesaants remained at left guard. Martinez threw a pick-six on the first play of the second half. Pleasants got blown up on first down, then missed a pressure, allowing a free rusher on the interception. Pleasants ended up leaving with an injury midway through the third quarter. It did not look good, as it looked like his knee buckled. Willis replaced Pleasants. Another sign that it’s not a three-man race. Ephesians Prysock made a nice pass breakup on third down. Martinez ended up scrambling for a 9-yard touchdown run. After Nick Martin forced a fumble on a kickoff, Martinez found Jordan Watkins for a 17-yard touchdown. That was the third consecutive scoring drive for the 49ers, and just like that, the score was 41-9. Rookie Jalen Stroman had a big hit on the ensuing kickoff. Deep into the fourth quarter, the Chargers had rushed for three yards. The score was 41-9. The Chargers added a touchdown and a two-point conversion late to make it 41-17.

summary: The San Francisco 49ers received good news before they took the field on Thursday night. ESPN’s Adam Schefter tweeted the following: 49ers tight end George Kittle visited Wednesday in Los Angeles with renowned orthopedic surgeon Dr. Neal ElAttrache, who performed the surgery on his torn Achilles in January. It was said to be an encouraging […]
full_text: Jan 11, 2026; Philadelphia, PA, USA; San Francisco 49ers tight end George Kittle (85) looks on during warmups prior to an NFC Wild Card Round game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field. Mandatory Credit: Eric Hartline-Imagn Images | Eric Hartline-Imagn Images The San Francisco 49ers received good news before they took the field on Thursday night. ESPN’s Adam Schefter tweeted the following: 49ers tight end George Kittle visited Wednesday in Los Angeles with renowned orthopedic surgeon Dr. Neal ElAttrache, who performed the surgery on his torn Achilles in January. It was said to be an encouraging visit. Kittle’s recovery is ahead of schedule, and it gives him a legitimate chance to play in the regular season opener in Australia against the Los Angeles Rams. Last Sunday, Kittle said he expects to return sooner than later and didn’t think about the possibility of beginning the season on the PUP list. One of Kittle’s lone concerns about being ready for Week 1 was getting enough practice time and building up his football shape ahead of traveling to Australia. He did not want the game to be his first time in pads. Kittle said you can train all you want, but you have to play football to get into football shape. The 49ers face the Rams exactly three weeks from Thursday night. The 49ers have been practicing about four times a week with two walk-throughs mixed in. But that has also included joint practices and preseason games. If Kittle returns to practice this Saturday, he’ll have about a week of practices to build his cardio. For what it’s worth, when he spoke this past Sunday, Kittle didn’t sound like it would be the end of the world if he missed Week 1. He understands it’s a 17-game season and this is a long, long season.

title: 5 players to watch in the 49ers second preseason game
summary: The San Francisco 49ers are back in action on Thursday, taking on the Los Angeles Chargers in their second preseason game after the two sides had a joint practice earlier this week. San Francisco is expected to play some starters, including potentially quarterback Brock Purdy, before giving way for the backups to see some opportunities. […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JANUARY 11: Renardo Green #0 of the San Francisco 49ers defends during the NFC Wild Card playoff game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on January 11, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The 49ers defeated the Eagles 23-19. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers are back in action on Thursday, taking on the Los Angeles Chargers in their second preseason game after the two sides had a joint practice earlier this week. San Francisco is expected to play some starters, including potentially quarterback Brock Purdy, before giving way for the backups to see some opportunities. Still, the eyes will be on the younger players who are looking to prove things and get more reps under their belts. Who are five players to watch for the 49ers against the Chargers on Thursday night? RB Kaelon Black Black was held out of San Francisco’s first preseason game with an adductor injury, which caused him to miss two weeks, but he returned to practice on Tuesday and made some plays working in with the top offense. Christian McCaffrey won’t play, and Jordan James is out, so Black will have a big chance to put his foot forward in the running back competition in his first NFL snaps. Eyes will be on him both in the backfield and as a pass-catcher. WR De’Zhaun Stribling Staying on the rookie page, De’Zhaun Stribling had quite the debut last week, shaking off some early issues to catch seven of his eight targets for 63 yards. On Thursday, Stribling will likely get a chance to work with Brock Purdy, and he could even be the focal point with Mike Evans out. If the 49ers see enough from Stribling, this could be it for him in the preseason. OL Carver Willis If there’s a dark horse candidate to win that left guard competition, it’d be Willis, who has started to get some left guard reps in the three-way battle with Robert Jones and Connor Colby. Now, he should get extended run here on Thursday, giving the coaching staff a better look at whether he’s ready to work more with the starters, or if he’s better suited as a backup for the time being. Colby seems to be trending down in the competition. Perhaps Willis can put himself firmly in the battle on Thursday. DL Gracen Halton Halton had an impressive start to the preseason last year, and he seems to be one of the ready-now contributors in the 49ers rookie class. He should factor in a ton again on Thursday as the 49ers continue to figure out their defensive tackle rotation behind Osa Odighizuwa. There’s a lot of young talent in the room with Alfred Collins, CJ West, and Halton, but the 49ers need someone to step up from that group. S Ji’Ayir Brown Safety play has become a bigger talking point this week after the 49ers secondary faced trouble during Tuesday’s joint practice. The 49ers didn’t do much to add to the safety room this offseason, leaving Malik Mustapha, Ji’Ayir Brown, and Marques Sigle as the top competitors there. But free agent signee Ashtyn Davis played well in the first preseason game, and he could be an option in the room as well. Heading into the second preseason, there’s still a good amount to figure out about this room. Let’s see if Brown plays better here on Thursday night. CB Renardo Green Along with the left guard battle, another ongoing one has been the cornerback battle between Jack Jones and Renardo Green. Jones, a free-agent signee, has been praised by defensive coordinator Raheem Morris and has made plays in camp, while Green is looking to bounce back from an inconsistent sophomore season. In an ideal world, we see Green be the cornerback that he displayed on tape coming out of Florida State. But both players should see the field a good amount on Thursday, giving more information on how the battle could play out.

title: Kyle Shanahan’s pessimistic injury update places extra pressure on 49ers rookie
summary: It was not exactly a surprise this week when Kyle Shanahan gave a pessimistic outlook regarding Mykel Williams’ status for the 49ers’ regular-season opener with the Los Angeles Rams. Williams being ready for Week 1 always seemed unlikely after he tore his ACL in the Week 9 win over the New York Giants last November, […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 13: Romello Height #94 of the San Francisco 49ers rushes pass Dan Moore Jr. #75 of the Tennessee Titans in the first half at Levi's Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images It was not exactly a surprise this week when Kyle Shanahan gave a pessimistic outlook regarding Mykel Williams’ status for the 49ers’ regular-season opener with the Los Angeles Rams. Williams being ready for Week 1 always seemed unlikely after he tore his ACL in the Week 9 win over the New York Giants last November, and Shanahan confirmed last year’s first-round pick will probably not be involved when San Francisco faces its division rivals in Melbourne, Australia. “He’s further away than those other guys you guys just asked about, but we do think he’s close,” Shanahan said on Tuesday. “I do think Week 1 would be a long shot, but we haven’t ruled it out yet. But, he’s progressing very well.” With Williams seemingly out of the picture for Week 1, the 49ers’ depth chart at defensive end beyond Nick Bosa — himself coming back from a serious knee injury — looks sparse. Somebody will need to step up to take Williams’ place as one of the two starting defensive ends. Right now, the most likely scenario would be that Keion White or Sam Okuayinonu play on base downs with rookie Romello Height coming in on true pass rushing downs. But, for the 49ers to have confidence in such a plan, they will likely need to see more from Height. On paper, Height checks all the boxes as a 49ers pass rusher, having excelled in all the drills that measure explosiveness during pre-draft testing. But the third-round rookie showed little of that explosiveness in his preseason debut for the 49ers, with his impact minimal as he was outshone by other rookies up front in the form of defensive tackles Gracen Halton and Bryson Eason. Of course, life for the other members of the defensive line becomes a lot easier when Bosa is on the field because of his ability to collapse the pocket often single-handedly and draw attention from multiple pass protectors. As such, Height can afford to have hope of profiting from the disruption Bosa can cause in the regular season. Still, the 49ers cannot solely rely on Bosa and a hopefully improved interior pass rush to boost their fortunes rushing the passer. They need more contributions from their other edge rushers, including Height and Williams when he gets healthy. Williams returning to full fitness is not imminent. There is, therefore, increased pressure on Height to display his pass-rushing promise as the 49ers play their second preseason game against the Los Angeles Chargers on Thursday. Should he do so, then the Niners will be able to feel a little better about their options on a depleted defensive front.
