title: 2026 Seattle Seahawks training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Catch up on our daily updates from Seahawks training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The  Seattle Seahawks ' camp is taking place in Renton, Washington, and Seahawks reporter Brady Henderson has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Seahawks camp. What is new with the defending Super Bowl champions? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Catch up on all the updates, including the Packers' top camp performer and biggest lingering question as preseason games begin.

 
 Camp previews for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Seahawks camp 
 
 CB Trevon Diggs signing 1-year deal with Seahawks 
 Sources: Seahawks still plan on signing Terrion Arnold 
 Cooper Kupp's latest route? Opening a new coffee shop 
 Seahawks, Witherspoon reach extension: 4 years, $132M, sources say 
 Seahawks' DeMarcus Lawrence confirms 2026 season his last 
 Facing charges, Terrion Arnold set to join Seahawks 
 WR Tory Horton healthy after cracking tibia last season 
 Seattle Pro Bowl DL Williams confirms deal talks 
 Seattle's Nick Emmanwori has ankle surgery, expected to play W1 
 Who are the Khoslas? Meet the family set to buy the Seahawks 
 
 

 Thursday. Aug. 20 
 What is Trevon Diggs ' mindset after joining the Seahawks?

 "I just want to come here, compete, earn my keep," the former Dallas Cowboys cornerback said Wednesday, "just do everything I can to earn a spot here and help this team win."

 Exactly what the Seahawks have in mind for Diggs will become more clear when the details of his one-year deal emerge. The fact that they were not initially reported seems telling in and of itself. So does the ending of Diggs' tenure in Dallas last season, as well as what he said after arriving at Seahawks headquarters about how he wants to "earn" a spot in Seattle.

 Nothing about the situation suggests the Seahawks view Diggs as an immediate, surefire upgrade to their current options at CB3. Rather, he looks like someone who could reinforce Seattle's secondary depth for now, and potentially work his way into a bigger role.

 With the Seahawks off to Nashville Thursday for a joint practice and a preseason game against the Tennessee Titans , the Diggs signing invites a day-after look at Seattle's cornerback room.

 The only real certainties are that the newly-extended Devon Witherspoon and Josh Jobe  -- whom Seattle re-signed in March -- will fill the top two spots. Noah Igbinoghene seems to have at least a slight edge over Nehemiah Pritchett in the battle for the No. 3 job.

 The Seahawks seem to think that Terrion Arnold could eventually be an upgrade there, but with a stay on the commissioner exempt list coming and a suspension potentially to follow, there's no telling when he'll be available. Julian Neal figured to be part of the No. 3 cornerback competition when the Seahawks drafted him in the third round, but he's been sidelined for much of camp with an undisclosed injury. While Neal has been in uniform in recent days and took part in the walkthrough Wednesday, rookies who miss as much time as he has tend to fall far behind.

 The Diggs signing might have as much to do with Neal's extended absence and strengthening the bottom of the depth chart than it does the question of whether Seattle will be vulnerable at CB3 regardless of who wins that job.

 Below them are seventh-round picks Andre Fuller and Michael Dansby , who have each cooled off after strong starts to training camp. They've always seemed like candidates for the practice squad more than the 53-man roster. The Seahawks had a fifth-round grade on Fuller, but the fact that each lasted to the seventh round suggests there's a good chance Seattle could get them through waivers.

 Seattle recently placed Shemar Jean-Charles on season-ending injured reserve, but he wasn't likely going to make the 53-man roster even if he'd stayed healthy.

 More observations: 

 
 G Bryce Cabeldue was on the field for the walk-through Wednesday after going down with a neck injury Tuesday. He appears to be OK. 
 The Seahawks will hold one practice against the Titans on Friday. They'll practice by themselves on Friday before the preseason game Sunday. 
 

 

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 18 
 There are so many ways in which Mike Macdonald coaches the Seahawks differently from his predecessor, and this week is about to bring another example.

 Whereas Pete Carroll was staunchly against joint practices -- he never held one in 14 seasons in Seattle -- Macdonald is a proponent. It's why the Seahawks will head to Nashville on Thursday to practice against the Tennessee Titans on Friday, two days before their preseason game at Nissan Stadium.

 The Seahawks held joint practices in each of Macdonald's first two seasons -- in Nashville in 2024 and against the Packers in Green Bay last summer.

 Macdonald sees a best-of-all-worlds appeal in getting reps against another team in the controlled setting of a practice, where the two sides can simulate certain situations, and where the quarterbacks are not to be touched. Teams can also run plays that they wouldn't call in preseason games lest they put them on film for the rest of the league to see.

 "It's a lot of intentional reps," safety Julian Love said. "You're not just going through a game setting. You're doing one-on-ones against these guys, you're doing third-down period, certain concept periods against them, but you're going full go. It's cool where you get intentional work. It's always good to see other [starters] just so you can read and react. Me as a DB, it's nice when you can play a ball in a different setting against different people, get some different tendencies.

 "We're going to value it. The whole team is going to really take advantage of these reps because they're important."

 Fights are a common occurrence in joint practices. That's likely one reason the Seahawks have opted for just a single session after doing two of them against the Titans in 2024. Punches flew even in their lone practice against the Packers. 

 When things aren't getting out of hand on the field, another benefit of joint practices is the opportunity they provide for team bonding.

 "Two years ago in Tennessee, last year in Green Bay, it was the first time everyone let their hair down and enjoyed hanging out with each other," Love said. "Traveling with the team is always fun. We love traveling with each other just because it's a time where guys can just get a break and be with each other. Playing against another team in that kind of competitive space is fun. Then we go out to dinner, do the rookie [talent] show, all that stuff is a lot of fun. I know a lot of the guys are really excited about it."

 More observations: 

 
 RB Jadarian Price practiced for a second straight day. Seattle's top pick didn't practice for over a week due to what Macdonald called lower-body soreness. 
 RB Emanuel Wilson remains sidelined for undisclosed reasons. 
 CB Josh Jobe made the play of the day when he jumped in front of Rashid Shaheed and intercepted a short throw from Sam Darnold for what likely would have been a pick-six in a game. Darnold and Shaheed connected earlier on a deep throw that traveled about 45 yards in the air. 
 Backup G Bryce Cabeldue left practice with an apparent neck/head injury. 
 

 

 

 Sunday, Aug. 16 
 One lesser-known player who's making his best case for a job with the Seahawks in 2026 is Montorie Foster Jr . The second-year receiver continued his strong summer with a touchdown catch in Seattle's preseason opener, a 17-7 loss to the Dallas Cowboys .

 This time last year, he was unsigned and thinking about giving up football.

 Foster joined the Seahawks as an undrafted free agent in 2025. But after he…

title: 49ers return their 'bullies' in Deebo Samuel, Dre Greenlaw
summary: Greenlaw and Samuel are back in key roles for the 49ers. How will Greenlaw slot in at linebacker? Will Samuel be a rushing threat again?
full_text:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- After wrapping up his reunion with the San Francisco 49ers early in free agency, linebacker Dre Greenlaw quickly turned his attention to recruiting.

 More specifically, Greenlaw thought the offense could use an enforcer similar to him. He soon reached out to wide receiver  Deebo Samuel Sr ., who, like him, had once been a focal point of the 49ers' culture, departed for one season and was a free agent.

 Greenlaw's message was simple: There's unfinished business in San Francisco, and he and Samuel can help the team finish it.

 "[I said] 'Let's have a reunion, let's do this thing together,'" Greenlaw said. "This place is just about football ... Sometimes you got to go and go see what's out there, but once you go, you realize, hey, it ain't nothing like San Fran."

 Although Samuel didn't re-sign with the Niners until July 30, the warm reception he got when he returned to the building was similar to the one Greenlaw got when he arrived for the offseason program in April.

 "It felt like I never left," Samuel said. "They were happy. I was happy. We were ready to get the ball rolling."

 Both Samuel and Greenlaw are slated to slot back into their prominent roles for the 49ers. Greenlaw will start at weakside linebacker, which was further solidified when the 49ers traded away his replacement ( Dee Winters ) in April. Samuel will again have a varied role at receiver, running back and kick returner for a depleted skill group.

 

 And while they might not be as impactful as they were in their first stint with the team, there's no denying the intangible boost that San Francisco sought in adding Greenlaw and Samuel back into the fold.

 "Those are two just bullies on the offense and the defense," fullback  Kyle Juszczyk  said. "Guys that set the tone, guys that really motivate others just by the way that they play, the physical nature that both of them play with. And I'm so happy to have both of them."

 It was about a year and a half ago that Samuel and Greenlaw, both members of the 49ers' 2019 draft class, departed for other opportunities. The Niners attempted to keep Greenlaw in free agency, but he ultimately opted for a three-year, $31.5 million deal with the Broncos. Samuel, meanwhile, had requested a trade after a turbulent 2024 season, and he was eventually traded to the Commanders for a 2025 fifth-round pick.

 Neither player necessarily found the grass to be greener elsewhere.

 In Denver, Greenlaw again dealt with injuries. He missed eight games of quadriceps and hamstring issues, and he served a  one-game suspension  in Week 8 for unsportsmanlike conduct toward a referee. Greenlaw called the season "real tough" and acknowledged that he often found himself longing for what he had in San Francisco alongside Fred Warner , his close friend and fellow linebacker.

 By the end of the regular season, Greenlaw had 43 tackles, a sack, an interception and a forced fumble while playing 38.6 snaps per game. The Broncos released him on March 12, and he agreed to a one-year, $7.5 million deal with the Niners the next day.

 There's never been a question of Greenlaw's impact -- including the postseason, the 49ers were 52-24 and allowed 20 points per game when he played -- but injuries have long been an issue. He missed 36 games in his first six seasons with the team because of various injuries. After tearing his Achilles during Super Bowl LVIII, Greenlaw only made two more appearances for San Francisco before departing for Denver.

 The 49ers have been accordingly cautious with Greenlaw in hopes of having him healthy to open the season.

 "I haven't felt this good since about a month before the Super Bowl," Greenlaw said. "It's been just one [injury] after one after another, one after another. And I just been playing catch up the whole time. But now I just feel like I'm where I need to be now as far as just body, health wise, everything."

 Samuel's lone season in Washington was more fruitful than Greenlaw's in Denver. Samuel played in 16 games, leading the Commanders in catches (72), receiving yards (727) and receiving touchdowns (five). Of course, he made an impact on the ground with 17 carries, 75 rushing yards and one rushing touchdown. Despite the Commanders letting him walk, Samuel had nothing negative to say about his time in Washington but made it clear he was happy to be back with the 49ers.

 

 Over the past couple of seasons, questions about Samuel's conditioning have arisen as he's struggled to produce consistently. According to left tackle Trent Williams , one of Samuel's closest friends who was in contact with him weekly throughout his time in Washington, that could change this season. Samuel returned to the Niners in what Williams calls "probably the best shape I've seen him in since I've known him."

 "I know he's coming from a situation where he feels people doubt his ability," Williams said. "You put that extra doubt to him, that extra fuel to his fire, I think he's going to be a lot better."

 Throughout the preseason, those who have played with Samuel and Greenlaw before recognize many of the tone-setting traits they brought to San Francisco the first time. They also see a renewed chip on the shoulder, in no small part because of San Francisco's inability to win a Super Bowl, that should only further inflame the fuel Williams mentioned.

 "The good thing about it, they got something to prove," safety Ji'Ayir Brown said. "Deebo has something to prove. Dre has something to prove. And not to nobody else, not to no outsiders, more to themselves."

 In this training camp, Samuel has lined up at running back again and got the ball in space in a variety of ways. He is also taking on the kick return role, which he only did sparingly in his first stint but featured in for the Commanders last season (30.1 average yards per return).

 Greenlaw has resumed his role as the enforcer, though age (29 years old) has brought the wisdom to know when to pump the brakes. At one practice, he hit star running back Christian McCaffrey near the sideline. McCaffrey took exception, threw the ball and shoved Greenlaw back. Greenlaw didn't retaliate, realizing what he'd done and who he had pushed.

 McCaffrey didn't mind and counts Greenlaw among his favorite players in the league. That's a sentiment shared by the entire team, which is looking forward to Samuel leading them out of the tunnel pregame and Greenlaw flying around the field unafraid to take on anyone who tries him or his teammates.

 "To be able to bring back some enforcers like that who play exactly how we want everybody to play, those are two special dudes," coach Kyle Shanahan said. "I haven't been around two people like that in my career, really, who play that way. That stuff's huge. Just knowing they're in here gets guys pumped up. They've been away for a year, but to see them out there, they look exactly like the guys I remember."
